But I looked at her. Really looked at her.
Her entire body was trembling from the strain. The emerald light of her aura was flickering like a dying candle. A thin line of blood trickled from her nose, a stark crimson against her pale skin.
She wasn't just holding back a stampede anymore. She was in a psychic war, and she was losing.
(Shouting back at Eve) I can't leave her like this! She's barely holding on!
(Through gritted teeth) You have to! It's the only way... to save them all! Go, Cyan... Please!
Her plea was full of pain, but her eyes were a clear, hard command. She was giving me an order. The same kind of order Eve would give.
But my promise wasn't to a soldier. It was to a friend. My anchor.
I'm not leaving you! I'm your anchor, remember?!
I drew my sword, planting my feet beside her, a useless piece of steel against an ocean of rage. A foolish, heartfelt, and ultimately fatal act of defiance.
Lyrel saw my stupid, stubborn resolve. She saw me choose her over the mission.
And in that split second, her expression changed. The strain vanished, replaced by a profound, heartbreaking sadness. A look of weary acceptance.
She had a new plan.
(A sad, determined whisper that cut through the chaos) Then I'll make sure you get there.
She dropped the calming ritual.
The horde roared back to full, uncontrolled madness. But Lyrel ignored them.
She focused all of her remaining life force, all of her love and her pain, into one final, desperate gambit.
The ground beneath my feet exploded. Massive, ancient roots, glowing with an impossible emerald light, erupted around me, faster than I could react.
(V.O., screaming, his fists banging uselessly against the roots) Lyrel! What are you doing?! Let me out! LYREL!
It was a prison of love, woven from her own life force. And it was perfect.
Beyond my cage, I saw it: a second wall of colossal roots had burst from the ground, physically halting the horde's advance, creating a clear, empty path between me and the south ridge.
She hadn't just protected me. She had completed the mission.
She placed a hand on my cage, her form already starting to fade, becoming translucent.
(V.O., her voice weak, but clear in my mind) I've bought you time... It's all I have left to give.
(V.O.) Now go. Keep your promise.
(V.O.) Be the heart.
(V.O., screaming) Lyrel! NO! Let me out! LYREL!
My fists hammered against the glowing roots, but it was useless. I was a prisoner in a cage woven from her love and her life force.
And then... the chaos vanished. The roars, my own screams, the sound of my fists... it all faded into a profound, humming silence.
I wasn't in the cage anymore. I was... somewhere else. A quiet, peaceful grove that felt like the heart of the Oakhaven wishing tree and the Eldertide forest, all at once.
Cyan.
Her voice wasn't in my ears. It was inside my head. Calm. Serene. And so, so tired.
Lyrel? What is this? Where are we? Let me out! I have to help you!
You are helping me. You're safe. That's all that matters now.
No! We're supposed to be anchors for each other! We do this together!
(A sad, gentle smile) And we are. You were my anchor, Cyan. You anchored me back to myself, back in our forest. You taught me how to be whole again.
Now... it's my turn to be yours. Just for a little while.
I tried to step towards her, but I couldn't move. I was just a consciousness, floating in her final, peaceful thought.
Don't do this. Please. You're going to die.
My life force is already spent. This... all of this... is just the last echo of the song. But I wanted to see you one last time.
I'm sorry I can't keep our promise. The quiet home, the warm fire... you'll have to build it with someone else.
I don't want it with someone else! I want it with you!
I know. And you have no idea how much that means to me.
But now you have to make me a new promise. You have to go to the ridge. You have to stop the voice. You have to be the heart, even when yours is broken.
Promise me you'll live, Cyan. Promise me you'll keep fighting to heal the sad places.
Tears were streaming down my face. I couldn't speak. I could only nod.
(Her smile is radiant, beautiful, and final) Thank you. For everything. For the festival... for seeing me.
I love you.
Her form began to dissolve into motes of emerald light, like fireflies in the dusk.
Now go. Live.
The vision shattered. I was back in the cage, the sounds of the horde crashing down like a physical blow. Her final 'I love you' was still echoing in the ruins of my heart.
It took less than twenty minutes. The ravine was clear. The Northern army was in full, disorganized retreat.
I ran back to the courtyard, my heart light for the first time in days. A wide, stupid grin was plastered on my face.
She was right where I had left her. Her head was tilted back against the wall, her eyes closed. A faint, peaceful smile was on her face.
She looked like she was finally getting the rest she'd more than earned. I felt a surge of affection for the stubborn, brilliant woman who had saved my life.
I'm back. You were right, the path was totally clear. They're all running. We can get out of here, no problem.
She didn't stir. She must have been more exhausted than I thought.
You were amazing back there, Eve. Truly. Like a hero from one of my mom's stories. You saved me.
We both need a long rest after this. A really long one. And then... we can still find that tavern by the sea, right?
The promise hung in the quiet air between us.
It'll probably take a while for you to heal up, but that's okay. I can handle the foraging. I'll even find some of those tasteless roots you like so much.
And I'll make sure you don't do any 'threat assessments' for at least a week. Doctor's orders. My orders.
I chuckled, waiting for a sarcastic retort. But none came.
The silence stretched. The only sound was the lonely wind.
...Eve?
Her peaceful expression didn't change. The faint smile was still there. But it was... too still.
A cold knot of dread began to tighten in my stomach.
Hey. I told you not to fall asleep.
I reached out a hand to gently shake her shoulder.
My fingers touched her arm.
She was cold.
Ice cold.
A deep, primal horror washed over me, so absolute it stole the air from my lungs. My voice was a choked whisper.
Eve...?
I shook her shoulder, a little harder this time.
Her head lolled to the side, slumping forward at an angle that wasn't natural. That wasn't sleep.
Her eyes were slightly parted, vacant. The peaceful smile was no longer peaceful. It was a hollow, empty mask.
She wasn't resting. She hadn't been resting at all.
I saw it all in a sickening flash. The cough. The way she'd leaned back. The lie.
'I'll be right behind you.'
She had sent me away.
She had sent me away so I wouldn't have to watch her die.
Her final 'I love you' echoed in the ruins of my heart.
I was back in the cage of green light. The sound of the horde thundering past was a distant, fading thunder. And then...
Silence. A silence more horrifying than any scream.
Slowly, the roots around me withered, turning to grey dust and crumbling away. The prison of her love released me.
I stepped out into a world made new. The horde was gone, its path of destruction a scar on the horizon.
But where she had stood... where she had faced the storm for me... there was an impossible garden.
A perfect circle of beautiful, otherworldly flowers, glowing with a soft, emerald light, fed by her final breath. They had purified the very ground the monsters had corrupted.
It was the most beautiful, and the most hateful, thing I had ever seen.
My feet moved on their own, drawn to the center of the garden. Lying on a small, perfect patch of soft moss was the Heartwood seed she had given me.
I picked it up. The warmth was gone.
It cracked in my hand, crumbling into cold, grey dust that the wind carried away.
She had done it. She had healed the earth, one last time. She had kept her promise to be the heart.
And I had broken mine. I hadn't been her anchor. I had been the reason she had to burn herself away.
My gaze drifted past the garden, to the south ridge. The path was clear. Her final gambit had worked.
'Promise me you'll live,' she had said. 'Promise me you'll keep fighting to heal the sad places.'
I stood there, frozen in her garden of sacrifice, her last command echoing in my head. But how could I move on? How could I live in a world that she had died to give me?
(V.O.) That's not a wish, Lyrel. That's a promise.
The memory of the future we had promised each other, so warm and perfect just a day ago, was now a source of unbearable agony.
A single, choked sob tore itself from my throat. The sound of a world breaking. Of a promise turned to ash.
(Voice - a raw, desperate whisper) How can I...? How can I heal anything... when you're the one who's broken?
I clutched the dust of the seed in my fist. Her last wish against my own selfish, desperate heart.
No... I won't accept it. I won't live in a world that you're not in.
It wasn't a shout. It wasn't a roar of anger. It was a denial of reality itself. A quiet, insane refusal to accept her sacrifice.
I would give anything...
I looked up at the grey, unforgiving sky.
(His whisper builds, cracking with absolute, soul-deep conviction) ...*anything*... to do it all again. To be the anchor you deserved.
We reached the river crossing just as the horde appeared, a seething tide of claws and fury under the crimson glow of the Blood Moon.
Eve moved like a phantom, setting sonic traps and explosive runes to divert the edges of the stampede. My job was simple, and terrifying: protect Lyrel.
Lyrel closed her eyes, and a soft, emerald aura pulsed outwards. A silent lullaby in the face of a roar.
And for a moment... it was working. The beasts at the front of the horde slowed, their maddened red eyes flickering, their roars softening into cries of confusion and pain.
(VOICE, shouting from a distance) She's doing it! The madwoman is actually doing it! The front line is turning towards the marshes!
For a heartbeat, I felt a surge of pure, triumphant hope. We were going to win. Her way. The way of the heart.
(Gasping, through gritted teeth) No... wait...
Her face went pale. The calming aura around us flickered violently.
Lyrel! What is it? What's wrong?
It's not... them. Their rage... it isn't their own.
Her eyes shot open, wide with a horrified, dawning realization.
There's a voice. A single, powerful voice... screaming in all of their minds at once. It's... forcing this madness on them.
It's coming from the south ridge!

The south ridge... where the Southern command was supposed to be. A cold, sick feeling washed over me. I had a terrible idea of who that 'voice' could be, but there was no time to even form the thought.
Eve must have heard her through our comm-runes, or just understood the shift in the battle.
(VOICE, sharp and urgent) A psychic controller... Damn it! Lyrel can't fight a whole horde *and* a psychic at the same time! The lullaby is just a bandage on a severed artery!
Eve was right. Calming the horde was a temporary solution. As long as the 'voice' was screaming, the rage would never truly end. We had to stop the source.
(VOICE) Cyan! You're the only one who might be able to get close! The monsters are focused on Lyrel! You have to get to that ridge and stop that voice! NOW!
The 'Good End' path was clear. A desperate, targeted strike. But it meant leaving Lyrel alone, the sole focus of a psychic storm and a thousand raging beasts.
The morning after the festival was quiet, the sound of a soft rain drumming against the inn's windowpanes.
It felt... peaceful. Like the world outside couldn't touch us.
I can't believe you actually got her to hang a wish-lantern! You never told us what you wished for, did you, Helmet Hair?
(A small, genuine smile) And I never will. But...
(She looks at Cyan) It was a good wish.
Yeah. It was.
Looking at her, at the relaxed set of her shoulders, I felt a warmth that had nothing to do with the inn's fireplace.
The door to the inn creaked open, letting in a gust of cold, wet air. A figure stood silhouetted in the doorway.
Can we help you?
Her voice was sharp, a layer of ice instantly forming over the morning's warmth.
The figure scanned the room, their eyes landing on Eve. They took a hesitant step forward, pulling back their hood. Her face was young, rain-plastered, and etched with exhaustion and fear.
Shadow...? Is that really you?
My blood ran cold. 'Shadow' was Eve's old code name. One she hadn't used since she deserted.
You have the wrong person.
(Taking another step, her voice a desperate whisper) Commander. Please. We didn't know who else to turn to. The High Command...
I am not your commander. Not anymore. Now get out.
It's the Northern Star. It's Anne.
Eve went completely still. It was like the agent had spoken a magic word that could turn a living woman to stone.
She's back, Commander. The resurrection... it worked. For a few weeks, she was... her. Confused, but it was her.
Then the High Command took her. For 'amplification'. For the war effort.
Amplification? What does that mean?
(Shaking her head, tears welling in her eyes) They broke her. They turned her into a weapon. A mindless puppet that answers to them and burns everything it touches.
She's not a hero anymore, Commander. She's a monster they're pointing at the South. And she's winning the war for them.
The agent's words hung in the air, more chilling than the rain outside. They hadn't come to conscript a soldier. They had come to beg a friend.
They had come to ask Eve to save Anne from a fate worse than death.
Why me?
Because you're the only one she might remember. Because you're the only one strong enough to get close. And because... you're the only one who ever cared more about Anne than about the North.
The silence that followed was absolute. A war of loyalties raging within her. Her hatred for the military she'd fled, and her love for the friend they had just enslaved.
I'm going.
Eve, wait! This is insane! Going back there is a death sentence! You hate the North!
This isn't about the North. Or the war. This is personal.
(She looks at Cyan and Lyrel) This is *my* fight. You are not required. You should stay here, where it's safe.
No.
You're not doing this alone.
I remembered my wish at the festival. To be strong enough to protect the people I care about. It wasn't just a hopeful dream. It was a promise.
She's a soul in torment. We don't abandon those. We're The Strays. We go where we're needed.
Eve looked at us, a flicker of something—gratitude? pain?—in her eyes before she crushed it.
...Don't slow me down.
After Eve's... forceful wakeup call, we gathered in the common room. The tension of the night before had melted away, replaced by the easy comfort of a shared meal.
The memory of the festival, of the wish we made, was a warm, pleasant glow in my mind. It was a perfect, funny, completely normal morning.
It was the last one we would ever have.
The door to the inn didn't just open; it was thrown open. A family, their faces pale with terror and streaked with dirt, stumbled inside.
More people began pouring in from the street, their voices a rising chorus of fear.
I looked at Lyrel. Her face was a mask of empathetic pain. She could feel the chaos.
(Voice - a quiet murmur) They're in pain... raw, blind terror...
Forget the handlers. If a horde of berserk war-beasts hits a civilian town like Oakhaven... it'll be a massacre.
We can't let them get here. We have to intercept them.
There was no debate. No discussion of sides. This wasn't war. This was disaster relief.
The refugees are coming from the east. The horde will be following the main road. If we cut through the Whisperwood, we can get ahead of them, try to divert them at the river crossing.
Can we stop them?
We can't 'stop' them. Not with force. But maybe... maybe I can calm them. If I can reach the heart of the stampede, I can try to soothe their rage.
(A grim look) And if you can't, I'll be there to put down whatever you can't control. Let's move. Now.
We left the panicked villagers behind, running against the tide of refugees, heading directly towards the screams and the chaos.
The journey north was a descent into a fresh hell. The further we walked, the more the world seemed to die around us.
The green forests of Oakhaven were a distant memory, replaced by skeletal, black trees and the lingering smell of smoke.
(Voice - quiet, trembling) The earth here... it's screaming. There's so much pain in the soil.
Stay alert. We're in her territory now.
Eve's voice was sharp, cutting through the wind. She hadn't relaxed for a single moment since we'd left the inn. She was a coiled spring of deadly tension.
Up ahead, the source of the devastation became clear. We crested a hill and looked down upon a small, ruined valley.
It wasn't a battlefield. It was a slaughterhouse.
By the gods...
Dozens of soldiers lay scattered across the valley. But it was wrong. Utterly wrong.
Eve... their uniforms... some are Northern, some are Southern.
They weren't fighting each other... They were all... running. In the same direction.
She was right. It wasn't a battle line. It was a rout. Soldiers of two opposing armies, united in a desperate, failed attempt to flee a single, overwhelming threat.
Eve was already moving, her face a mask of grim determination. She knelt beside a fallen Northern officer, then a Southern footsoldier, her eyes scanning, analyzing.
No sword wounds. No arrow fire.
(She touches a patch of scorched armor) Just this. Overwhelming, raw power. No precision. No strategy.
She stood up, looking out over the field of the dead, her expression hardening into something colder than stone.
This wasn't a soldier. It wasn't even a berserker.
This was a storm. A natural disaster in the shape of a person.
The way she said it... it wasn't an exaggeration. She was giving us a technical assessment. The friend she knew was gone, replaced by a force of nature.
Can we even fight something like that?
We can't. Not head on.
But a storm has an eye. A moment of calm. If she's in there, somewhere... there has to be a moment of weakness. A flicker of recognition.
And if there isn't?
Then you find the heart of the storm... and you stop it. Permanently.
The finality in her voice was terrifying. She wasn't talking about defeating an enemy anymore. She was talking about putting down a rabid animal.
She was preparing herself to kill her best friend. Again.
Eve's plan was simple: cut through the Whisperwood to get ahead of the horde. But the forest itself seemed to be in agony.
Lyrel, are you okay?
(Wincing, one hand pressed to her temple) It's so loud... The trees, the soil... everything is screaming in terror.
It's not just the monsters; the whole land is panicking. I've never felt anything like it.
Focus. Use it. Let the fear guide us. Which way is the 'screaming' loudest?
Eve's question was blunt, but practical. Lyrel closed her eyes, taking a shaky breath.
...This way. It's getting stronger.
We pushed on, the distant roars growing steadily louder, the very air vibrating with a primal terror.
Soon, we found the first signs of the horde's passage.
It wasn't a clean kill, like the soldiers Eve had analyzed before. This was pure, mindless destruction.

Massive, ancient trees were snapped in half like twigs. Boulders were overturned. And the bodies of woodland creatures—direboars, shadow-cats, even a great bear—were savaged, torn apart and left where they fell.
They're not even eating them...
A predator kills for food. A soldier kills for a goal. This... this just kills to kill. It's a force of nature. A wildfire with claws.
They're not killing, Cyan. They're lashing out.
This isn't rage. This is what absolute, world-ending terror looks like when it's given claws and teeth.
She looked so sad. So deeply, profoundly sad for the very monsters that had caused this destruction.
And you think you can soothe *that*? Lyrel, this isn't a lonely ghost in a chapel. This is madness.
Madness is just a kind of pain, Eve. The deepest kind.
I have to try.

There was no arguing with the look in her eyes. It was the same look she'd had when she'd faced the 'cancer' in her own forest. The fierce, stubborn empathy of a healer who refuses to believe any wound is fatal.
We found a small, hidden cave overlooking the valley. The fire cast long, dancing shadows on the stone walls. It felt less like a camp and more like a tomb.
Lyrel was murmuring a quiet elven prayer. I was just trying to stop my hands from shaking. But Eve... she was perfectly still, staring into the flames.
Eve...
She didn't look up, but I knew she was listening.
That... thing out there. The White Phantom. It's really her, isn't it?
It doesn't matter who she *was*, Cyan. What matters is the storm she is *now*. Don't get sentimental. Sentimentality is a weapon the enemy will use against you.
It matters to you.
The fire crackled. The wind howled softly outside. For a long moment, she said nothing.
Then, she spoke, her voice so quiet it was almost lost in the flames.
(Voice - quiet, brittle) When you're in the special forces... they teach you to sever all ties. Your past is a liability. Your feelings are a weakness.
There is only the mission... and your partner.
The way she said 'partner' was different. It wasn't about a mission. It was something sacred.
You're two halves of the same blade. One is the edge, the other is the shadow. The light that everyone sees, and the darkness that keeps it safe.
A shadow... is supposed to follow its light into the dark.
(She finally looks at him, her eyes filled with a deep, ancient guilt) I ran instead.
I finally understood. This wasn't just a friend or a squadmate. This was a part of her soul that she had left behind to die. And now, it had come back to haunt her.
She looked away, her composure returning, but the confession lingered in the air between us.
That thing out there... it's a storm. And we are not strong enough to stop it. We are only fast enough to survive it.
She pressed the cold, tarnished silver coin into my hand.
Tomorrow, my job is to be the distraction. To draw its attention, to give it the ghost it wants to hunt.
When I do, a window will open. It will only be for a moment. In that moment, your job is to get yourself and Lyrel out. You fall back. You survive. That is the only victory possible here.
Promise me you won't get caught in my storm. Promise me you will survive.
The irony was crushing. She was begging me to do the one thing she couldn't—run and survive—so that she could finally stop running from her past.
She was asking me to abandon her.
...I promise... I'll be there for you, Eve.
I knew, even as I said it, that those were two very different promises.
And I knew, with a certainty that chilled me to the bone, that tomorrow, I would only be able to keep one of them.
We reached the cliff overlooking the river crossing just as the full weight of the Blood Moon crested the horizon, bathing the world in blood.
And below us... was the storm.
It wasn't an army. It was a river. A living, breathing, screaming river of monsters, flooding the valley from edge to edge. Their eyes glowed like a thousand red coals in the darkness.
In the distance, I could just make out the faint, twinkling lights of Oakhaven. They looked so small. So fragile.
We'll never stop all of them.
We don't have to stop them. We just have to turn them. If we can create enough of a panic at the front, we can divert the stampede into the Dead Marshes. Let them exhaust their rage on the swamp.
Lyrel. You're the key. You have to get to the heart of the stampede, the alpha beasts at the front. If you can soothe or disorient them, the rest will follow.
Cyan, your job is to guard her. Nothing gets close. Nothing breaks her concentration. I'll handle the flanks, create the diversions they need.
It was a desperate, insane plan. And it was the only one we had.
Are you sure you can do this, Lyrel? That rage... it's what almost consumed you.
(Her face is pale, but her eyes are clear and resolved) I'm not the same person I was then. And I'm not alone this time. You're my anchor, remember?
She pressed the Heartwood seed into my hand. It was faintly warm, a tiny spark of life in a world gone mad.
Hold onto this. It's our anchor. A piece of the quiet forest, the one we healed together. It will remind their rage of what peace feels like.
Her words reframed the memento. It wasn't a lifeline to pull her back from the brink. It was a tool for their victory.
(Closing my fist around the seed) It'll work. We'll make it work.
(A bright, confident smile) I know we will.
She gave me a smile so full of hope and conviction that it chased away the chill of the Blood Moon. In that moment, facing a tide of monsters, I had never felt safer.
We were The Strays. This is what we did. We walked into the storm and sang it a lullaby.
Warm...
That was the first thing I felt. A gentle, comforting warmth.
We must have talked for hours after we released the lantern. About the future. About everything and nothing.
At some point, without even realizing it, we had fallen asleep right there, under the watchful eyes of the wishing tree.
It was the most peaceful I had felt in my entire life.
(VOICE, off-screen, sharp and loud) There you are!
My eyes snapped open. Eve was standing over us, her arms crossed, her foot tapping impatiently. If looks could kill, we would have been twin piles of ash.
I spend half the night thinking you've both been kidnapped by a cult or eaten by a grue, and I find you sleeping on the job. Sleeping! Outside! Without a perimeter!
(Yawning, stretching like a cat) Mmm... good morning, Eve. Did you know the sunrise is extra pretty from up here?
Lyrel's complete lack of alarm only seemed to make Eve angrier.
Don't 'good morning' me! We had a watch schedule! I was on post for six hours straight! Do you have any idea how many 'situational assessments' I had to perform on the local honey-cake economy?!
We're sorry, Eve. We just... lost track of time.
Lost track of time," she muttered, rolling her eyes. "You're both hopeless.
She sighed, the anger draining out of her, replaced by that familiar, long-suffering exhaustion.
Here. I saved you some bread from the inn. Eat. We're leaving in twenty minutes.
She turned to leave, her lecture seemingly over.
(Without looking back) And Lyrel.
Yes?
...You've got a leaf in your hair.
And then she was gone. The 'I'm mad at you' was real. But the 'I was worried about you' was real, too.
That was our family.
(Blushing, trying to find the leaf) Oh, spirits, how embarrassing...
I just laughed, feeling the warmth of the morning sun on my face. It was a perfect, funny, completely normal morning.
It was the last one we would ever have.
You're all in one piece. Barely. Was it worth it?
We found it, Gabe. We found everything.
Cyan, with Lyrel's help, laid out the proof for Brandt: the scorched ledger, a vial of the synthetic reagent, and their harrowing story of the monster farm and the 'Withering War'.
Brandt listened with quiet, focused intensity. His calm exterior never cracked, but Cyan could see a new, hard light in his eyes.
You have done the kingdom a service beyond measure. The danger you faced... it is not something that can be repaid with coin.
But you have my word, this information will reach the highest authorities. You have my gratitude.
What will happen now, Magistrate?
Now? Now you rest. You have earned it. You have risked everything, and now your part in this is done. Leave the rest to me.
His words were meant to be a comfort. A promise that their burden was now lifted.
Hear that, kid? Our part is done. Means we can finally get a real drink.
We almost died! Shouldn't we be more careful?
A moment of respite is strategically sound after a prolonged engagement. Even if Eve's idea of 'respite' is questionable.
They left the guild, the familiar rhythm of their bickering a comforting sound in the quiet night. For the first time in weeks, it felt like it was finally over.
Eve waited until the sounds of sleep had settled over the inn. She slipped out of her room, a shadow in the moonlight.
Her part wasn't done. Not yet.
I had a feeling you would request a more... private debriefing.
Cut the act, 'Magistrate'.
The dead drop you suggested after the smuggler incident. The cipher protocols for the ledger. You're sloppy.
Sloppy? I received my information.
You're using outdated techniques. The Coiled Snake seal for field reports? That's ten years out of date. It was the signature of the Revenant Division.
The air grew thick with unspoken words. The weary magistrate persona melted away from Brandt, leaving behind the chilling stillness of a professional spy.
I'll ask you once. Who are you, *really*? King's Eyes? Royal Intelligence?
My employers value discretion. As I believe, do you.
And there it was. A perfect, non-answer that confirmed everything. The old Eve—the killer, the weapon—would have seen this as an opportunity or a threat.
But she wasn't that person anymore. She had a bar to run. A promise to keep. Two idiots to look after.
I don't care who you work for. I don't care about your war with the South. This is the last time we speak alone.
You can use the 'Strays'. You can use the idealistic kid and the elven knight. Point them at the heart of the Southern Alliance and they'll probably thank you for the opportunity.
But my name—the *real* one—stays out of your reports. My face stays out of your files. As far as the Northern Kingdom is concerned, I'm just a retired adventurer who runs a quiet inn.
Am I clear?
Crystal.

She had drawn her line in the sand. But she knew, with a certainty that chilled her to the bone, that the world of spies and shadows she had tried so desperately to escape had finally found her again.
I swear, if that lopsided mud statue is still in the inn when we get back, I'm using it for target practice.
It was a gift, Eve. Rejecting it would be... culturally insensitive.
The goblins don't have a culture, they have a concussion.
Come on, you two! We've got a goal now! Gabe! We're ready! What have you got for us? Something to test my new path? A B-Rank, maybe?
Settle down, kid. You just got back from a B-Rank that the client stiffed you on, remember? Paying quests don't grow on trees.
I've got something. A solid C-Rank. Good pay, low risk.
A lumber merchant needs an escort to the Stonecreek Quarry and back. Worried about bandits.
Lumber. We're guarding lumber. We have officially peaked as adventurers.
While the task lacks... grandeur, a successful contract is a successful contract. And bandits are a more conventional threat than our recent assignments.
Oh. Bandits.
Gabe... can I ask something?
Shoot.
It's just... all the stories I heard about the North... they were full of heroes fighting Griffons, Manticores, Wyverns... My propaganda was full of it.
We've been here for weeks, and the most dangerous thing we've fought was a mutated rat in a basement.
Where are all the monsters?
Gabe sighed, a deep, weary sound that seemed to carry the weight of the entire guild. He had clearly heard this question before.
You want the official story? The army did its job too well. For the last ten years, they've been running 'pacification campaigns'.
Clearing out nests, securing the trade routes, pushing the big beasts deep into the Dragon's Tooth mountains where they can't bother anyone.
It's a good thing, kid. The North is safer than it's ever been.
Safer just means... boring. Now, are you taking the lumber job or not?
Cyan looked around the quiet guild hall. It wasn't just boring. It felt... hollow. Like a legend that had been forgotten.
He opened his mouth to reply, but was cut off by a harsh, bitter laugh from a dark corner of the bar.
Safer? Heh. That's a good one.
The guild hall was quiet, but the air around the Strays felt electric. They slammed the heavy research tome and the smuggler's ledger onto the bar.
It's done. The mine is gone. The lab is destroyed.
And the Saboteur?
Buried under a thousand tons of rock. Along with his 'abominations'.
This... is exceptional. You have not only neutralized the immediate threat but provided us with the intelligence needed to track down the rest of the network.
The 'Withering War' ends tonight, thanks to you.
We actually did it. We stopped them.
I admit, when you three walked out of here chasing a rumor, I thought I'd be drinking to your memory. I'm glad I was wrong.
Cyan, come here.
I already filed the paperwork based on Brandt's preliminary report. You're officially C-Rank. And... honestly? You earned it.
I couldn't have done it without them.
It was an adequate performance. Your adaptability in the mine was... commendable.
Don't get a big head, kid. You're still paying for the drinks.
Your payment. Plus the hazard bonus. You are wealthy adventurers now.
I suggest you rest. You've changed the fate of the North today.
They celebrated. They drank. For a moment, the world was simple. Good defeated Evil. The monsters were avenged. The town was safe.
Cyan looked at his friends, flushed with victory. He didn't see the cold calculation in Brandt's eyes as the 'magistrate' pocketed the research notes on biological warfare.
He didn't see the gears of the military machine turning. He just saw the light.
Alright. I'm crashing. Don't stay up too late, heroes.
I suspected you might follow me. You have a good instinct for loose ends.
Cut the act. The 'Magistrate' routine worked on the kids. It doesn't work on me.
I'm sure I don't know what you mean.
The tactical assault on the mine. The heavy infantry you had on standby. Magistrates don't have strike teams. Spies do.
You're King's Eyes. Royal Intelligence.
And if I am?
Then you played us. You knew about the Whispering Wood. You knew about the capture squads. You just needed a deniable asset to kick the door down so your team could sweep in.
We weren't heroes. We were bait.
You were effective. That is all that matters in war.
Listen to me closely. We did your dirty work. We saved your kingdom.
But my name stays out of your official reports. I'm just a retired adventurer helping some rookies. You leave me, and you leave them, out of your war games.
I can keep your name out of the files, Mistress Eve. I can respect your privacy.
But you should know... the logs you recovered mentioned the 'Mother'. The leader of this operation.
Our profile suggests she isn't a general. She's a martyr. And martyrs don't retreat when you burn their temples.
They escalate.
The North will strike back for what we found today. And the South will answer. The real war hasn't even started.
Sleep well, Eve.
Eve stood alone in the silence. She had won the battle, but she knew the war was coming for them.
She looked back toward the inn, where Cyan and Lyrel were sleeping, dreaming of their victory.
I'm sorry, kid. I don't think I can protect you from this.

A man stepped out of the corner. He looked like he was carved from old, scarred wood. One eye was milky white, a long scar cutting through the eyebrow above it. He wore the patched leather of a lifelong adventurer, but he moved with the stiff gait of someone whose fighting days were long behind him.
Don't start, Corvin.
Safer? Heh. Kid, you got sold a nice story, but you're living in the punchline. Let me tell you what 'safer' really means.

It means the Great Guild Hall in the capital—the place where kings used to award medals—had to sell half its building to the Merchant's Collective just to keep the lights on. It means the Adventurer's Academy in Silverpeak, where they trained the best of the best, shut down two years ago for 'lack of enrollment'.
Shut down? But... why?

Why? Because this business doesn't run on protecting lumber. It runs on two things: quest fees from monster hunts, and the monster parts we sell after. The first is a living. The second is a fortune. Both have dried up like a riverbed in a drought.

You want to talk economics? Five years ago, a single Griffon feather was worth twenty silver. Standard reagent for potions of speed. Now, you can't find one for a thousand gold. Alchemists are trying to get the same effect with mountain herbs and bat wings. It's not working.
So... that's why everything is so expensive?

Expensive and shoddy. Blacksmiths are using reinforced leather instead of proper Basilisk hide for armor. Enchanters are using flawed gemstones because they can't get the Manticore eyes they need to focus their spells. You think the army is 'efficient'? They're sending soldiers into battle with gear that would've been considered garbage a decade ago.
It's a resource crisis, kid. A rot, eating the kingdom from the inside out. And it's getting people killed.
Corvin's hand subconsciously went to his milky eye, the gesture full of a pain that had never faded.

My last crew... we went after a Manticore in the foothills. The bounty was a king's ransom, enough to retire on. We were good. A-Rankers, all of us. But our gear failed. The strengthening potions burned instead of healed. My shield, supposedly reinforced with Wyvern scale, shattered like glass when the beast swiped at me.
I was the only one who walked away.
Your equipment failed. This rot you speak of... it seems to be accelerating. And the monsters... you don't believe the army's official explanation?
The army can't kill what they can't find. I've talked to other old-timers, hunters, trackers from the borderlands to the coast. It's the same story everywhere.
The monsters didn't get pushed back. They didn't migrate south for the winter. That's the story they tell children.
They just... vanished. All at once, over the last few years. One season, the plains were teeming with Gorgons. The next? Nothing. Not a single track. It's like the land itself was swept clean.
It's not natural.
Not natural. The words hung in the air, shifting the mystery from an economic problem to a chilling, unnatural event.

Cyan's idealistic vision of the North lay in shattered pieces at his feet. Lyrel's sacred mission to investigate an unnatural magical event had just found a potential new, massive lead. And Eve was staring at a man who was a ghost of a future she desperately wanted to avoid.
They left the guild, but they didn't go home. Corvin's words—'A rot eating the kingdom'—pushed them out into the streets.
They wanted to see if it was true.
They passed the local apothecary. A young mother was pleading with the shopkeeper, clutching a sick child.
Please! The fever won't break! You must have a restoration draught!
I don't, ma'am. I haven't had a shipment of Siren Scale in six months. All I have is this willow-bark tea. It... it might help with the pain.
Tea? He needs magic! He's burning up!
She's right. That kid needs a potion, not tea. But there are no ingredients.
Further down, the ring of the blacksmith's hammer was notably absent. The smith sat outside his forge, staring at a pile of rusted scrap.
Hey, Smithy. Quiet day?
Quiet year, Eve. Can't make B-Rank plate without Gryphon leather straps. Can't make swords without flux. I'm reduced to sharpening kitchen knives.
If this keeps up, I'm packing up. Heading south. Heard there's work there.
They walked in silence until they reached the edge of town, looking out at the vast, quiet forest.
The flow of mana in the town is stagnant. The economy is collapsing. Corvin was not exaggerating. The North is bleeding to death.
We can't just guard lumber, Eve. We can't. If we don't find out where the monsters went, this whole town... everything we're trying to build... it's gone.
Fine. You win, kid.
We're not doing this for glory. We're doing it because I like having a blacksmith who can actually repair my daggers.
So we're doing it? We're investigating?
We're doing it. But we're not stumbling around in the woods blind. We need a lead.
Let's go ask the expert.
Back already? Lumber merchant fire you?
We're not taking the lumber job. We want to find the truth.
Corvin, if you were going to look... if you thought there was even one monster left in this region... where would you look?
You're looking for trouble, kid.
We are looking for answers. The disappearance cannot be absolute. There must be an epicenter.
The Whisperwood.
The Whisperwood?
It's a dense patch of old forest, two days east. Always had weird magical currents. Hunters usually avoid it.
But a few weeks ago, before I hung up my sword... I heard something. Not the silence. A roar. Just once. Distant, but deep.
Sounded like a Manticore. If anything survived the purge... it's hiding in there.
Then that's where we go.
The Whisperwood. Creepy name. I hate it already.
Gear up. We leave at dawn.

The Whisperwood earned its name. The wind moved through the ancient pines with a sound like hushed voices. But today, there were no other sounds. No birds. No insects. Just a heavy, suffocating silence.
It's... really quiet. Is it always like this?
(Memory) It's like the land itself was swept clean.
No. A forest this old should be teeming with life. The magical background radiation here is unsettled. Something has disturbed the ecosystem on a fundamental level.
Keep your eyes open. If there is a Manticore here, it's hiding. And if it's hiding, it's scared.
They tracked for hours. Lyrel found broken branches high up in the canopy—signs of a large, winged creature crashing through in a panic.
Here. Look at the soil.
The tracks are erratic. Deep impressions. The creature was fleeing, dead weight hitting the ground... then taking off again.
Maybe it was fighting another monster?
There are no other tracks. Only... these.
Boots. Heavy ones. But the stride is wrong. Too wide for a human. Too disciplined for a goblin.
Blue. Up there.
It's... an arrow? No, it's too thick.
It is a projectile. But not designed to kill.
There is a reservoir here. It smells of... Dreamroot and Viper venom. A paralytic agent. Strong enough to drop a Giant.
This isn't a hunt. Who brings tranquilizers to fight a Manticore?
Cyan turned the heavy dart over in his hands. Etched into the cold metal near the base was a tiny, singular symbol.
There's a mark here. A single red drop.
A blood drop? Maybe a poacher clan?
No... it looks precise. Deliberate. Like a teardrop.
It feels... sad.
Sad or not, this confirms our fears. Someone is not slaying these beasts. They are capturing them.
Down!
We're not alone. And I don't think they're happy we found their toy.
From the mist, figures emerged. Tall, furred, and armored in strange, patchwork leather. They moved with military silence.
The figures stepped out of the mist, surrounding them. They were Beastkin, but not the ragged bandits Cyan had read about in stories.
They wore matching leather armor reinforced with iron. They moved with silent, disciplined signals.
Beastmen? Here? They're so organized...
Capture Squad. Look at the nets and the bolas. They aren't here to kill the Manticore. They're here to bag it.
Interlopers. You have seen too much. Secure the assets. Silence the witnesses.
My, my. Look at that posture, the raw power, the... excessive amount of hair.
I must admit, Eve, seeing your 'dream' in person... it is quite imposing.
I swear to the gods, Elf, if you don't shut up and shoot him, I'm going to stab *you* first.
Come now. Do you not wish to ask him for tips on his technique? Perhaps he can teach you how to howl properly.
I hate you. I hate you so much.
Die!
The Wolf charged. Cyan stood his ground, weaving a complex pattern in the air. Rune of Gravity.
The air around the Wolf turned heavy. The beast was forced to its knees, struggling against the sudden weight of the world.
Whoa. Heavy stuff, kid.
The Wolf charged. Cyan dashed backward, snapping his fingers to fire three Runes of Force like invisible arrows.
The bolts slammed into the Wolf's knees, shattering his momentum and sending him skidding into the dirt.
Excellent precision, Cyan. Finish it!
The Wolf lunged. Cyan didn't try to block. He slapped a Rune of Flash onto the ground and rolled away.
A blinding burst of light erupted. The Wolf howled, clutching his sensitive eyes.
Eve! His eyes! Go!
On it!
The Wolf brought his greatsword down. Cyan didn't flinch. He slammed his hand onto his own chest, activating a Rune of Iron Skin.
Get back!
He caught the blade on his reinforced forearm, sparks flying, stopping the massive beast in its tracks.
Nice block, kid! Now hit him!
Disengage! Fall back to the Forward Camp! Alert the Commander!
They're running. Do we chase?
They mentioned a 'Forward Camp'. If we follow, we may find the source of this operation.
Then let's go. Before they...
Impressive. Very impressive.
Discipline, magic, and banter in the face of death. I see the rumors were understated.
Who's there? Give me one reason not to gut you.
I can give you three. One, I am not your enemy. Two, I know where those Beastmen are going. And three...
I am looking to hire a team exactly like you.
Who are you?
My name is Brandt. I am a... concerned magistrate. And I believe we have a mutual interest in what is happening in this forest.
You found the dart. Good. That saves me the trouble of explaining why this isn't a normal poaching ring.
Those soldiers were not poachers. They are a paramilitary extraction team. And I need someone to find out who is signing their paychecks.
A magistrate who knows about paramilitary ops? You're full of surprises.
And you are full of potential. Help me locate their base, and I will ensure you are paid... handsomely.
We were going to follow them anyway. Might as well get paid for it.
Agreed. His intelligence could prove useful.
Fine. But you walk in front where I can see you, 'Magistrate'.
A wise precaution. Shall we?
Guided by the retreating Beastmen's tracks—and Brandt's surprising knowledge of military diversion tactics—the Strays reached the edge of a ravine.
Below them sat the Forward Operating Base.
That's... that's not a camp. That's a fortress.
Standard perimeter spacing. Two-man patrols. Shift changes every hour. These guys aren't bandits, they're soldiers.
Precisely. This is a logistical hub. They bring the 'assets' here to be processed before transport.
The magic in the air is stifled here. Dampening wards. Those cages... they hold magical creatures, but I sense no agitation. No roars. Just... silence.
They are heavily sedated. The South prefers their cargo docile.
I cannot risk exposure. I will maintain the perimeter and ensure your escape route is clear. You must go in.
I need two things: Proof of where they are taking the monsters, and the identity of their commander.
Convenient. You stay safe, we do the dirty work.
I am paying you for the risk, Mistress Eve. And your particular talents are better suited for infiltration than mine.
Hmph. Fair point. Alright, Strays. We go in quiet. Cyan, stick to the shadows. Lyrel, watch for magical alarms.
They moved through the camp, dodging patrols. They stopped near a row of cages.
It's a young Wyvern. It's breathing, but barely. It looks... thin.
These are not just cages. They are siphons. Look at the runes. They are slowly draining the creature's mana to keep it weak.
Wait. That guard. What is he doing?
The Beastman touched the Wyvern's snout through the bars. He whispered something in a guttural tongue, clutching a small pendant around his neck.
Mother... bear this burden... forgive us...
He's praying? To a dark god? Probably asking for a safe sale.
Perhaps. Or perhaps it is an act of contrition. It is... unexpected behavior for a slaver.
Save the sociology lesson. The Command Tent is up ahead. That's where the answers are.
The camp wasn't a savage gathering. It was a military installation. Patrols moved in perfect sync. Supply wagons were lined up with mathematical precision.
These are not poachers. This is a forward operating base.
Look. The cages.

Dozens of cages were stacked in the clearing. Inside were the 'vanished' monsters of the North—Gorgons, Basilisks, even a young Wyvern. But they weren't roaring. They were silent, drugged into a stupor.
That's a lot of firepower. If they wake those up, we're dead.
The Strays crept closer to listen.
The shipment is ready. But the price has gone up. The... 'Mother' does not know we are holding back this inventory.
Careful, Grog. If your 'Blood Sovereign' finds out you're selling her children to the North, she'll skin you alive.
She sits in her throne of pain and weeps. We are out here doing the work. We deserve our cut. Just take the crates and leave the gold.
They're selling them. They're stealing monsters and selling them back to us for profit. It's just greed.
Curious. That totem... it depicts a human. But the iconography is one of reverence, not capture.
Probably some dark witch they worship. Or a trophy of a victim. Sick.
Focus. We need proof. That ledger on the table.
Got it. The Silver Mine to the east. That's where they're taking the main haul.
Then that's where we go. We end this.
Voices drifted from inside the large tent. One was a deep, growling bass—a Beastman. The other was human, oily and sharp.
The shipment is prepped. But the price has gone up. You want the Wyverns? You pay double.
Careful, Grog. You're getting greedy. Does the 'Blood Sovereign' know you're skimming off the top?
She sits in her tower, weeping black tears for every beast we bag. 'Do not hurt them,' she says. 'Share their pain,' she says.
She is soft. I am the one out here in the mud. I am the one building the army. If I sell a few beasts to the North to line my pockets, it is my right.
Lower your voice! If the Foxian Guard hears you call her soft, you're dead. They worship that girl.
Let them worship. I want gold. Just take the crates to the Silver Mine and be done with it.
They're stealing them... and selling them back to us? It's just greed. Pure, sick greed.
And this 'Blood Sovereign'... she sounds like a religious figurehead. Someone they fear, yet revere.
She sounds like a problem for another day. We have a location. The Silver Mine.
We need to stop this deal. We can't let them take those Wyverns.
No. Too many guards. If we start a fight now, the alarm goes up, and the smuggler gets away with the location of the main base. We need the intel more than the monsters right now.
Fine. But we're taking proof.
Eve sliced a slit in the tent fabric. While the Commander and Smuggler argued over gold, Lyrel used a Mage Hand cantrip (or simple telekinesis) to slide the ledger off the table and through the slit.
Got it. Let's move.
Look at that. That must be her. The 'Blood Sovereign'.
It is... haunting. The iconography suggests suffering, not triumph. Why worship a weeping god?
Because they're monsters, Lyrel. They probably enjoy the suffering. Come on, let's get back to Brandt.
Cyan turned away from the totem, disgusted. He saw a witch worshiped by savages. He didn't see the desperate hope of a people clinging to the only being who ever loved them.
The mine had been hollowed out and filled with humming machinery. Green liquid bubbled in massive glass vats.
What is this place?
It smells of... corruption. Alchemical runoff.
On the table lay a Northern potion—the cheap, toxic kind found in Porthumming—next to a pristine monster organ.
I get it now. They aren't just hoarding the real parts. They're using them as templates.
They study the real thing, create a cheap, toxic copy, and flood our market with it.
Precisely. Why fight an enemy when you can simply sell them their own slow death?
Welcome to the future of warfare, adventurers. No swords. No fireballs. just supply and demand.
We starve you of resources, then sell you poison to fill the void. By the time your army realizes their shields are brittle and their potions are toxic, the war will already be over.
You're monsters! You're poisoning innocent people!
Innocent? Your kind hunted mine for sport for centuries. We are simply... adjusting the market value of a life.
An Elf... and a Human boy with Southern Runes? How ironic. You fight for a Kingdom that would put you in a cage if they knew what you were.
Less talking. More smashing.
The lab began to collapse. Explosions rocked the mine.
We have the ledger! We have the samples! Go!
You can't stop the tide! She is coming! The Mother is coming!
Brandt studied the ledger the Strays had stolen from the smuggler. He traced a line on the map with a gloved finger.
Excellent work. This ledger confirms it. The 'Money Grubbers'—this splinter faction of Beastmen—aren't just selling monsters to random buyers.
They are delivering them exclusively to the Old Silver Mine.
Corvin mentioned that mine. He said it was the only place to process Sunstone Dust.
And Sunstone Dust is the catalyst found in the toxic potions. The connection is undeniable. The monsters go in, and the poison comes out.
So it's a factory. Which means it's going to be guarded like one. We saw the camp—that was just the logistics hub. The mine itself will be crawling with soldiers.
Three of us can't take a fortress, Brandt. Not unless you're hiding an army in your pocket.
As it happens, Mistress Eve, I am not without resources. My... associates... have been staging nearby, waiting for a target.
Associates? You mean mercenaries?
Let's call them 'specialists'. Heavy infantry.
Here is the plan. At dawn, my team will launch a frontal assault on the main mine entrance. We will make a lot of noise. We will draw every guard from the perimeter to the gates.
A distraction. Loud and messy. I like it.
While they are occupied with us, 'The Strays' will infiltrate here.
This is an old ventilation shaft. It leads directly to the lower levels—the Refinery Core.
Your mission is surgical. Get in, secure the research data on the synthetics, and disable their production capability. Do not engage the main force. Leave the army to me.
A logical division of labor. We strike the head while you occupy the body.
We get the proof, stop the poison, and get out.
Precisely. But be warned. The leader of this operation—the one designing these synthetics—will likely be in the Core. He will not be a simple smuggler.
Don't worry. We've dealt with mad scientists before.
Then prepare yourselves. We move at first light.
They laid it all out. The capture operation. The toxic synthetics. The Saboteurs.
Incredible. You have uncovered a plot that threatened the very foundation of the Kingdom.
Because of you, we can neutralize this threat. We will seal the mine. We will burn the corruption.
And as promised. Payment for services rendered. Plus a significant bonus for the intelligence on the 'Mother' cult.
We did it. We actually saved the North.
You did good, kid. Real good. I've already filed the paperwork. You're C-Rank now. Officially.
See? We're the good guys. We stopped the bad guys. It's just like the stories.
The enemy was... organized. Intelligent. But we prevailed.
Yeah, yeah. We're heroes. Now, are we drinking or what?
They celebrated. They laughed. For a moment, the world was simple. Good defeated Evil.
Cyan didn't see the cold calculation in Brandt's eyes. He didn't see the gears of the military machine turning, preparing to use this information to start a counter-offensive.
He just saw the gold, the rank, and the smiles of his friends. And he believed.
I don't care who you work for... This is the last time.
My employers value discretion. As I believe, do you.
My name stays out of your reports. I'm just a retired adventurer.
Crystal.
One thing, Mistress Eve. Before you go.
The 'Mother' mentioned in the logs. The one commanding the Beastmen.
What about her?
The psychological profile suggests she isn't just a tribal leader. She's a unifying symbol. A martyr.
When we strike back... and we will strike back... she won't retreat. She will escalate.
Enjoy your peace while it lasts. The real war hasn't even started.
She walked back to the inn, to the sleeping 'heroes' who thought they had won.
She knew better. They hadn't stopped the storm. They had just signaled the lightning.
This is the story of {player_name} Bernalette — a young man determined to live his life to the fullest.
This is the story of {player_name} Bernalette — a young woman determined to live her life to the fullest.
{player_pronoun_subj_cap} had {player_appearance} and eyes the color of clear morning skies.
The clothes were new — rougher, tougher — but the eyes were the same. The eyes of someone who hadn’t given up.
Thank you for letting me aboard your ship.
The sailor only laughed, boots thudding against the wooden planks as he disappeared with his crew.
This is it. My journey starts here.
The town felt half-asleep — shops shuttered, dust clinging to the cobblestones.
It looked like a place that had been waiting for someone to care again.
After a few minutes' walk, {player_name} stopped at a small inn and peered through the window.
Need something?
(Whoa—Did she just appear out of nowhere?)
Umm… sorry. I was just looking for the guild.
Guild, huh. You sure you can handle one of their jobs? Kids these days—
I'll give it my best shot. Could you point me to it?
Well, the guild moved down the lane — old hall's empty, they work out of a house now. Not much pay, but you'll meet characters.
Thanks. I’ll check it out.
Name's Eve. I run this place. Rooms are cheap — and I put up with idiots for free. If you need a bed, say the word.
I'm {player_name}. I'll see you at the inn if I find work. Thanks, Eve.
Don't die out there. We get enough of that already.
(That was... encouraging.)
The 'Adventurer's Guild' in Porthumming was less a hall of heroes and more a bar that refused to die.
Broken chairs, a sun-faded noticeboard, and the steady smell of cheap rum filled the place.
…Is this really the guild?
You'd be surprised what people call a guild these days. The real guild closed two winters ago. This one just refuses to die.
Are you… the guild master?
Guild master, bartender, janitor — depends on who’s asking.
He grins, pouring himself a drink.
So, which are you? A {cps=*1.8}dreamer or a {cps=*1.8}runaway?
I'm {player_name}. I'm looking for work — anything to get started.
Then you came to the right place. I'm Gabe. We got all kinds of work here — drinking, sweeping, and occasionally fighting oversized rats.
...If you can pay your own tab, that is.
A few of the regulars in the back snorted and returned to their drinks. They'd seen hopeful faces before.
I can handle rats. I just need a quest.
Quest, huh? Haven’t heard that word in a while. Let me see what we have.
Let’s see… Monster subjugation? No budget. Escort job? Client got eaten. Ah—here we go.
‘Missing cat’ — pays one silver coin and eternal gratitude. Straightforward, minimal risk. Interested?
...A cat?
Not just any cat — my cat. Anne. She ran off last night. Cute little menace with more brains than half my regulars.
He glares at the snoring adventurers in the back.
...You’re serious.
Dead serious. Bring her back and you’ll get your coin. And maybe… a drink on the house.
Rumor says she 'teleports' when she wants to skip dinner. Sounds like a tavern tale to me—
...but if you come back and tell me she vanished into another dimension, I might finally believe in miracles.
Gabe's laughter hid a tired gratitude — the kind of man who'd pawn his pride for one fewer empty chair.
At the far corner, hood drawn low, a lone figure watched quietly. She said nothing — only listened.
The road south of PortHumming wound into a dense forest, where even the wind sounded tired.
A missing cat shouldn't be this mysterious...
{player_name} tightened his pack and scanned the underbrush.
You're not the only one who thinks it's a small job, kid. But I'm coming along.
Why? You don't exactly look like a field agent.
Because that cat's the closest thing I have to 'home' left. If something's happened to her, I don't want to find out from a rumor at my counter.
The laugh in his voice faded. For once he sounded like a man who'd lost more than his coin.
They walked. Gabe pointed to an old notice nailed to a tree: a faded poster for the Northern 'Protection Route'.
Once this place was busy as a hive. After the war, the north cleared the roads and—well, life left with the ships.
So that's why the guild's empty.
That, and the king's taxes.
Keep your steps light. This path used to be crawling with scouts during the war.
You talk like you’ve walked it a thousand times.
Try five hundred. I used to run missions here before the army gutted the place.
{player_name} scanned the trees, {player_pronoun_poss} hand brushing the hilt of {player_pronoun_poss} sword.
Hard to imagine monsters living this close to town.
They don’t anymore. The north’s army burned everything that moved— monsters, beasts, even half the trees.
What’s left now is silence. And silence is worse.
The trees grew denser. Moss and rot replaced sunlight.
No bird sounds.
Exactly. Keep your eyes open.
Wait. I can check something.
{player_name} tore a thin strip of parchment and began drawing glowing sigils with sharp precision.
Rivirä.
Light flared briefly, forming a translucent green map above {player_pronoun_poss} palm. Lines pulsed outward like veins, marking traces of life in the forest.
...I'll be damned.
That’s real rune-craft. Not the academy tricks they sell in town.
Basic tracking spell, really. It just reads life signatures.
Don’t downplay it. I’ve only seen a handful who could do that without blowing off a finger.
{player_name} tried to hide a small smile. Praise wasn’t what {player_pronoun_subj} expected from a man who smelled like whiskey and smoke.
There. A small life signature northwest of here. Probably a cat.
Good eyes. I’ll take point — you cover my back.
He moved ahead with the calm gait of someone who’d been in a hundred forests before. Despite his ragged clothes, his grip on the dagger was steady — a soldier’s reflex that never died.
(He may look like a drunk, but his footing’s solid...)
The deeper they went, the heavier the air grew. The path ended at a clearing half-choked by roots.
A faint mewl echoed back — then silence.
That was—
Anne! Anne, you little furball, is that you?
Something’s off. The echo’s too deep.
Probably she’s stuck somewhere. Let’s look.
They pushed through thick brush until the earth dipped ahead, where a dark crack split between the roots of a dying tree.
This… wasn’t here before, was it?
No. The ground’s been dug up recently.
By what?
Hopefully something smaller than me.
{player_name} knelt, feeling the warm air seeping from the hole.
This isn’t natural. It’s giving off heat — a lot of it.
Underground vent maybe. Or something living.
You sound way too calm about that.
Calm keeps you alive. Panic gets you buried.
We should check inside.
We will. But slow. I’ll go first — you watch our backs. If anything moves, don’t chant — stab first, spell later.
...Got it.
{player_name} followed as Gabe descended into the dim passage, his steps sure and deliberate. For a man who called himself washed up, he didn’t move like one.
The forest swallowed their trail behind them, leaving only the faint echo of their steps — and the whisper of something shifting below.
They pushed deeper until the passage opened into something wrong — like a wound in the earth.
The air was thick with rot. Every step made a wet sound against the slick stone.
It reeked of decay and something far older — like the earth itself was decomposing.
By the gods…
Even Gabe, who had seen the aftermath of war, looked pale. His dagger stayed close to his chest — not from fear, but disbelief.
Stay sharp. Something made this.
Could be an old burrow... or—
A rancid stench rolled over them, cutting his words short. The cave walls pulsed faintly, slick with green mucus that reflected the light from {player_name}’s rune flare.
No normal monster does this kind of thing...
If the northern army really cleared this route, then—
He stopped mid-sentence, eyes catching movement in the shadows.
Gabe?
Anne!!
Gabe broke into a run before {player_name} could stop him.
Slumped against the cave wall, half-buried in slime, was a small black cat. Its fur was matted and dull, breath faint — barely alive.
Easy! You’ll alert whatever did this!
She’s alive— she’s still alive!
Give her this.
{player_name} pulled a small vial of shimmering red liquid from {player_pronoun_poss} pouch and tossed it to him.
Thank you…
He poured a drop between Anne’s lips. The cat twitched, faintly, a fragile mewl escaping her throat.
For a second, hope flickered.
Keep quiet. Your shout didn’t help.
Sorry. I just— I thought—
He couldn’t finish. The silence pressed down again.
Then, the ground moved.
A deep vibration crawled through their feet, low and rhythmic. The cave trembled like an arena crowd roaring for its champion.
That’s… not wind.
Move!
The ground exploded beneath them. Massive fangs shot upward, snapping at where Gabe stood seconds before.
{player_name} rolled aside, blade flashing as {player_pronoun_subj} caught a glimpse of the horror emerging — rugged flesh, ringed teeth, the glisten of wet muscle.
A Tesák-Worm. Blind, ancient, and hungry — the kind miners whispered about in their drink but never truly believed existed.
You’ve got to be kidding me—!
Stay behind me!
The cave roared, the worm lunging again. The air turned hot and rancid from its breath.
And in that chaos, Anne’s eyes flared faintly blue… the first hint of something neither of them understood.
From the pit ahead, a monstrous shape surged upward — pink flesh slick with bile, a ring of teeth glinting in the gloom.
Oh, hell—
Stay back, I’ll— Anne?! Where’s the cat?!
In the bag! Still breathing!
Good. Try not to get *her* killed too.
Priorities, huh?

options.text: Rivirä — reveal its movement
Firä — burn its hide
Volitare — hurl the rocks

steps.text: Rivirä!
Runes spiraled across the ground, showing faint tremor lines where the worm shifted.
Neat trick. Can you do that faster next time?
Next time? You’re assuming there’ll be one.
Firä!
Flames licked up the creature’s flank, leaving a smoking welt.
You trying to roast it or anger it?
Little of both.
Volitare!
Nearby stones lifted and smashed into its face.
So... we’re just throwing the cave at it now?
Resource management.
Gabe dashed in, dagger flashing. He carved into the soft tissue under the beast’s jaw.
Got you, you slimy bastard!

options.text: Encourage him
Mock him

steps.text: That’s it! Keep it distracted!
Easy for you to say!
Wow, a knife. Against *that.* Bold choice.
You want the knife? Be my guest!
The worm recoiled and spat bile — a wide spray of hissing green acid.
Poison! Don’t let it touch the floor—
Already not standing there, thanks!
Gabe shielded Anne’s carrier bag, turning away as drops sizzled on his armor.
She okay?!
Still alive. Pissed, but alive.
Great. One of us is.

options.text: Meteorä — go for a full strike
Volitare — use it defensively
Rivirä — track it if it burrows

steps.text: Meteorä...!
{player_name}’s hands burned with runic light. Circles of flame spiraled in the air, drawing sigils that pulsed hotter with each breath.
Uh—how long does that take?!
Just—just a second—!
The worm shrieked, sensing danger. It reared and slammed its body into the cavern floor, shaking loose a rain of stones.
We don’t *have* a second!
{player_name}’s concentration broke as the ground pitched. The half-formed rune shattered, flaring wildly before dissipating in a burst of sparks.
Damn it—! I almost had it!
Great plan, slow burn! Maybe next time start with something that *exists* before we die!
It’s a tier-three spell, okay?!
You’re a *tier-one!*
The worm lunged again, undeterred — and {player_name} grit his teeth, switching to something faster before it was too late.
Volitare, barrier form!
Floating debris formed a brief wall as the worm slammed against it.
You sure you’re not just making this up?
Fake it till it holds!
Rivirä!
Lines spread wider, mapping its every subterranean twitch.
So it’s running?
Or thinking.
Gabe charged, boots sliding over the wet stone. He drew his last throwing knife — the one he swore he’d never waste on a monster’s hide — and hurled it straight into the worm’s gaping maw.
The blade disappeared into the darkness. A beat of silence—then a muffled *crack* erupted from within.
Did you just—did that actually work?!
If it didn’t, I’m suing the blacksmith!
The worm shrieked, thrashing wildly, before pulling itself backward — half its body retreating into the broken earth.
Wait… it’s running?
Ha! Maybe I *am* due for that promotion—
Then, silence. The tremor faded.
Ha! Look at that. It’s retreating!
Or digesting.
Hey, optimism, kid.
You think the guild’ll promote me for this?
For killing an urban legend? Maybe.
And the quest was for a *missing cat*... one silver coin reward. Absolute robbery.
You can complain to accounting after we live through this.
You got accounting in the guild?
Hi! I'm Gabe the accounting.
I’ll take my bonus in *not being eaten.*
They shared a quick laugh. The kind that shakes loose tension but doesn’t erase it.
Then Anne hissed — the sound sharp and wrong. Her eyes flared faintly blue.
...Anne?
What’s she—
The floor split open.
MOVE!
The worm exploded upward from below, fangs first. The earth folded, and the world turned black with motion.
Stone, screams, fur — all gone in one collapsing instant.
Outside the city wall, two drunk adventurers stumbled home.
Did you see that? The ground just—just ate someone!
Sure it did. You gonna blame the tavern stew next?
No, I swear—Gabe and that weird kid—gone!
Hell of a way to skip your bar tab.
By the time they reached the guild, their story had doubled in size.
And when Eve heard Gabe’s name among the rumors—she stopped laughing.
{player_name} gasped awake, choking on air that tasted of pine and damp earth. His head rang like a bell.
Sunlight filtered through a canopy overhead—forest. Not cave. The impossible overlap made his vision blur.
Gabe—?! Where are we?!
Still here. Still too handsome to die. Also... very, very lost.
He was leaning on his dagger, breathing hard. His armor was half gone, and blood traced down his sleeve. A fern tickled his neck.
Beside him, Anne lay limp, faint blue sparks fading from her fur like spent magic.
Anne… she’s not—?
Alive. Barely. Last thing I remember is darkness. Being crushed. Then... birdsong.
Either my cat rewrote reality, or being swallowed whole comes with a very weird aftertaste.
{player_name} tried to stand, but his legs trembled. His mana felt scraped raw.
We need to move. Now.
Agreed. And we need to call reinforcements from the guild to kill the big ugly guy
They didn’t get ten steps before the ground shuddered.
Dust fell like rain. Stones cracked.
The ground behind them rippled — a massive shape tunneling fast.
…You hear that?
Oh, for the love of—don’t tell me—
The earth split open behind them—the same monstrous roar tearing through the forest.
Gabe drew his blade, stepping between {player_name} and the shaking ground.
Take Anne and run. Call some drunkards from the guild to help. I’ll buy you time.
No way! I’m not leaving you—!
{player_name}, this isn’t a debate!
You’re young! You’ve got that fancy runes, the future ahead of you. Me? I’m the discount meat shield!
Now move it before I actually start feeling heroic!
Shut up, idiot! You think I’m—
{player_name}! GO!
His legs moved before his mind did. The ground tore open behind him, spraying dirt and poison.
He didn’t look back. Couldn’t.

options.text: Run faster and trust Gabe.

steps.text: {player_name} clenched his teeth, forcing his legs to move faster. His chest burned—not from exhaustion, but guilt.
The forest fell silent again. Only the sound of {player_name}’s ragged breath remained.
Then, the rumble came again.
The ground beneath his collapsed. He rolled, barely dodging the gaping maw bursting from below.
He hit the dirt hard, Anne slipping from his grasp.
No—no no no—!

options.text: Firä — burn it alive!
Volitare — throw it off balance!

steps.text: ‘Firä!’ He cried, but only smoke escaped his hands. His magic was gone.
He forced the rune—stones floated, then fell uselessly. Mana empty.
The worm tore through the ground, its maw opening wide, the same nightmare again—
A streak of silver light cut through the air. The worm froze—then split cleanly in two, collapsing with a thunderous crash.
Through the rising dust, a woman stepped forward. Calm. Unshaken. His blade still humming with power.
Couldn’t even let me finish my drink, could you?.
E-Eve…?
{player_name} could barely form words. His chest still heaved, mana dry as stone.
You can breathe now, rookie. You’re safe.
Eve’s gaze flicked to Anne, then to {player_name}’s shaking hands.
She’s drained. Cat too. You did well, getting this far.
…Where’s Gabe?
{player_name} blinked — realization crashing back.
He— he stayed behind. He—
Stay put.
Eve turned sharply, blade still drawn, following the faint trail of crushed soil and blood.
She found him a few meters away — slumped against a tree, still breathing, dagger planted in the ground beside him.
The worm’s remains smoked nearby, its body twitching as if still remembering pain.
Idiot.
You promised me you’d quit getting eaten.
She knelt beside him, checking his pulse, then looked back toward {player_name} and Anne.
He’ll live. Barely. Let’s move before something else wakes up.
…Yeah.
{player_name}’s voice was barely a whisper, his eyes flicking between Eve, Gabe, and the cat that had saved them all.
And somewhere deep under the forest, another tremor rolled — faint, but alive.
The fire crackled weakly, the smell of smoke blending with damp earth. Gabe’s breathing was steady again, Anne still motionless, faint traces of blue light flickering around her body.
{player_name} poked at the campfire with a stick, stealing glances at Eve, who sat quietly across from him—arms resting on her knees, eyes distant.
You really did a number on that worm. I blinked and it was... gone.
It’s easier when you don’t hesitate.
That looked like more than 'not hesitating'. You were... terrifying.
Heh. I get that a lot.
You’ve got to be at least—what, A-rank? Maybe S?
Don’t throw that word around, {player_name}.
A-rank?
No. The other one.
Eve’s smirk faded.
And don’t repeat it at the guild. Or anywhere.
Her voice was low. Flat. Like steel ground against stone.
{player_name} straightened unconsciously.
S-sorry. I didn’t mean—
It’s fine. Just… forget it. There’s a lot about the world you’re better off not knowing.
You sound like someone who’s seen too much.
Maybe I have.
For a moment, Eve’s eyes drifted toward the darkness beyond the trees. The firelight painted faint scars on her arms—old, pale lines half hidden under leather and cloth.
You ever fight in the war?
Eve didn’t answer immediately. She reached for her flask instead, took a slow drink, and then said,
Once. Long ago.
Which side?
Wrong question.
{player_name} shut up instantly.
The silence that followed wasn’t awkward—it was heavy.
I quit. Walked away before they could decide my conscience wasn’t convenient anymore.
So the inn’s just... your way of keeping busy?
My way of pretending I’m still human.

options.text: You saved us. Whatever you did before… it doesn’t change that.
If you ever want to talk about it… I’ll listen.
You quit on a war? That takes guts.

steps.text: You saved us. Whatever you did before… it doesn’t change that.
You sound like her.
Who?
Someone who didn’t make it out.
If you ever want to talk about it… I’ll listen.
Heh. Brave offer.
But trust me, you don’t want those stories in your head.
You quit on a war? That takes guts.
Takes fear, actually. Guts come after.
{player_name} looked at her for a long moment. There was power in Eve, yes—but also something else. Something cracked and tired, like a sword left too long in its sheath.
You and Gabe go way back, right?
Yeah. Before all this. He’s the only reason I still talk to people.
You mean drink with people.
Same thing.
{player_name} chuckled weakly. The humor was dry, but it kept the fire from dying.
Get some rest. We’ll head back when the sun’s up. Don’t mention what happened tonight to anyone—not the worm, not me, not the thing you saw.
Why?
Because there are people in the capital who’d rather pretend I died years ago.
The flames popped, and for just a heartbeat, {player_name} saw it—the look of someone who’s killed too many people for a flag that didn’t deserve them.
Understood.
Eve nodded once, satisfied.
Then she stood, walked toward Gabe, and covered him with her cloak.
...Still cleaning up your messes, huh, idiot.
Morning crawled over the forest canopy. Too bright for people who’d survived being eaten the night before.
Eve walked ahead. Gabe dragged his boots behind her. And {player_name} trailed along with Anne snoozing on her arm.
I still can’t believe that thing didn’t chew us twice.
It tried. You were just too bitter to swallow.
Funny. Last I checked, *you* were the one doing the slicing.
Old habits.
You mean war crimes.
Semantics.
{player_name} snorted before she could stop herself.
You two sound like an old married couple.
Watch it, kid.
She wishes. I’d rather wrestle another worm.
You barely survived one. Don’t make me help the next.
Anne meowed — somewhere between agreement and mockery.
Anne says you both sound ridiculous.
That cat can talk?
Probably judging you, too.
They walked on in reluctant silence — the air finally safe enough to breathe.
So… that swing you did. The one that cut the worm in half. That wasn’t normal, right?
Define normal.
Normal as in, doesn’t split monsters like firewood.
Then no. Not normal.
You’re really something, Eve. They should make you an S-rank or something.
Don’t joke about that.
The edge in her voice killed the humor instantly.
…Sorry.
Don’t be. Just—don’t bring that up anywhere. Ever.
{player_name} nodded quietly. Even Gabe had no comeback.
By noon, the rooftops of Porthumming appeared. The guards waved them through.
They just let us in? No papers?
Perks of having a face the guards remember.
Yeah, they remember the face that broke their captain’s arm.
He asked for a rematch.
And you took his job.
He should’ve trained more.
You two are *unbelievable.*
You’ll get used to it. Or die trying.
At the fork of the street, they stopped.
Alright. {player_name}, with me. We’ll go back to the inn and rest.
Wait — seriously? I thought you were going drinking.
Later. My liver filed a complaint.
Coward. I’ll drink for both of us then.
Good. Try not to choke on the mug this time.
Anne leapt onto Gabe’s shoulder — apparently declaring her allegiance.
Figures. Even your cat prefers chaos.
She’s got taste.
{player_name} blinked. 'Old friends' didn’t even begin to cover it.
You were really in the same party before?
Long time ago.
When she still had manners.
When he still had hair.
Hey!
Gabe grumbled something about 'bossy women' as Eve rolled her eyes and tugged {player_name} along.
Come on, kid. Before you start growing mushrooms on your boots.
Do you always insult people you save?
Only the ones still breathing.
Don’t let it go to your head, old hag, but… thanks.
Too late. My head’s already higher than your aim.
For a moment, warmth flickered under Eve’s usual steel. Then she masked it with a smirk.
Eve collapsed into a chair, throwing her daggers aside.
{player_name} sat on the bed, still clutching Anne’s ribbon.
You sure you don’t want to rest too?
I’m fine. Just… everything’s starting to sink in.
It’ll sink deeper tomorrow. Go wash up before you start philosophizing.
So about that training—
No.
Not even a maybe?
Ask again after you stop shaking when you say the word 'worm'.
…Deal.
A faint warmth glimmered behind Eve’s tired eyes.
The guild was already loud when Gabe entered.
Anne hopped onto the counter like she owned it.
There he is! The worm’s lunch!
And he crawled back out!
Keep talking, I’ll feed you to the next one.
So how’d it taste?!
Like your breath. Poisonous.
Laughter exploded.
Relax, I didn’t fight anything. Fell down a well. Passed out. End of story.
The room booed him. One drunk hid under a table.
But one person wasn't laughing.
Lyrel watched quietly, eyes fixed on the faint acid burns on Gabe’s arm.
(No fall makes scars like that.)
(Interesting.)
