She stood, slung her bow over her shoulder, and left without a word.
Evening settled. From her inn a few blocks away, Eve watched the lanterns flicker outside.
The world moved on. But the war still lingered behind her eyes.
And for the first time… {player_name} realized: being strong didn’t mean being free.
Morning sunlight filtered through the trees. Dew still clung to the grass.
{player_name} followed Eve out of the inn, half-jogging to keep up.
Eve, wait up! About that training—
No.
You didn’t even let me finish!
I don’t need to. You’re still in one piece, aren’t you? Good enough.
C’mon! I almost got digested by that worm! I need to get stronger!
And I need a quieter morning. We all have dreams.
{player_name} pouted, hugging his sword like a sulking child.
What if I told you… Anne teleported us out of the worm’s mouth?
Eve stopped mid-step, exhaling sharply.
You hit your head harder than I thought.
I’m serious! Everything went white, and suddenly we were outside the cave.
Cats don’t teleport, kid. They nap, eat, and vomit in corners.
Then explain how we survived!
Eve’s pace slowed. The casual disbelief in her eyes faded, replaced by a quiet, calculating stillness.
...Fine. If your furball can do miracles, prove it.
Wait—you’re actually going to train me?
I said prove it, not train you. But fine, let’s see your ‘miracle’.
Eve crossed her arms, a hint of a grin tugging her lips.
If it turns out you’re crazy, I’ll just add ‘delusional’ to your file at the guild.
You keep files on me?
You’d be surprised what I keep.
{player_name} rolled his eyes but couldn’t hide the grin spreading across his face. For the first time, Eve hadn’t completely shut her down.
The two turned back toward town.
Come on. If we’re doing this, we’ll need the cat.
So we’re actually borrowing Anne?
Borrowing. Not adopting, not summoning. Borrowing. And you’re explaining it to Gabe.
Why me?
Because you’re the one with the miracle story. I’m just the chaperone.
The guild was already alive with noise — chairs scraping, drunks snoring, and a few unlucky ones cleaning up the mess from last night.
Gabe stood behind the counter, bleary-eyed but awake. His expression soured the instant he saw Eve and {player_name} together.
The guild was already alive with noise.
Oh no. Whatever this is, I don’t like it.
Relax. We’re just here for the cat.
You’re kidding.
It’s for… research.
You’re *definitely* kidding.
Anne lay curled atop a stack of request papers.
You, furball — field trip.
She’s not a broom, Eve. And no, you can’t—
Anne jumped down, stretched, and landed neatly on {player_name}’s shoulder.
Looks like she wants to go.
See? Voluntary abduction.
I swear, one day that cat’s gonna turn into something else entirely.
Wouldn’t surprise me.
That’s what I’ve been saying!
Gabe just sighed, rubbing the bridge of his nose.
Fine. But if you break her, you’re both cleaning up the mess.
Deal.
The clearing behind the town stretched quiet and open — a perfect place for bruises and bad decisions.
Eve stood with her hands on her hips while {player_name} tightened the strap on her short sword.
Alright, magical girl. You said the cat can blink you around?
Yeah. You don’t believe me, huh?
Nope. So prove it.
Eve tapped her boot twice against the dirt — drawing an invisible line between them.
Here’s your test. Try to land a hit on me.
Wait, that’s the training?!
You wanted training, didn’t you? Congratulations — you’ve got a moving target.
{player_name} glanced at Anne sitting on a rock nearby. The cat gave her the flattest look imaginable.
You heard her, Anne. Let’s not embarrass ourselves.
Anne yawned, unimpressed.
Whenever you’re ready, rookie.

options.text: Charge straight in.
Cast Spark to distract.
Try Blink.

steps.text: {player_name} lunged forward, short sword flashing in the sun.
Too predictable.
Eve sidestepped with lazy grace, caught {player_name}’s wrist, and tapped his forehead with a finger.
Dead.
You’re not even taking this seriously!
Neither are you. Next.
Fira!
A flash of light burst from her blade — but Eve was already gone, the spark sizzling harmlessly through empty air.
Pretty fireworks. Planning to blind me or court me?
You could at least *pretend* to get hit!
Pretending’s for drunks and nobles. Try again.
Alright, fine… Anne. Let’s sync up.
The cat’s tail flicked once — a silent acknowledgement.
{player_name} whispered a short incantation; runes along his blade glowed faint blue.
Blink!
The world snapped. A streak of light — {player_name} vanished and reappeared behind Eve, sword swinging down.
Eve twisted at the last instant, evading the blade — the shock of the rune pulse pushing her back a step.
Eve blinked once, her smirk fading for the first time.
You actually did it.
Told you!
Don’t get smug. Once is luck. Do it again.
{player_name} nodded, this time holding Anne tighter.
Blink!
Another flash. The grass flattened where she’d stood, wind rushing outward in a pulse.
...Well, I’ll be damned.
Eve stepped back, brushing her palms. The faint blue shimmer still clung to her gloves.
You and that cat — that wasn’t a normal spell. You’re syncing mana across two sources. Dangerous trick for someone your level.
But it worked!
Yeah. Until it doesn’t and you end up inside a wall.
I’ll take my chances.
Eve’s smirk softened, just a little.
You pass. For now. But next time, you aim for the heart — not my shadow.
Wait, so that means—?
You’ve got yourself a teacher. Or a sparring partner, depending on how annoying you get.
{player_name} grinned, wiping sweat from his brow. Anne meowed once, smugly.
Keep going rookie. Make it count.

options.text: Charge straight in.
Cast Fira to distract.
Try Blink.

steps.text: Eve’s smirk faded into a thoughtful frown.
Keep going. I want to see how stable it is.
{player_name} grinned, adjusting his stance as Eve gestured for another round.
Anne meowed, faint blue light flickering again.
Steel met wind. {player_name} blinked and swung, blinked and stumbled, blinked and fell — each attempt sharper, faster, closer.
Good. Again.
Eve’s movements stayed effortless, yet there was respect now — the kind reserved for people worth teaching.
Sun climbed higher above the trees, painting long shadows across the clearing.
By the time the breeze turned warm, their duel had evolved into rhythm — strike, vanish, recover, repeat.
And somewhere in town, a certain guild master named Gabe yawned, grabbed a frying pan, and started packing lunch — blissfully unaware that two maniacs were turning the forest into a training arena.
The guild smelled like fried eggs and butter. Gabe hummed as he flipped something golden in the pan.
And... perfect. Two lunch boxes, one extra for the bottomless stomachs out there.
He packed roasted meat, fresh bread, and something suspiciously close to stew.
Eve better not throw this one at me again.
He slung the bag over his shoulder and stepped outside, whistling.
Across the street, a pair of emerald eyes peeked over a windowsill.
Lyrel kept her distance — eyes sharp, steps light.
The man disappears for a day, nearly dies in the woods… and now he’s packing lunch for someone?
Her tone was flat, but curiosity pulled her forward like a hook.
The scent hit her next — warm bread, butter, a hint of pepper.
Oh, come on… really? Roasted meat too?
Her stomach growled, loud enough to make her grimace.
Not now. I’m on a mission. Focus, Lyrel.
By the time Gabe turned the corner toward the forest path, Lyrel was already slipping along rooftops, silent as a cat with a guilty conscience.
Sunlight dappled through the leaves. The sound of steel and breath echoed faintly ahead.
Gabe stopped just before the clearing, catching sight of the two figures training.
Eve and {player_name} were already there — weapons drawn, dust rising around them.
{player_name} swung his short sword clumsily, his breathing heavy but determined.
Tighter grip. You’re not fanning a fire, you’re trying to stay alive.
Easy for you to say, you *are* the fire!
Gabe chuckled, setting down the lunch bag.
And here I thought you two would’ve killed each other by now.
Gabe! Food!
Ignore her. She hasn’t earned it yet.
You can’t just starve your student!
Watch me.
Anne hopped onto the lunch bag, tail flicking possessively. Gabe sighed.
Lunch time before she faints, yeah?
I said—
A faint growl escaped {player_name}’s stomach.
—fine. Ten minutes. Eat before you start crying.
{player_name} grinned in victory, grabbing the lunchbox.
See, even warriors need fuel!
You’re not a warrior yet, kid.
Anne meowed in agreement, hopping onto {player_name}’s lap.
Gabe chuckled, dusting off his hands.
You two behave. I’ve got drunks to wrangle.
Try not to drink with them this time.
No promises.
He left down the dirt path, the leaves rustling behind him.
Lyrel stayed hidden, adjusting her position for a clearer view.
So that’s where he went… babysitting duty, huh?
She exhaled quietly, resting her chin on her hand.
Hmph. I could’ve been eating that bread right now.
Her stomach gave another protest. She pressed her palm against it, cheeks flushing slightly.
No. I’m here for information — not free meals.
{player_name}, starving from the training, tore into a piece of bread. Eve watched him, her expression unreadable as she took a more measured bite of an apple.
This is the best meal I've ever had.
You say that now. Wait until you've been eating nothing but dried rations for a week.
{player_name} chuckled, but Eve didn't smile. Her eyes were sharp, analytical. She was no longer just the innkeeper; she was the veteran assessing a new asset.
You drop your vowels when you're tired. 'Training' comes out 'trainin'.
{player_name} froze mid-chew, the bread suddenly tasting like ash.
The only people I know who talk like that are from the Southern Reach. Way down south.
The silence stretched. It wasn't an accusation, just a statement of fact. {player_name} swallowed, his mind racing. He hadn't thought he had an accent.
Oh. Yeah. I guess I am.
He tried to make it sound casual, unimportant. Just another fact, like his hair color.
Risky time to be a Southerner this far north. Tensions are high. People are getting nervous.
What made you cross the border? Looking for trouble?
Here it was. The real question. {player_name} looked away, toward the trees, avoiding her gaze.
The opposite, actually.

Where I'm from... your path is set for you. There's no choice. But here... here you can be anything. You can become a hero if you're strong enough. I saw it once, during the Lothern Campaign. I saw what a real adventurer could do.
Eve stopped eating. Her hand tightened slightly around her apple. The name of that campaign hung in the air like a ghost.
An adventurer?
Yeah. Someone like... Anne the Hero.
The change in Eve was instant and chilling. The casual curiosity in her eyes vanished, replaced by a deep, familiar cold. The mask was back, thicker than before.
The North isn't what you think it is, kid.
Her voice was low, flat. All the earlier warmth was gone.
And heroes... heroes are just the ones with the prettiest graves.
{player_name} didn't know what to say. The shift was so sudden it felt like whiplash. The easy camaraderie of the training ground was gone, replaced by a heavy, uncomfortable silence.
He looked down, picking at a loose thread on his tunic. He had said something wrong. Something that had touched one of those old, pale scars he'd seen on her arms.
A few minutes later, Eve and {player_name} finished their lunch. {player_name} stretched, wiping her mouth.
Alright! Round two?
You sure you can move with that stomach full of mine stew?
Watch me!
Eve smirked, stepping back and crossing her arms.
Fine. Show me your miracle.
{player_name} inhaled, gripping her short sword tight. Runes faintly glowed along her arm — then—
—the air snapped. {player_name} vanished in a pulse of azure light and reappeared ten feet to the left, his sword held at the ready.
In the trees, Lyrel's breath caught in her throat. Her eyes widened, first in shock, then in a blaze of pure, undiluted rage.
(That signature... It's HIM! It's that magic!)
The air felt colder all of a sudden. A memory flashed — screams, light, soldiers half-merged with earth and trees, the rest crawling, twisted, screaming to die.
Before {player_name} could even catch his breath, a figure in green and brown burst from the forest.
YOU!
Lyrel's voice was a low growl, trembling with fury. Her bow was in her hand, though not yet drawn.
Your magic! I saw it! That's Northern military teleportation! That's the magic that murdered my home!
Where did you learn it?! Tell me NOW!
Huh? Who—?
Eve moved before {player_name} could finish, stepping between them like a shadow. Her posture was relaxed, but her eyes were like chips of ice.
You’ve got one chance to walk away, stranger.
This doesn't concern you, butcher. I want answers from the boy.
Lyrel took a step forward. Eve didn't flinch.
You're not getting near him.
Then I'll go through you.
In a flash, Lyrel nocked an arrow. Before she could draw, Eve lunged.
The world became a blur of silver and green. A flash of steel, the whistle of an arrow, the sharp tang of ozone from a deflected spell.

{player_name} couldn't even track their movements. Eve was a shadow, her blade a seamless extension of her will. Lyrel was a whirlwind, firing arrows that curved in mid-air while weaving defensive runes.
This wasn't a spar. This was a battle between two apex predators. And {player_name} was completely, utterly outclassed.
The chaos stopped as suddenly as it began. Eve's blade was pressed against Lyrel's bow, their faces inches apart, both breathing hard.
You're fast, tree-hugger. I'll give you that.
And you fight like a cornered animal.
Last warning. Stand down.
Not without answers!
Eve’s patience thinned. Her tone dropped cold.
You don’t want to see what serious looks like.
Eve’s next strike — strong enough to split the giant worm ——
—— and then, a sound louder than any clash echoed through the clearing.
Grrroooowwwwwwl.
Both women froze. Lyrel's face, a mask of furious determination a second ago, turned a shade of crimson that had nothing to do with anger.
The sound came not from the forest, but Lyrel’s stomach.
…Was that your attack skill?
Shut up— it’s tactical hunger!
Eve blinked twice, lowering her guard.
Tactical hunger. That’s new.
{player_name} laughed, rummaging through the leftover lunchbox.
You can join the post-battle meal if you stop trying to stab us.
I don’t need—
Her stomach growled loud enough to make the birds scatter.
...Alright. Maybe one bite.
They sat in the grass — tense silence broken by the crunch of bread and the faint hum of wind.
No one said it, but something had shifted.
A confrontation had turned into a strange, quiet truce — born from curiosity, and maybe just a bit of hunger.
Eve watched, still wary, while {player_name} sat down a safe distance away.
(Munch)... That magic. The Blink... (Munch)... It's the same energy signature that poisoned my home. A Northern military signature.
You don't know what you saw.
(Munch)... Yes, I do. I have spent years tracking that magical poison. It's why I'm here. Are you a Northern soldier?
No! I'm not a soldier! I'm just... training to be an adventurer. Anne—the cat—is the one with the real power.
Lyrel paused, looking from {player_name} to the cat, then to Eve.
And you're training with her? I felt her killing intent. She's no adventurer. She's a butcher.
Heh. Takes one to know one, tree-hugger.
Lyrel glared at Eve before taking another angry bite of cheese.
The cat... the energy comes from the cat, but you channel it. How?
I don't know! We're connected somehow. We're still figuring it out.
Lyrel finished the last of the bread, her energy returning. The anger in her eyes was replaced by a steely resolve.
I apologize for attacking you, {player_name}. My reaction was... extreme. But my mission is not.
This teleportation magic is a poison to the world. But you... you are not a soldier. I don't believe you are the cause.
You may, however, be the key to the cure.
She stood up, dusting crumbs from her tunic.
I want to join you. I will travel with you and observe this power. I need to understand it.
Really? That would be great!
Absolutely not. We're not collecting strays.
I wasn't asking for your permission, helmet hair.
...What did you just call me?
{player_name} looked between the glaring assassin and the stubborn elf, a slow smile spreading across his face.
His party was finally coming together.
The leftover food sat between them, the easy mood of the morning completely gone.
Eve stood up, her movements sharp and efficient.
Break's over. Get up.
Right...
{player_name} scrambled to his feet, grabbing his short sword. He could feel the shift in her — the friendly mentor was gone, replaced by a hardened drill instructor.
You want to learn? Then learn. The battlefield doesn't care about your feelings. It only cares about results.
Show me the Blink again. And this time, make it count.
From the deep shadows of the forest's edge, Lyrel watched, her hand resting on her bow. She had followed them, her suspicion now a burning certainty.
(There it is again... that faint magical residue. What are they doing?)
{player_name} took a deep breath, pushing aside the confusion from their conversation. He focused on Anne, who sat on a nearby rock, alert and ready.
Okay, Anne... like we practiced.
He whispered the incantation. Blue runes flared to life along his blade.
Blink!
The air snapped. {player_name} vanished in a pulse of azure light and reappeared ten feet to the left, his sword held at the ready.
In the trees, Lyrel's breath caught in her throat. Her eyes widened, first in shock, then in a blaze of pure, undiluted rage.
(That signature... It's HIM! It's that magic!)
Before {player_name} could even catch his breath, a figure in green and brown burst from the forest.
YOU!
Lyrel's voice was a low growl, trembling with fury. Her bow was in her hand, though not yet drawn.
Your magic! I saw it! That's Northern military teleportation! That's the magic that murdered my home!
Where did you learn it?! Tell me NOW!
W-what? Who are you?

ENOUGH!
Eve and Lyrel stopped, both turning to look at him, surprised by his sudden fire.
Arguing isn't going to work. Your plan failed, Eve. My plan failed. And Lyrel, your plan failed too. We can't do this alone. So let's stop trying to.
Let's just... talk. What do we actually know?
He took the lead, not as a commander, but as a moderator trying to stop a fight.
My scouting rune worked for a second. There are dozens of small ones, four or five of those big mutated ones, and one huge nest deep in a crack in the back foundation. The nest is the source.
The smaller creatures are no threat if they can be pacified. My spores will work on them, but they had no effect on the mutated ones. Their magical resistance is too high.
And those mutated ones are the real problem. They're fast, and that acid can melt steel. The wards on this place prevent any large-scale attacks.

I could fight them all, but I can't guarantee this place would still be standing. If I'm dodging acid and fighting off a horde, I can't afford to hold back. Gabe's 'no S-rank solutions' rule goes out the window.
Okay... so we have a horde that needs to be controlled, and elites that need to be distracted, all so we can hit a single target without bringing the house down.
Lyrel closed her eyes, thinking.
If I could focus just on the horde, I could create a 'path of peace' through them. But I'd be completely exposed to the mutated ones.
And if I had a clear path, I could get to that nest and finish this in under five seconds. But I can't do that while fending off those acid-spitters. I need a diversion.
A moment of silence hung in the air as the pieces of the puzzle clicked into place. {player_name} looked at Eve, then at Anne the cat, who was watching them with intelligent eyes.
A diversion... Eve, you need something that can get their attention but can't be easily hit, right?
Yeah. Something impossibly fast.
A slow grin spread across {player_name}'s face. He looked at Anne.
We can do that. Anne and I. We'll be the diversion. We'll Blink around, keep the big ones busy. They can't hit a moving target.
Lyrel's eyes widened as she saw the full picture.
It could work! While you have the elites' attention, I will pacify the horde. That will give Eve...
...a clean run straight to the nest.
Eve finished the thought. A rare glint of professional respect flickered in her eyes as she looked from {player_name} to Lyrel.
It's a risky plan. If your timing is off by a second, kid, you're acid-bait.
We can do it. Together.
They looked at each other, a silent agreement passing between them. No one was giving orders. It was their plan.

They moved as one. Lyrel went first, casting her spores in a wide, sweeping arc. A wave of calming green energy washed over the basement, and the horde of smaller rats instantly slowed, their aggression fading.
The mutated rats hissed, unaffected. Just as they were about to lunge at Lyrel, the air snapped.
{player_name} appeared directly in front of them. 'Hey, ugly!' he yelled, waving his arms.
As they spat acid, he vanished again, reappearing safely on the other side of the room. Anne and {player_name} became a blur of blue light, a constant, impossible-to-hit distraction.
It was all the opening Eve needed. With the horde pacified and the elites distracted, she exploded into motion.
She was a silver streak, her twin daggers a blur. She ran through the path Lyrel had cleared, vaulted over a sleeping rat, and reached the back wall.
Without hesitating, she plunged both daggers deep into the pulsating, fleshy nest.
A piercing shriek echoed through the basement. The mutated rats froze, their glow fading, and collapsed. The magic holding them together was gone.
The silence that followed was absolute. The basement was still, the threat neutralized.
{player_name} leaned against a wall, breathing heavily. Lyrel was already kneeling, checking on the sleeping rats.
Eve calmly wiped her daggers clean.
Job done.
Before they left, Lyrel walked to the cage at the back of the room. She placed a hand on the whimpering creature, a soft green light flowing from her palm, healing the worst of its wounds.
{player_name} followed her. He didn't say a word. He just lifted his boot and brought his heel down hard on the cage's rusty lock.
The door swung open. The small creature looked at him for a long moment before scurrying into a dark crack in the wall, and to freedom.
Eve watched from the stairs, rolling her eyes. But she didn't stop them.
They met Valerius outside. He handed them a paper with his stamp, a proof for a finished quest to the guild without asking for details.
As they took the proof, {player_name} looked the alchemist directly in the eye. He didn't say anything, but his cold, disappointed stare said everything that needed to be said.
You're right, boy. I should have been more careful.
The old man turned and went back inside his quiet cottage, closing the door on his secrets.
The Strays walked back to Porthumming. They didn't talk much on the way.
They weren't friends yet. But the silence between them was no longer hostile. It was the quiet of a team that had survived its first test.
The next morning, the air in Eve's inn was thick with the smell of stale ale and silence.
A massive, bearded man with the physique of a bear was fast asleep, his head pillowed on his arms at a corner table. His snores sounded like a distant thunderstorm.

Ever since their formation as the Strays, {player_name} and Lyrel had been staying at Eve’s inn — part home, part base of operations. The place had become their quiet shelter between missions, where mornings began not with orders, but with the clatter of mugs and Eve’s dry sighs.
Eve stood behind the bar, methodically cleaning a mug with a worn rag.
Morning, Eve! Ready for our debriefing at the guild?
Should we not wait? You seem to be... working.
Lyrel gestured vaguely at the empty, silent room.
This is it. This is the morning rush. Him.
She nodded toward the snoring drunk.
That's Borin. He's my best customer. Pays his tab once a month and serves as a free security system.
(mumbling in sleep)...I'll fight the whole lot o' ya...
See? Low maintenance.

Eve finished cleaning the mug, hung it up, and pulled a small, dusty wooden sign from under the counter. She flipped it over. On it, crudely painted, were the words: GONE HUNTING. POUR YOUR OWN. LEAVE COIN IN JAR.
Wait, that's it? You're just... leaving?
This place doesn't make money, kid. It's a place for me to drink in peace. If anyone wants a room, they can fight Borin for it. If they win, they've earned it.
She walked to the front door, flipped the 'Open' sign to 'Closed,' and hung her new sign on the inside.
She turned to them, completely deadpan.
Let's go. I'm missing out on valuable time I could be spending getting lectured by Gabe.
The guild hall was moderately busy. The Strays, still covered in grime from the basement, walked up to the counter where Gabe was sorting papers.
He looked up and did a visible double-take.
You're back already? And the town's still standing?
What did you break? Did you burn it down? I know you burned it down, Eve.
My professional integrity is wounded.
You don't have any. Report.
{player_name}, standing a little taller than before, stepped forward.
Mission complete, Guild Master. The nest has been eradicated.
He proceeded to explain their 'Trinity Strike' strategy, detailing each member's role.
Huh.
Gabe leaned back, genuinely impressed.
A three-pronged synergistic assault... for rats. You three don't do anything halfway, do you?
The kid's scouting rune saved us from walking in blind. It's a solid strategy. He's not as useless as he looks.
{player_name} beamed at the backhanded compliment.
And we couldn't have done it without Lyrel! Her spore magic was incredible! She handled the whole horde by herself!
Lyrel, unaccustomed to such direct praise, looked away, a faint blush on her cheeks.
It was a team effort... And... I suppose... Helmet Hair's final strike was... undeniably efficient.
Damn right it was.
Gabe was speechless for a moment, a rare sight. He expected them to fail, or worse, succeed by causing thousands in property damage.
He shook his head, a real smile breaking through his usual cynicism, and slid a heavy pouch of coins across the counter.
I'll be damned. You didn't kill each other. That's a first.
Go get a drink. My treat. You look like you've earned it.
A short while later, the four of them were gathered at a corner table. The mood was lighter than it had ever been.
So she really got drenched? The whole 'cabbage water' thing?
Completely! You should have seen her face!
Keep talking, kid, and I'll show you again up close.
I must admit, for a moment, I believed justice had been served.
Even Eve cracked a small, reluctant smile. For the first time, it felt less like a business arrangement and more like... a party.
From a nearby table, a loud, drunken voice cut through the chatter.
And then the bastard... my own partner... took the Eye of the Gorgon and ran! Left me for dead in that goblin nest! Can you believe it? Betrayed by my own friend of ten years!
The mood at their table instantly shifted.
Happens all the time. Never trust your partner more than you trust your own blade.
How could someone do that? A bond of trust is sacred. To break it is unforgivable.
Sounds like you picked a bad partner, old man.
{player_name} was quiet. He wasn't cynical like Eve or morally outraged like Lyrel. He looked genuinely, deeply confused by the concept itself.
He turned to the group, his voice quiet and earnest.
But... why? Why would a friend do that to someone they trust?
The question hung in the air, heavy and out of place. It wasn't philosophical; it was personal and painful.
Eve's faint smile vanished. She gave {player_name} a long, searching look, sensing again that there was a deeper wound there.
Lyrel saw his genuine pain and offered a reassuring smile, though she didn't understand its source.
Gabe, completely missing the subtext, just clapped him on the back.
Because people are bastards, kid. Welcome to the real world.
The laughter from the other table seemed distant and hollow.

They were closer now, yes. But {player_name}'s simple, painful question was a stark reminder that the greatest dangers they faced weren't in monster-filled basements, but in the pasts they were all running from.
Well, well. If it isn't my favorite band of walking disasters. Good news, your reign of terror on my booze supply is being put on hold. I've got a job for you.
Pass. I've met my quota for weirdos this month.
That's a shame. It's your first official B-Rank offer. I guess I'll give it to that group of rookies who call themselves the 'Crimson Blades'...
B-Rank?! For us? Gabe, you're serious?
A B-Rank designation implies a significant threat. What is the nature of the quest?

Now that I have your attention... The client is one Baron Von Hess. Pompous fellow with more money than sense. Seems a tribe of goblins has taken up residence in his logging woods and are 'disrupting his vital economic endeavors'.
Goblins. You're giving us a B-Rank for *goblins*. That's pest control, Gabe. You hired S-Rank and A-Rank talent to go squash some green rats.
But goblins can be dangerous in large numbers! And it's for a Baron! It's a classic adventurer quest! This is great!
The Baron's involvement is what concerns me. A task's rank is often inflated by a wealthy client's ego. Goblins are a nuisance, but they are rarely a B-Rank threat on their own.
Hey, his money is good. He's paying B-Rank price, so it's a B-Rank job. All you have to do is go to the logging camp east of here, find the tribe, and... persuade them to leave. Permanently.
Fine. Let's go get this farce over with. But if I get even one drop of goblin guts on my boots, you're paying for a new pair.
It is our duty. Let us hope this Baron is not as trying as his reputation suggests.
The Strays' first B-Rank mission! Let's go!
Heh. 'Classic adventurer quest'. This is gonna be good.
Doesn't smell like a warzone. I was expecting more screaming and... well, goblins.
Look. Tracks. Dozens of them. They are small, chaotic... and lead deeper into the woods. But there are no signs of a struggle. No blood, no broken weapons. Strange.
They must have a hidden base! A goblin fortress! We've got to be careful.
Sure, kid. A 'fortress'. Let's go find your fortress. Just try not to trip over any roots on the way.
What... in the world...?
The clearing was dominated by a haphazardly built stage. On it, a bizarre play was in full swing, and its stars were goblins.
The first 'act' was a chaotic re-enactment of the Giant Worm battle...
...ending with one goblin throwing a very angry badger at the hero in a baffling interpretation of teleportation magic.
I can't believe this. They're making us look like fools.
But the show wasn't over. The actors reset for a new scene, this one apparently set back at the guild.
The large 'Goblin Eve' staggered to center stage, clutching her side as if wounded. She then picked up a wooden bucket filled with muddy water and wilted leaves.
She took a huge, dramatic gulp... then, with a look of utter disgust, spat it all out in a massive spray.
Hey! That was one time! And it was Gabe's fault for calling that swill 'ale'! It was basically cabbage water!
Ah, yes. I believe I do recall something about 'questionable refreshments'. To see it immortalized on the stage...
{player_name} clamped a hand over his mouth, but a muffled chuckle escaped anyway.
I... uh... did think Gabe's ale tasted a bit off that day.
Wipe those smirks off your faces, both of you. Your turn's coming.
As if on cue, the 'actors' prepared for their grand finale. The 'Goblin {player_name}' stood opposite the skinny 'Goblin Lyrel'.
A goblin offstage began to beat a hollow log, creating a loud, rumbling growl that echoed through the clearing.
On stage, 'Goblin Lyrel' clutched her stomach, doubling over in supposed agony.
That is... an outrageous exaggeration.
HAHAHA! Oh, this is the best thing I've ever seen! They even got the sound right!
Eve's explosive laughter was infectious. A surprised, genuine laugh burst out of {player_name} before he could stop himself.
Eve, tears streaming from her eyes, clutched her own stomach and let out a loud, mocking gurgle, perfectly imitating the goblin's drum.
Grrrowwlll... Oh, the great Elven Warden, felled by a bit of hunger! Priceless!
It was NOT that loud! And you can stop laughing too, {player_name}! This is hardly heroic behavior!
You're right! Sorry! Guys, guys! Focus! We're on a job!
Alright, alright. I've had my fun. But now this whole circus has to end. I'm tearing it all down.
After you just finished enjoying the performance? You would attack our... our admirers?
They're not admirers, they're a security risk and a source of deep, personal embarrassment. They need to go.
And I maintain that a diplomatic approach is the only honorable one! We cannot resort to your brutish methods!

They tried to bow like Lyrel, but being goblins, they just ended up headbutting each other and falling over.
In the commotion, several goblins tripped backwards into the stage's main support beam. It groaned, swayed, and then collapsed.

Alright, watch a master at work. I'm just going to dismantle their little stage. They'll get the message.
Eve shot forward like a shadow. But as she vaulted onto the stage, the goblins didn't scream or flee. They gasped in awe.
WOOOW! THE SHADOW-STAB!
The large 'Goblin Eve' saw her idol in action and decided to join in. He copied her leap... but with none of her grace.
The brutish goblin landed squarely on the stage's weakest point, which collapsed with a splintering crack, starting a chain reaction.
The wiggling worm log rolled off its platform and flattened the cabbage-water bucket. The badger, finally free, went on a vengeful rampage through the goblin audience.
Well... that didn't go according to plan.
This is a disaster! If you'd just let me handle it properly...
Me?! Your 'plan' resulted in the exact same outcome! This is what happens when you refuse to consider the honorable path!
The two women squared off amidst the wreckage, their patience completely gone. The comedic music fades out, replaced by a tense silence.
My methods are efficient. Your methods are naive.
My methods have integrity. Yours have none.
That's it, elf. You and me. Right now.
Just as they were about to come to blows, a familiar, loud, rumbling growl echoed through the clearing.
You have got to be kidding me.
Lyrel clutched her stomach, her face a mask of pure mortification. It had happened again.
I... had a light breakfast.
YAY! THE WARDEN'S ROAR!
HAHAHA! Not again! The timing! It's too perfect!
The tension shattered instantly. But before anyone could say another word, a new, pompous voice cut through the air.
What is the meaning of this disaster?!
I hired you to eliminate these pests, not throw a festival with them! Look at this mess! Guards, kill every last one of these vile creatures!
Wait! You can't!
And why not? They are goblins! Worthless! Now, out of my way!

options.text: Eve's Plan: Deception. (This will earn a heart for Eve)
Lyrel's Plan: Honor. (This will earn a heart for Lyrel)

steps.text: (Whispering) Eve, can you create a distraction?
(Whispering) Better. Watch.
Baron, I would not take another step if I were you. We didn't destroy their camp. We were forced to quarantine it.
Quarantine? What nonsense is this?
They're afflicted with Scrofulous Pox. Highly contagious. Causes boils in... very embarrassing places. We were trying to contain it when you arrived.
The Baron, a man who clearly valued his vanity, turned pale and took a step back.
P-Pox?! Disgusting! Very well, burn the whole forest! I don't care, just keep them away from me! I'm leaving!
(Whispering) Lyrel, can you reason with him?
(Whispering) Reason is for reasonable men. He understands only reputation.
Baron Von Hess! These goblins are now under the official protection of the Adventurer's Guild. Any hostile action against them will be considered a direct assault on the Guild itself.
The Guild? You can't be serious!
I am. Word of a nobleman who hires adventurers and then tries to slaughter them while they work travels fast. Your reputation would be in tatters. Is that truly worth it?
The Baron sputtered, his face turning red with fury and indignation. He valued his reputation more than anything.
This is an outrage! An insult! Fine! Keep your filthy pets! But I am NOT paying you!
Well, we saved them. Now what?
{player_name} stepped forward, facing the Goblin Chief. He pointed a finger at him, then deep into the forest, away from the logging camp.
LEAVE.
Then he pointed at their stage props.
AND STOP COPYING US.
The goblins, finally getting a command simple enough to understand, nodded frantically, gathered their things, and scurried off into the deep woods.
Well... that's that. You think they'll actually stop?
Nope. Not a chance.
I am less concerned with *if* they will stop, and more concerned with *what* their next performance will entail.
They have just witnessed two spectacularly failed strategies, a direct confrontation, and a... a biological interruption.
Great. I can't wait to hear the goblin tribute ballad of 'The Warden's Roar'.
Please, do not call it that.
Let's just... let's just go home.
So. The great heroes return from the big B-Rank goblin hunt. Judging by your faces, I'm guessing you don't want a celebratory drink.
We failed, Gabe. The job's a bust. The Baron walked. We're not getting paid.
Hold on. There's a difference between 'failing a job' and 'not getting paid by a cheapskate nobleman'. Are the goblins still causing a problem at his logging camp?
No. We... convinced them to relocate.
And you did it without a massacre?
Yes. But the Baron wanted us to kill them, so when we refused...
So let me get this straight. You were hired to solve a pest problem. You went there, found out the 'pests' were just a bunch of brain-dead fans putting on a terrible play...
{player_name}, Eve, and Lyrel recounted the entire absurd story. With every detail—the badger teleportation, the cabbage water, the 'Warden's Roar'—Gabe's amusement grew.
Hahaha! So you solved the problem, stood up to a pompous noble, and accidentally started a goblin cargo cult. That's not a failure! That's the most Strays-ass victory I've ever heard of!
It doesn't feel like a victory when we don't get paid for it.

Good thing I know my clients. I took a 'non-refundable security deposit' from the Baron before you even left. For 'potential property damage'. He was so furious he forgot to ask for it back. This should cover your fee.
And speaking of a job well done... Eve, Lyrel. Your report mentioned the kid handled himself.
He didn't panic when the plan went up in flames. And he stood his ground against the Baron. That takes guts.
His judgment in a chaotic social situation was sound. He chose a path that, while unconventional, prevented bloodshed. It was commendable.
A few days later...
A nervous-looking delivery boy entered the guild, dragging a large object covered by a burlap sack. He dropped it in the middle of the room, handed Gabe a note, and ran.
Huh. It's for 'The Strays'.
{player_name} pulled off the sack. Underneath was, without a doubt, the single ugliest statue ever created.

It was a lopsided, life-sized sculpture of the three of them, made of mud, twigs, and stolen junk. The 'Eve' was a lump with two bent spoons for daggers. The 'Lyrel' had a ridiculous cape made of leaves. The '{player_name}' was just a smaller lump holding a shiny rock.
And at their feet, represented by a particularly spiky pinecone, was 'Anne the badger'.
I'm getting the firewood.
While aesthetically... challenging... it is a testament to the impact we have on the world. A terrible, terrible testament.
They... sent us a gift.
Looks like we're stuck with a reputation, kid. Whether we like it or not.
Is that... a bad thing?
It's a leash. But as long as you know how to use it... maybe it's not the worst thing in the world. Just don't expect me to pose for their next masterpiece.
This is the burden of being a hero, {player_name}. Your actions are no longer your own. They become stories, symbols...
Even the embarrassing ones?
(A small, sad smile) Especially the embarrassing ones. But as long as we strive to make the story a good one... that is what matters.
Alright, I'm done for today.
As am I.
Right. See you tomorrow.
The morning after the goblin statue's arrival was heavy with an unspoken question.
The sheet-covered lump in the corner served as a silent, ugly monument to their chaotic existence.
Eve stared at it, her breakfast untouched. The weariness of the past few weeks seemed to finally settle on her shoulders.
What are we doing?
What do you mean?
This. The Strays. Stumbling from an alchemist's disaster to a goblin fan club. We almost get killed, we barely get paid... What is the *point* of all this?
The point? Eve, we're helping people! The ones nobody else will. We freed that creature, we saved those goblins from being slaughtered.
Isn't this what real adventurers do? It's exactly what a hero like Anne would have done!
The name hit the air like a shard of glass. A flicker of raw pain crossed Eve's face before a cold, bitter mask slammed down in its place.
You have no idea what you're talking about, kid.
You think being a hero like Anne is a storybook? It's being a weapon for other people's wars until you break. That's the 'point'.
He is naive. Dangerously so.
But his naivete provides an unexpected tactical advantage.
Consider our recent missions. An illegal alchemy lab and a dispute with a minor noble. We operated completely beneath the notice of the military or any major political power.
Our reputation is not that of efficient mercenaries, but of chaotic, unpredictable eccentrics.
This... foolishness... is the perfect camouflage. By following his idealistic crusade to 'help the forgotten,' we become invisible.
No one of power would ever see 'The Strays' as a threat or a tool worth controlling. It grants us the freedom to move and act without scrutiny.
And so, an unspoken agreement was forged. It was not a shared goal, but a fragile symbiosis.
{player_name} would get to be the hero he always dreamed of being.
And in doing so, he would provide the perfect shield for the two deeply wounded people following in his wake.
Fine. Do whatever you want.
Just... don't use her name like that again.
The air was thick with the things left unsaid. Eve's warning to never use Anne's name like that again hung between them, heavy and cold.
{player_name} opened his mouth, the shape of an apology on his lips, but Lyrel spoke first, her voice cutting cleanly through the tension.
The issue of our 'camouflage' is settled. However, the mission at the Baron's logging camp revealed a significant tactical flaw in our operational structure.
Eve, your power is overwhelming but indiscriminate. My own skills are for precision and defense. In both of our recent missions, we have been a sledgehammer and a scalpel.
We lack versatility. We lack a proper vanguard.
We are a liability because you cannot keep up.

She's right, kid. The goblin thing was a joke, but if that Baron had been a real commander, you'd be dead. Your Blink is a great trick, but in a real fight, you're a glass cannon with a five-second fuse.
We need to get you to B-Rank proficiency. Not on paper, but in practice. If you're going to run with this circus, you need to be able to pull your own weight when things get real.
Okay... so how do I do that? What does a B-Rank test even look like?

There is no single test. One is recognized as B-Rank when one has survived a B-Rank threat. My own recognition came during the border skirmishes. My unit was tasked with holding a mountain pass against a full legion of Southern regulars for three days.
It was not about killing. It was about controlling the terrain, managing dwindling supplies, and outlasting a superior force. B-Rank, for a Warden, is about endurance and strategy.
And... and you, Eve?
A distant, almost fond look entered her eyes. It was a startlingly open expression, a brief glimpse of a person {player_name} had never met.
My test was... messier. Less strategy, more chaos.

It was before the war. Back when monster subjugation quests were still common. A whole clan of Orcs had migrated down from the Dragon's Tooth mountains and were terrorizing the northern farmlands. A real B-Rank threat.
A ghost of a smile touched her lips, tinged with a deep, unspoken sadness.
There were three of us. A loudmouthed warrior who was better at taking hits than planning...
She means Gabe.
...the shield of the party, calm and focused, the one who actually kept the warrior from getting himself killed...
She means Anne.
...and me.
The smile turned a little more real, a little more weary.

We were young, stupid, and thought we were invincible. The plan went to hell in the first five minutes. We were supposed to ambush them in a ravine, but our warrior tripped a rockslide and we ended up in a full-blown brawl with fifty angry orcs.

It wasn't elegant. It wasn't clean. We won because we refused to lose. He held the line, she picked off their shaman, and I just... caused chaos. Traps, smoke bombs, hamstringing their biggest brutes from the shadows. B-Rank, for us... it was about pure, stubborn teamwork. Watching each other's backs and pulling a win out of a complete disaster.
The room was silent. {player_name} was left with two starkly different images of strength: Lyrel's disciplined military operation, and Eve's chaotic, friendship-fueled trial by fire.
So... I just need to survive something impossible?
Pretty much. You're not a Warden and you don't have a party of idiots to watch your back... well, you've got two idiots now, I guess.
We'll have to find a job that tests *your* limits as a Rune Mage.
Indeed. A standard subjugation will not suffice. We need a mission that requires a unique application of your skills.
The weight in the inn's common room had been lifted, replaced by a new, tangible sense of purpose. For the first time, they weren't just reacting to chaos; they were actively seeking it.
As they walked through the streets of Porthumming, the morning sun casting long shadows, Eve broke the comfortable silence.
Alright, kid. Before we go looking for a B-Rank suicide mission, let's get one thing straight. What are you even trying to be?
Huh? I'm a Rune Mage.
That's not a thing. That's a title. I'm talking about your class. Your path.
My... path?
Your combat discipline. Most adventurers begin by mastering one of the Four Pillars. The Warrior, the Rogue, the Archer, or the Mage.
From there, one can either perfect their Pillar or walk an Advanced Path by combining two.
So a Mage can become something else?

Correct. A Mage who devotes themselves solely to the arcane arts may become a Wizard, a master of complex, learned magic. Conversely, a Warrior who studies magic can become a holy Paladin. That was Anne's path.
My own class, Arcane Archer, is the fusion of the Archer and Mage Pillars.
And some people are just born with it. They're Sorcerers. Magic in their blood from some long-dead dragon ancestor or whatever. They don't learn it, they just... are.
Wow. So what about you, Eve? You're a Rogue, but you fight more like a Warrior.
A pure Rogue is a backstabber hiding in the dark. Too fragile. I walk the path of the Duelist. It's a fusion of the Warrior's resilience and the Rogue's speed.
I even use a little magic, but not for light shows. Just enough to harden my skin or make my muscles fire faster. It's about ending a fight before the other guy even knows what hit him.
Wizards, Sorcerers, Paladins, Duelists... {player_name} felt a growing sense of unease. He didn't fit into any of these molds.
Which brings us back to you, {player_name}. Your 'Rune Magic' does not seem to be a Pillar, an Advanced Path, or a Sorcerous bloodline. What is its origin?
He was in exile, hiding from his past. But these two were his team. They deserved to know something.
It's... it's a Southern art.
From the Southern Alliance?
Yes. It was developed by the Rune Weaver tribe. I learned the basics from a guard I knew when I was younger.

It's not like your magic. We don't channel power from the world. The spells are pre-woven into runes, and we just... activate them. It requires high intelligence and a certain... compatibility. That's why not many can use it, even in the South.

The North's propaganda painted the Southern Alliance as a horde of savages. But Lyrel knew their military was brutally effective. To learn of a rare and powerful Southern magic from the boy in front of her was a paradigm shift.
Fascinating. A form of prepared, activated magic... The tactical applications are immense.
The Southern Alliance... The Five Tribes. The Rune Weavers are one... The Beastmen are another, aren't they?
Yes. The wolf-kin and the bear-kin are the strongest.
For the first time since he'd met her, {player_name} saw a look of genuine, almost childish wonder in Eve's eyes. It was completely unguarded.
So... you've seen them? The wolf-kin who walk the Warrior's path?
The Werewolves? Uh, yes. I have.
Hmph. In my younger days, I would always dream of being able to do that.
To just... let go. Transform into something else. Something wild and strong that no one could hurt.
Ho ho...
So the stray dog dreams of being a wolf.
Eve's head snapped back towards them, her face flushing a deep, embarrassed red as she realized how much she'd just revealed.
Shut it, elf!
Anyway. Southern magic, Beastmen... you're full of surprises, aren't you?
Great. So you really are in a class of your own. Class: 'Secret Southern Weirdo'.
Hey! Keep your voice down!
And I'm not a weirdo!
Oh, right. Gotta protect your little secret. My mistake, 'Mister Not-From-Around-Here'.
But the name doesn't matter. The path does. So forget the title for a minute, 'Secret Southern Weirdo'...
And tell me what you're going to *do*. You can't just be 'the guy with the cat' forever. You need a focus.
Are you going to learn how to take a hit like a Warrior? Use dirty tricks like a Rogue? Shoot magic from afar like an Archer? Or double down on that rune stuff like a proper Mage?
What path will {player_name} focus on?

options.text: The Warrior's Path. I'll use my runes to fight up close.
The Rogue's Path. I'll use my runes to control the battlefield.
The Archer's Path. I'll use my runes to strike from a distance.
The Mage's Path. I'll embrace my heritage and master my runes.

steps.text: If I'm going to protect people, I need to be able to stand on the front line. I'll focus on the Warrior's path. A Rune Knight.
Heh. A frontline magic-user. Bold. I can work with that.
A sound tactical choice. Your defensive capabilities will be a great asset.
Brute force isn't everything. I'll focus on the Rogue's path. Control the fight before it even begins. A Rune Trickster.
Smart. A battlefield is just a big trap waiting to be sprung. I like the way you think.
An unconventional but potentially devastating choice. Your ability to disable opponents without lethal force will be valuable.
You two are masters of close combat. The party needs someone who can provide cover from afar. I'll focus on the Archer's path. A Rune Caster.
Safe. Practical. Can't argue with it.
An excellent decision. A ranged fighter who can coordinate with a Warden is a powerful combination.
This power is my heritage. I need to understand it, not just imitate other styles. I'll focus on the Mage's path. A true Rune Weaver.
Doubling down on the weird, huh? Ambitious. Don't blow yourself up.
A bold path, and perhaps the most powerful. To master an entirely different school of magic... I will be observing your progress with great interest.
Alright. You've got your goal.
Now, c'mon. Let's go see if Gabe has a quest weird enough to test it.
He wasn't just a boy with a cat anymore. He was a Rune {cyan_path}. And he had work to do.
I swear, if that lopsided mud statue is still in the inn when we get back, I'm using it for target practice.
It was a gift, Eve. Rejecting it would be... culturally insensitive.
The goblins don't have a culture, they have a concussion.
Come on, you two! We've got a goal now! Gabe! We're ready! What have you got for us? Something to test my new path? A B-Rank, maybe?
Settle down, kid. You just got back from a B-Rank that the client stiffed you on, remember? Paying quests don't grow on trees.
I've got something. A solid C-Rank. Good pay, low risk.
A lumber merchant needs an escort to the Stonecreek Quarry and back. Worried about bandits.
Lumber. We're guarding lumber. We have officially peaked as adventurers.
While the task lacks... grandeur, a successful contract is a successful contract. And bandits are a more conventional threat than our recent assignments.
Oh. Bandits.
Gabe... can I ask something?
Shoot.
It's just... all the stories I heard about the North... they were full of heroes fighting Griffons, Manticores, Wyverns... My propaganda was full of it.
We've been here for weeks, and the most dangerous thing we've fought was a mutated rat in a basement.
Where are all the monsters?
Gabe sighed, a deep, weary sound that seemed to carry the weight of the entire guild. He had clearly heard this question before.
You want the official story? The army did its job too well. For the last ten years, they've been running 'pacification campaigns'.
Clearing out nests, securing the trade routes, pushing the big beasts deep into the Dragon's Tooth mountains where they can't bother anyone.
It's a good thing, kid. The North is safer than it's ever been.
Safer just means... boring. Now, are you taking the lumber job or not?
{player_name} looked around the quiet guild hall. It wasn't just boring. It felt... hollow. Like a legend that had been forgotten.
He opened his mouth to reply, but was cut off by a harsh, bitter laugh from a dark corner of the bar.
Safer? Heh. That's a good one.

A man stepped out of the corner. He looked like he was carved from old, scarred wood. One eye was milky white, a long scar cutting through the eyebrow above it. He wore the patched leather of a lifelong adventurer, but he moved with the stiff gait of someone whose fighting days were long behind him.
Don't start, Corvin.
Safer? Heh. Kid, you got sold a nice story, but you're living in the punchline. Let me tell you what 'safer' really means.

It means the Great Guild Hall in the capital—the place where kings used to award medals—had to sell half its building to the Merchant's Collective just to keep the lights on. It means the Adventurer's Academy in Silverpeak, where they trained the best of the best, shut down two years ago for 'lack of enrollment'.
Shut down? But... why?

Why? Because this business doesn't run on protecting lumber. It runs on two things: quest fees from monster hunts, and the monster parts we sell after. The first is a living. The second is a fortune. Both have dried up like a riverbed in a drought.

You want to talk economics? Five years ago, a single Griffon feather was worth twenty silver. Standard reagent for potions of speed. Now, you can't find one for a thousand gold. Alchemists are trying to get the same effect with mountain herbs and bat wings. It's not working.
So... that's why everything is so expensive?

Expensive and shoddy. Blacksmiths are using reinforced leather instead of proper Basilisk hide for armor. Enchanters are using flawed gemstones because they can't get the Manticore eyes they need to focus their spells. You think the army is 'efficient'? They're sending soldiers into battle with gear that would've been considered garbage a decade ago.
It's a resource crisis, kid. A rot, eating the kingdom from the inside out. And it's getting people killed.
Corvin's hand subconsciously went to his milky eye, the gesture full of a pain that had never faded.

My last crew... we went after a Manticore in the foothills. The bounty was a king's ransom, enough to retire on. We were good. A-Rankers, all of us. But our gear failed. The strengthening potions burned instead of healed. My shield, supposedly reinforced with Wyvern scale, shattered like glass when the beast swiped at me.
I was the only one who walked away.
Your equipment failed. This rot you speak of... it seems to be accelerating. And the monsters... you don't believe the army's official explanation?
The army can't kill what they can't find. I've talked to other old-timers, hunters, trackers from the borderlands to the coast. It's the same story everywhere.
The monsters didn't get pushed back. They didn't migrate south for the winter. That's the story they tell children.
They just... vanished. All at once, over the last few years. One season, the plains were teeming with Gorgons. The next? Nothing. Not a single track. It's like the land itself was swept clean.
It's not natural.
Not natural. The words hung in the air, shifting the mystery from an economic problem to a chilling, unnatural event.

{player_name}'s idealistic vision of the North lay in shattered pieces at his feet. Lyrel's sacred mission to investigate an unnatural magical event had just found a potential new, massive lead. And Eve was staring at a man who was a ghost of a future she desperately wanted to avoid.

They had left the guild without a word, the boring lumber quest completely forgotten. Corvin's story hung in the air between them, a dark cloud that had blocked out the sun of {player_name}'s simple worldview.
For a long time, nobody spoke.
We have to do something.
Do what, kid? Declare war on a ghost? You heard him. The monsters are gone. We can't solve a problem that doesn't have a body.

But that's just it! It's not just an economic problem anymore. Corvin's friends died. People are getting weaker, poorer... The North I read about, the one Anne the Hero fought for... it's dying. We can't just... guard lumber while that's happening.

His testimony was... compelling. A mass disappearance of magical fauna on a continental scale, happening 'all at once'. This is not a natural migration. It would require an immense expenditure of magical energy.
Her eyes gleamed with a familiar, obsessive light.
The kind of energy that can warp reality. The kind of energy that can poison a forest.
You think this is connected to your Eldertide incident?

The pattern is similar. A sudden, unnatural event that defies logical explanation. If there is a force capable of making thousands of monsters vanish, it may be the same force I have been hunting. This is a lead I must pursue.

Great. So he's on a crusade to save a dying dream, and you're chasing a ghost from ten years ago. And what about getting paid? What about staying alive? This sounds big, political, and messy. It's everything I came here to escape.
I'm out. You two can go on your wild goose chase. I'm going back to Gabe's to find a job that actually pays the bills.
I take it the 'let's save the world' meeting didn't go your way?
They're kids, Gabe. One's chasing a fairy tale, the other's chasing a nightmare. They're going to get themselves killed.
Maybe. But they're not wrong, Eve. Corvin's not the only one I've heard that story from.
And it's not just the gear. It's the medicine.
The watered-down potions? Old news.

No. Something new. Cheap 'herbal remedies' that have been popping up in the markets. Supposed to be a replacement for monster-based salves. People are saying they don't just 'not work'. They're making people sicker. Old Man Hemlock down at the docks used some on a cut... the fever almost took him.

This was different. A grand conspiracy was an abstraction. A war from her past was a ghost. But sick people? A tangible, immediate problem that had nothing to do with politics and everything to do with a predator preying on the desperate.
It was the kind of small, dirty problem that pricked at the edges of her buried conscience.
Fine.
Tell the kids I'll help them look into the 'bad potions'.
But that's it. No grand crusade. We're just... quality control.
Whatever you say, Eve.
The fire popped. The scent of iron lingered from the fight. Eve sat apart, her leg bent, cleaning a shallow wound with frightening calm.
You’re treating it yourself again?
It’s just a scrape. Don’t bother.
She spoke flatly, eyes on the blade she used to pry out the shard of metal. No flinch. No hesitation.

options.text: Offer to help her bandage it
Respect her space and stay silent

steps.text: At least let me wrap it. You’ll reopen it tomorrow.
You don’t trust me to handle my own body?
I don’t trust anyone who bleeds and calls it fine.
Eve’s eyes lifted — a slow, unreadable look. Then she turned her leg slightly, wordless permission.
Hold still… this might sting.
Tch… careful.
You hide pain too well, you know that?
Pain is just noise. I learned to ignore noise.
The words were simple, but they felt like a wall. Still, she didn’t pull away.
Thank you… I guess.
Guess?
Don’t make me say it twice.
Her tone was dry, but her hand brushed his wrist for a second too long.
Fine. Do it your way.
He leaned back, watching her work — every motion efficient, too practiced for a simple traveler.
(She’s done this too often… too calmly.)
The fire cracked. Anne stirred beside her, curling around Eve’s boots as if guarding her from the world.
What?
Nothing. Just… you’re scaring the cat.
The cat’s smarter than most people.
She finished tying the bandage, perfectly tight. Not a sound of pain escaped her lips.
The night settled again. Lyrel was asleep. Only embers and breath filled the silence.
You should rest. I’ll keep watch.
You always do.
She didn’t answer.
You’re too kind for this world, {player_name}.
And you’re too numb for it.
Eve’s lips twitched — almost a smile.
Gabe’s guild was as noisy as always — tankards clinking, rookies bragging, and someone crying over a failed slime hunt.
Ah, the hero squad returns! No broken bones, no missing limbs — that’s a record for you three.
We were hunting goblins, not dragons.
Still, with you around, Eve, I half-expected the whole forest to disappear.
I told you that fire wasn’t—
—your fault, sure, sure. It just *mysteriously combusted* the moment you sneezed, right, Helmet Hair?
Watch it, Tree Hugger, or I’ll start a campfire with your hair next time.
You two sound more married than teammates.
Don’t tempt fate, {player_name}. The betting pool’s still open for who snaps first.
Put me down for Eve. She looks five seconds away from homicide.
Make it three.
Gabe laughed, slapping a parchment onto the counter.
Alright, before someone gets stabbed — got a new job for you. Simple recon mission. Weird mana readings near the Vaelwood perimeter.
Vaelwood? That’s the forest the Northern army sealed after the war, right?
Mhm. Some researcher wants it surveyed. Says the energy’s been ‘reactivating’ lately.
He slid the quest form toward {player_name}. Eve’s eyes flicked to the top of the page.
"Survey of Abnormal Mana Readings in the Vaelwood Perimeter." Fancy title, huh?
The client is... eccentric. Some recluse from the capital using a proxy. He just calls himself 'The Curator.'
Insisted the logs found at the site were the real prize. Said they were tied to an old R&D project. Lazarus, or something.
Eve’s hand froze mid-reach. Just a twitch — so small most would’ve missed it.
You okay?
…Fine. Just bad handwriting.
‘Lazarus’? Sounds like another human word for ‘play god and ruin everything.’
You’re not wrong.
It pays triple the rate, and the client asked specifically for a discreet, high-skill party. That’s you guys.
Since when do you accept jobs that shady, Gabe?
Since rent’s due and my best assassin turned innkeeper keeps drinking my liquor instead of paying tab.
I could just stop coming altogether.
Don’t you dare, I’d lose half my entertainment.
Eve sighed, rubbing her temple. {player_name} could tell something about this mission bothered her, but she didn’t push it.
Alright. We’ll take the job.
Gabe nodded, his grin fading slightly as he looked at Eve.
Hey. If that place really is as bad as the rumors say… you sure you’re up for it?
I’m not the one you should worry about.
Her tone was calm — too calm. The kind of calm that sounded practiced.
Out back, a man in worn Northern armor left through the side door, a faint smirk tugging at his lips.
Let’s see if you’re still my Commander, Eve.
The Vaelwood road smelled of damp wood and old iron. The day's light filtered like gauze through the trees.
Gabe made it sound like a simple recover-and-escort. Research cargo, a strained parchment, and some dusty logs.
Logs from Project Lazarus. That's the name I keep hearing. Dangerous work, if the old files are true.
It was never 'just paperwork' when it came to those projects.
Anne sat on {player_name}’s shoulder, ears twitching. When the group moved, she kept watch — alert and oddly tense.
They rounded a broken stone checkpoint where rusted pikes still leaned like accusing fingers. Scattered around were torn crates and a toppled cart.
These crates look recent. Not decades-old at all.
Any markings?
{player_name} crouched and wiped grime from a crate stamp. A black sigil stared back — the Revenant Division mark, half-obliterated by rust.
Revenant Division... these crates are stamped with their emblem. And — wait — there's a transport manifest.
"Transport Log — Project Lazarus — Container #A3-9. Authorized: Northern R&D."
The name hit Eve like a hard thing. She didn't move; the world seemed to blur at the edges.
That's not supposed to be here.
You know these marks?
You don't want to know. Pack light.
Figures stepped from the treeline — scavengers in mismatched armor, faces braided with zealotry. One of them tossed a small, black canister onto the path and kicked it toward them.
For the Revenant! Purge the trespassers!
The canister spun, hummed, and a high, thin tone filled the clearing — not a sound but a memory, like a chorus of distant screams.
For a dizzying second the trees burned and voices braided into one: orders, laughter, a woman crying a name. Eve staggered, eyes wide as the past superimposed itself on the present.
A woman's laugh, bright and clear, twisting into static.
The smell of ozone and burning flesh. A sterile lab in flames.
A hand slipping from her grasp. A voice calling her name, drowned out by the roar.
Something bit into Eve’s thigh — a shard from the canister. She cursed, dropping to one knee, hand clamped at the wound.
…agh—
Lyrel rallied a web of mana, and {player_name} shoved a scavenger away. The attackers, startled by how their device worked, faltered and scattered.
Smoke and ringing filled the air. Eve sat, breathing hard, the wound bleeding but not critical. Her hands shook as if from cold.
Eve—you're hurt!
It's fine. Flesh wound.
She tore a strip from her cloak, poured a vial of cheap spirit over the shrapnel cut, and hissed between her teeth. The smell of burnt fabric and blood mingled as she pressed the cloth down.
‘Fine’? That’s half your leg bleeding, Helmet Hair.
I’ve had worse. Keep your herbs for someone who’ll use them.
{player_name} tried to help, but Eve brushed their hand away, tightening the makeshift bandage with a grimace.
We move once I can stand.
Her tone left no room for argument. The others exchanged uneasy looks but obeyed, scanning the battlefield for clues while Eve silently steadied her breath.
"Manifest: Transport Logs recovered from Vaelwood Transit — transfer authorized by Revenant Field Ops."

Lyrel’s voice was small. The pieces fit together like a cruel puzzle — Project Lazarus cargo being moved along Revenant supply lines. Either remnants were still active, or someone wanted it to look that way.
Burn it.
Burn— Eve, we can't just—
I said burn them. Now.
Eve seized the nearest loose sheet and shoved it into a brazier, striking a flint. The paper curled and blackened, the letters going up in angry smoke.
Eve—what are you doing?
These are research logs! Evidence! What gives you the right to destroy them?!
The right of someone who knows what happens when this kind of evidence sees the light of day.
That's not your call to make, Helmet Hair! We bring it back, we report it. That's the law. That's how justice works.
Justice has nothing to do with this. This is about burying a corpse so it can't be turned into a monster.
We're leaving. Now.
You were here before, weren't you?
Once.
What happened?
Nothing worth remembering.
Eve moved to the edge of the ruins, Anne padding to her side and curling at her boot. The cat’s purr was a quiet anchor.
I made sure it would never happen again.
They set a small camp near the ruined outpost. The fire’s glow made everything look older and smaller. {player_name} sat closer than before, thinking about the way 'Lazarus' had made Eve flinch.
The clearing smelled of ash and metal. The bandits were gone, their insignias charred beyond recognition.
{player_name} tightened the last of Eve’s bandages. Her thigh wound still oozed faintly, but the bleeding had stopped.
That should hold. You’ll be limping for a few days, though.
I’ve had worse.
You also just burned our entire paycheck.
You’re welcome. Those papers were poison.
Lyrel crossed her arms, but {player_name} caught the tremor in Eve’s hands — the same one she’d been hiding since the fight.
Whatever that was, it’s over now. We’ll report what we found and head back.
Good. The less anyone knows about 'Lazarus', the better.
Anne let out a small chirp from {player_name}’s shoulder — soft, questioning.
Eve glanced up, guilt flickering behind her calm mask. She didn’t answer.
Then, without warning, Anne leapt from {player_name}’s shoulder and dashed into the fog.
Oh, great. The furball’s gone feral again.
Anne! Wait—
The cat didn’t stop. Her tail bristled, ears flat, sprinting deeper into Vaelwood’s shadows.
Eve cursed under her breath and followed limping. The others ran after her.
They pushed through thick mist and dead roots until Anne stopped at what looked like a collapsed ridge.
The ground there pulsed faintly with mana, humming like a buried heart.
Hold up. You feel that? The energy readings here are... fresh.
A mana reactor underground?
...No reactor. A containment site.
Her tone dropped, low and cold. She stepped closer, brushing aside the roots until her fingers touched iron — an old service hatch half-buried beneath moss.
Eve's voice dropped to a barely audible whisper.
I sealed this place. I watched it burn.
You’ve been here before.

options.text: We have to know what's down there.
If you say we should leave, we leave.

steps.text: If something is active, we can't just walk away. It's our job to investigate.
Eve's jaw tightened. It was a clear rejection of her warning.
Your 'job' doesn't cover poking through old graves.
Then we should leave it sealed. I trust your judgment, Eve.
A flicker of surprise—or perhaps relief—crossed Eve's face before it was hidden.
Are you serious, {player_name}? After all this? We can't just turn back!
And Eve is saying it's a mistake. That's good enough for me.
I said we shouldn’t be here.
Then why does this cat look ready to claw her way through solid steel?
Anne scratched at the hatch, tail lashing, eyes glowing faintly in the dark.
A faint spark of magic rippled from her paw — the same blink energy she used to protect {player_name}.
Anne... what are you trying to show us?
The ground vibrated softly. Something deep below responded — an echo from the dark.
Enough. We’re leaving. Now.
{player_name}—
If someone’s still down there, we can’t just walk away.
You don’t understand what that place is.
Then maybe it’s time you explain it, Helmet Hair.
Later.
Eve’s voice cracked faintly on that word. Even Anne hesitated — ears twitching, eyes on the hatch.
Then {player_name} knelt beside it and pressed their hand to the cold metal.
There’s a way down.
Eve exhaled sharply, resignation cutting through her calm.
Stop. Whatever it is — we don't need to go digging.
You sure? Those readings are… odd. Fresh mana, too.
Lyrel crouched and brushed moss aside, revealing scorch marks that were newer than the rest — and a faint overlay of a sealing glyph that hummed with residual energy.
These burn marks… they're recent. And this glyph — it's an overlay, more modern than the old Northern work. Someone topped up the seals not too long ago.
So it's not dead then.
Eve listened like someone being told their wound had reopened.
If someone tampered with it, I’ll make sure it’s closed. But we're not looting curiosity.
Deal.
With a hiss of rust and mana, the hatch creaked open, revealing a staircase descending into faint blue light.
The air was thick, sterile — reeking of dust, iron, and memories Eve wished she’d buried.
Anne stepped forward first, tail raised, vanishing into the dark.
Guess that’s our cue.
You’d better pray she’s wrong about this place.
The party descended — unaware that the shadows below were already stirring.
The stairs opened into a wide, ruined atrium. Pipes hung like broken ribs, and frost traced the edges of long-dead consoles. Somewhere under the dust a faint hum pulsed like a heartbeat.
This place still holds energy. Not full power — but someone fed it recently.
So somebody didn't forget this place like it was supposed to be forgotten.
They moved among ruined desks and shattered containers. Lyrel's hand brushed the corner of a scorched binder wedged beneath a console.
Field notes — 'Phase two reclamation. Transfer manifest…'
{player_name} peered over. The manifest listed container IDs, dates, and destinations — and one line in particular snagged at him.
"Transfer record: Subject A. Lysandria — transferred to Vaelwood Relay — Received by: Unknown. Authorization signature: (redacted)."
Lysandria? Wait—Anne the Hero? Why is she on a transfer record?
Lyrel lifted a corroded hatch and peered into a maintenance conduit. A strip of clean metal — fingerprints recent, a sealing glyph overlay — glowed faintly.
Someone reopened a transfer channel not long ago. Whoever moved Subject A didn't use the old route. They moved her to somewhere else — perhaps this relay.
They followed the corridor until the stone widened into a cavernous hall. The air was colder here, as if the earth itself kept its breath.
These runes… they’re old, but not the kind found in any archive I’ve read. Someone blended sigilcraft with mechanical thinking.
Looks like something someone wanted forgotten.
It was. I made sure parts of it were.
Her voice carried an edge {player_name} had rarely heard — not anger, but the weight of a promise kept in darkness.

Pillars of veined crystal stood around the chamber; within the hollows of some, glass-like cylinders drooped with slow, inner light. Frost clung to cracked seals and ancient lacquered plates lay half-buried in dust.
Anne padded forward from {player_name}’s shoulder and nosed at a seam in the floor — her tail twitching like a compass.
We don’t need to go down there. Whatever this was — I burned the essentials. I left nothing useful.
Then why is the place humming? Why did the air change the moment we stepped in?
Someone's been here more recently than you remember. If there’s a pulse, we should know what it is.
Eve didn’t answer at once. Her hands curled at her sides, knuckles white.
A carved panel at the far end flared — runes shifting like written breath. A line of light coalesced into letters: Incoming Transmission — and a voice threaded through the hall.
Commander. How nice of you to come see what you thought you buried.
Roland.
The name landed like a stone. No one here knew the Revenant Division's history except a few old ghosts.
You should be dead.
So should you, perhaps — but here we both stand. Funny, isn't it?
But fear not I’m alive, yes. Present, not quite. I prefer working through arrangements.  The guild’s little breadcrumb trail was… efficient.
You set them on us. You dragged me back.
I arranged a door and left it unlocked. You opened it. That’s your choice, as always.
Burned...? What is he talking about?
Eve, who is this man?
Eve said nothing. Her eyes stayed fixed on the projection, every line of her body locked in ice.
Hello. My name is Roland Veyra. Once vice-commander of the Revenant Division — the unit Eve herself led into the dark.
We didn’t stumble on anything. We were led here—by chance, by her injuries, by—
By design. Everything circles back to her, sooner or later.
Enough riddles. Speak clearly.
Clarity is cruel, kid. You wouldn’t want it. Not yet.
If you came here to gloat, you’ve done it. Now vanish.
Still giving orders. I missed that tone.
You taught us how to end things cleanly. I simply wanted to show you what refuses to end.  Call it test, call it mercy — either way, it will reveal what you truly are.
Stop talking like you know my heart.
I don’t know your heart — I know your hands. They remember what to do.
As his image vanished with a crackle of static, a final door at the end of the hall slid open with a soft, clinical sigh.
The chamber beyond was circular and sterile. At its center stood a single, frost-rimmed stasis tube. A tiny monitor beside it rhythmically beeped, tracking a fragile life sign.
Vital stabilization: intermittent. Neural signature present... Subject A. Lysandria...
The Hero…
Inside floated a pale human form, her face horribly young. The hero from the songs.
Eve’s face changed as if the world had folded inward. She didn’t speak. The breath left her like a confession.
I burned it. I burned it with my own hands. I made sure—
Her practiced calm shattered into a thousand pieces. Grief, guilt, and a fresh, terrifying fury warred in her eyes as she stared at the ghost she had failed to put to rest.
The chamber hummed faintly, indifferent to sorrow.
Silence. The only sound was the soft, rhythmic beep of the life support and the blood pounding in {player_name}'s ears.
Eve was still on her knees, her reflection trembling on the frost-coated glass beside Anne's serene face.
It can't be... 'Declared martyred at Lorthen's Gate.' Every history book says so.
But it is. That's her.
…Anne.
A flicker of memory—a smile through smoke, a hand slipping away. Then the present rushed back like a blast of cold air.
Eve? You knew her?
I buried her.
A figure stepped from the darkness — robes tattered, eyes bright with tired conviction.
Please… lower your blades. Her sleep is fragile.
Who are you?
I am merely a caretaker. She has been sleeping peacefully for a long time. You need not disturb her.
Peacefully? This is necromancy. A perversion.
No. It is devotion. The Saint deserves rest until the world is worthy of her return.
Saint? Is that what the North is calling her now?
You speak her name as if you knew her. As an equal.
Eve pushed herself to her feet, her voice cracking under the weight of memory.
She fought beside me. And Gabe. She was my friend. She believed the world could still be kind.
But... you said you buried her…
I did. I made sure she could rest.
Then your efforts were in vain, child. The North wouldn't let their savior rest. When your fire was extinguished, they came to collect what was left.
They hired you? You worked for them on 'Project Lazarus'?
I was the lead researcher on the original project. She... she saved my village during the Lorthen campaign. I owed her a debt that could never be repaid.
When they came to me, proposing to... continue the work, I saw my chance. I took their funding. I used their labs.
You took their blood money to continue their defilement.
I took their resources to protect her! They saw a weapon; I saw a soul to be preserved.
I delayed their progress with false reports and fabricated data for years.
I told them the vessel was too unstable, that the spirit was gone, all while I worked to keep her safe here, hidden away.
I am not their pawn. I am her shepherd, using the wolf's own den to guard the lamb.
