She's not a lamb, she's a person! And this is still a cage, no matter how much faith you wrap it in.
Faith is what keeps a soul alive when the body cannot! And it is my faith that has kept her pure, away from their generals and their battle plans!
By keeping her here? Like a relic in a tomb?
I kept her *pure*. The Northern generals sought to make her a weapon. I rescued the vessel and brought her here, to keep her soul safe until her purpose could be reclaimed by a world at peace.
That's still defilement, whatever faith you wrap it in.
Faith is what keeps a soul alive when the body cannot. Tell me, elf—is that defilement, or is it hope?
Eve took a step closer to the cylinder, her hand rising to touch the cold glass.
Anne...
Their voices clashed quietly, echoing through the chamber’s hollow hum.
She moved—!
Do not fear. It is her spirit remembering warmth. Nothing more.
No… she’s reacting to me.
Corin stepped forward, his expression torn between awe and fear.
Whatever binds her spirit to this vessel is fragile.
Fade? You mean die again.
And who decided that? You?
Rest… That’s all she ever wanted.
Then let her have it. Go. Don’t wake her before her time.
Eve said nothing, but her jaw clenched — torn between guilt and the echo of old duty.
Somewhere deep within the crystal, something stirred — or dreamed.
They retreated to a small alcove outside the chamber. Corin's voice — a prayer, pleading — had followed them, asking them to leave Anne to her sleep.
Eve — you have to tell us. What did you mean before when you said you 'buried' her?
{player_name}'s voice was steadier than his hands. Lyrel's eyes were flames.
You told us to burn the logs, to forget Lazarus — but you didn't tell us about this. You kept this secret.
Eve remains silent a beat, then closes her eyes as if drawing a wound inward.
You were... part of them? You led a covert unit?
I led the shadows that erased other people's sins. We were called when the kingdom needed someone to make terrible decisions.
She tried to make it small — three images, sharp as knives: Anne smiling through rain, the teleportation failing like a storm swallow, Eve carrying something that had been broken.
Anne was my friend. Gabe's fiancee. She was light.
During the war, the North got desperate. They attempted a mass-teleportation of the Seventh Battalion to break the Lorthen stalemate.
The words hit Lyrel like a physical blow. The Seventh Battalion. The Lorthen campaign. She knew this story. This was the military operation that had bled into the Eldertide.
This was it. The event she had spent years chasing. Her mind raced, but she forced herself to remain still, to listen.
The portal... it collapsed. The official report called it a 'catastrophic mana inversion.' It didn't just kill them. It... changed them. She was declared dead on site.
But it was worse than that. She wasn't just hurt. She was used.
Lyrel's voice was quiet, dangerously steady. She was no longer just a friend listening; she was an investigator who had just found her key witness.
What do you mean... 'used'?
They wanted to fix their mistake. The northern labs wanted to patch their broken weapon and call it a miracle.
They were going to turn her body into a stabilizer. A living anchor to channel their teleportation magic. I learned that after… after the mission.
To turn a hero's body into a tool for the very magic that killed her... That's not just a crime. It's sacrilege.
So you found out what they would do to her — and you burned the lab.
I burned what I could. I destroyed the tools and the orders. I left nothing for them to salvage. I made sure no one would take her name and make it an order again.
So you decided life or death for her? You played judge over life and death, Eve.
Her words landed like iron. Eve's eyes skimmed past Lyrel to the sealed chamber where Anne slept.
It wasn't judgment. It was mercy. I couldn't let them make her into that. She begged me to let her rest.
The memory hurt in the soft places — Eve kneeling in smoke, Anne's hand slack in her palm, the world reduced to an ember and a promise.
You did what you thought was right back then. But now — now that her body is here and someone kept it — destroying it again won't undo the past.
No. It won't. But leaving it will let others play god with her name.
Eve — you can't be the arbiter of all that. Mercy or murder, it's not for one person to decree.
{player_name} steps closer, eyes searching hers.
We need to— we need to think. There might be another way. Burning everything won't heal you. It won't bring her peace for sure.
When I burned it, I thought I was putting a body to rest. I thought I had stopped the machine from using her. I told myself she could be buried in peace.
Her fingers found the hilt of her old blade, thumb tracing the worn edge as if it might remind her which self to be.
But if someone else keeps her alive, what then? If they wake her and she becomes something else — I can't let that happen. And yet... the thought of ending her again—
I don't know. I don't know which sin is smaller.
That's not an answer.
You don't have to decide now. But we need a plan — not just an oath to burn.
Eve's face was a map of old scars and fresh doubt. Her eyes flicked to the sealed glass once more, then to her hands.
I swore to end what tied her to that fate. I still believe that. But I won't throw myself into blind fury.
I am torn — half of me wants the fire to finish what it began. Half of me... wants to see if she can somehow be herself again.
The words hung between them like smoke. No resolution. No final verdict. Only a promise of hard choices to come.
Silence pressed down like old vows. Anne's crystal cylinder pulsed faintly. Dust motes moved in slow eddies. Eve's fingers flexed as if around an old wound.
You linger beautifully in the dark. But sentiment doesn't stop logistics.
I thought you'd appreciate haste. A retrieval party moves tonight — northern battleguard tasked to recover the vessel before anyone can destroy it.
The words landed like an order. Corin's face drained; Eve's jaw tightened.
I did. Consider it a precaution. If someone intends to burn what history covets, better to secure the asset first.
You forget how the world values a hero's body, Commander.
Something in Eve snapped like a brittle hinge. For a heartbeat she looked very old and very dangerous.
No. If they take her, they'll butcher her into an order. I won't let the north make a saint into a sword.
I'll end it. I will burn it all down again.
No! You cannot— You don't understand what it means for her—! I will not let you destroy what I kept.
Corin slammed both palms on a rune-altar. He chanted jagged syllables, hands trembling with fear and prayer.
Awake! Guardians of the ward — obey the keeper's oath!
Two hulking golems shifted from the gloom — iron-veined stone and crystal, runes along their joints flaring amber. They stepped between Eve and the cylinder, slow and absolute.
Please — leave. Take the child and go. I've kept her safe until now. I won't let her be taken or burned.
Eve — think. If you destroy this, you'll be doing the same thing you swore you'd never be.
Tch, what about you? You support this necromancy, Tree-Hugger?
All life should be preserved. ALL of it — even what you think should die.
Fine.
That single word was a declaration. The room tightened like a fist. The golems shifted, their runic eyes glowing amber. But Eve moved first.
She wasn't a warrior charging; she was a shadow flowing, her target not the party, but the golems' power source.
I won't let you!
Lyrel slammed her hand on the ground, and a barrier of thick, thorny roots erupted from the stone floor, blocking Eve's path.
Eve didn't even slow down. She used the new wall as a ramp, running horizontally for three steps before launching herself over the barrier, daggers flashing.
She's too fast!
{player_name} knew he couldn't match her speed. He needed information. He cast his unique spell.
He used Rivirä. The world dissolved into a sea of energy signatures. He saw Eve, a burning pinpoint of focused intent. He saw Lyrel, a steady green font of life. And he saw the golems...
They weren't independent. Their energy flowed from the same source as the stasis tube, a complex, interconnected circuit. They weren't just guardians; they were part of the life support.
EVE, STOP! THEY'RE LINKED TO HER LIFE SUPPORT! If you destroy them, the feedback surge could kill her!
For a fraction of a second, Eve faltered mid-air. The warning had registered. But her eyes flicked to the stasis tube, and her face hardened with grim resolve.
It's a kinder death than what the North has planned for her!
Eve landed and lunged for the left golem. Lyrel, unable to create another wall in time, loosed an arrow.
Not an arrow of death, but of binding. A shimmering green cord of energy trailed from it, aimed to ensnare Eve's wrist.
Eve parried it with her dagger, the magical energy dissipating with a sharp hiss. The deflection cost her a precious second, and the golem swung a massive crystal fist.
{player_name} saw his opening. While Eve was occupied, he slammed his palms to the floor.
Ligära!
A binding rune flared to life on the floor directly in Eve's path, spectral chains erupting to snare her ankles.

Eve, forced to choose between dodging the golem's fist and getting caught in the trap, twisted her body with impossible grace. The golem's fist grazed her shoulder, sending a shower of sparks from her armor, but she landed clear of {player_name}'s rune.
She was panting now, a flicker of frustration in her eyes. They couldn't beat her, but they could *hinder* her. And time was running out.
Seeing she couldn't get a clean shot at the golem's core, she changed tactics. She wasn't a brawler. She was an assassin.
With a sharp cry, she hurled one of her daggers not at the golem, but at a secondary power conduit on the wall.
The conduit exploded in a blinding shower of sparks, plunging their side of the room into momentary darkness and chaos. Lyrel and {player_name} instinctively flinched, shielding their eyes.
In that single, vital second of distraction, Eve moved.

She wasn't aiming for the golem's glowing core. She slipped past its guard and drove the tip of her remaining dagger into a tiny, almost invisible seam where the runic lines connected to its primary joint.
She didn't shatter it. She severed the connection.
The left golem's amber eyes flickered and died. It froze mid-swing, then sagged, becoming a lifeless statue of stone and crystal.
Lyrel's voice broke with a mix of fury and betrayal.
You said you'd stop the killing, but you turn into the thing that kills to stop it! How is this mercy?!
Eve panted, clutching her bleeding shoulder, but her voice was cold iron.
This is prevention. I will not let them make her a tool.
Roland's holographic form flickered back into existence. His previous calm was gone, replaced by a rapturous, almost unholy glee. His eyes were wide, his smile ecstatic.
Yes... YES! That's it! Perfection!
His voice was breathless, filled with the fervor of a worshipper witnessing a divine act.
Not brute force. Not blind rage. A prayer in steel. The divine efficiency that only you possess!
There she is! My goddess! The one who ends things so nothing worse can be born!
He leaned forward, his projection glowing brighter, his voice dropping to an intense, urgent whisper.
You've silenced the guardians. The path is clear. Now... complete the ritual. Finish your masterpiece.
Grant the hero your final, perfect mercy.
His words hung in the air, not as a suggestion, but as a zealot's blessing, urging her on.
His smile was a fine blade, watching, waiting, completely enthralled by the destruction he had set in motion.
The chamber's old wards trembled under the strain of fractured runes. Dust rained. Corin sank to his knees, hands pressed to the shattered stone of his guardian.
Why did you do it, Eve? Why now?
Because if they take her, they will not honor her. They will make her do things she would never choose.
And you decided that's your verdict? You decided to be judge and executioner?
No one had an answer. The chamber held only the echo of breaking and the thin, stubborn light from the surviving rune-plates.
The choice had been made in blood and stone. Above them, sirens wailed — or perhaps only fate answered. In the dark, every friend looked like a potential enemy.
Silence pressed down like old vows. Anne's crystal cylinder pulsed faintly. Dust motes moved in slow eddies. Eve's fingers flexed as if around an old wound.
You linger beautifully in the dark. But sentiment doesn't stop logistics.
I thought you'd appreciate haste. A retrieval party moves tonight — northern battleguard tasked to recover the vessel before anyone can destroy it.
The words landed like an order. Eve's jaw tightened.
You called them? You brought the army here?
I did. Consider it a precaution. If someone intends to burn what history covets, better to secure the asset first.
You forget how the world values a hero's body, Eve.
Something in Eve snapped like a brittle hinge. For a heartbeat she looked very old and very dangerous.
No. If they take her, they'll butcher her into an order. I won't let the north make a saint into a sword.
I'll end it. I will burn it all down again.
Eve — think. If you destroy this, you'll be doing the same thing you swore you'd never be.
Tch, what about you? You support necromancy, tree-hugger??
All life should be preserved. ALL of it — even what you think should die.
Words ended. The room tightened like a fist. Eve moved — fast as a blade-spark, a shadow with intent.
Don't make this choice alone.
{player_name} lunged, trying to hold her back. For a second his fingers closed around her wrist, a plea more than a grip.
I won't let them butcher her name.
Eve slipped beneath a swinging crystal limb with practiced precision. She struck the first rune-node — a seam of light that powered its ward.
The seam fractured. Sparks hissed.
Cyan — hit the runeforger while I hold it!
Eve found the core seam and drove her blade home with surgical force. The left golem sagged, stone grinding, then collapsed in a heap of dust and broken rune.
You said you'd stop the killing, but you turn into the thing that kills to stop it. How is this mercy?
This is prevention. I will not let them make her a tool.
So swift. So clean. There she is — the woman who ends things so nothing worse can be born.
You chose. You acted. That choice will echo. I only nudged the world to see what you would do.
His smile was a fine blade. He watched as the chamber filled with dust and the taste of iron.
The chamber's old wards trembled under the strain of fractured runes. Dust rained.
Why did you do it, Eve? Why now?
Because if they take her, they will not honor her. They will make her do things she would never choose.
And you decided that's your verdict? You decided to be judge and executioner?
No one had an answer. The chamber held only the echo of breaking and the thin, stubborn light from the surviving rune-plates.
The choice had been made in blood and stone. Above them, sirens wailed — or perhaps only fate answered. In the dark, every friend looked like a potential enemy.
The dust settled into a heavy shroud. The air tasted of ozone and broken stone.
Corin wept quietly over the remains of his guardians, his faith shattered into a thousand pieces.
But Eve's eyes were fixed on the stasis cylinder. Not with grief, but with the cold clarity of a mission nearing its end.
You... you didn't even hesitate.
You destroy everything that stands in your way. You burn labs, you shatter ancient guardians...
How is this any different from the orders you used to follow for the North?
Answer me, Eve! You've become the same monster you swore you'd escape.
That's not fair, Lyrel. She's trying to stop them from—
By becoming them? That's not justice, it's just another form of tyranny!
Eve, please. Listen to me. Just for a second.
This isn't about saving Anne from them. Not anymore.
This is about saving yourself from your guilt.
His words hung in the air, sharp and true.
Don't let the last thing you do for her be taking away her choice. Just like they did.
Choice...
She let out a breath that sounded like grinding glass.
You don't know what they planned. 'Project Lazarus' wasn't about bringing a hero back.
It was about creating a... a vessel. A living conduit for the souls of the soldiers lost in the Eldertide.
A puppet that would wear her face and answer their commands, fueled by a thousand screaming ghosts. That's the 'miracle' they wanted.
I held her hand as the light left her eyes. She made me promise.
'Don't let them make me a monster, Eve. Promise me.'
Her gaze returned to the cylinder, her resolve hardening again.
This isn't murder. It's keeping that promise. It's the only mercy she has left.
A touching debate, full of fire and conviction. But your time is running out.
I can hear their boots on the stone above. The Northern retrieval squad is here.
Make your choice, Commander. Before they make it for you.
The arguments fell away. The accusations, the pleas... they were just noise in the face of an oath.
Only the promise remained. Her hand reached for the cylinder's emergency purge console.
The final choice was hers. And yours.
Eve’s hand hovered over the purge console. The hum of the stasis cylinder was the only sound besides the frantic beating of {player_name}'s heart.
This was it. The moment where words failed. What {player_name} did next wouldn't just decide Anne's fate. It would decide who they were.
Anne the cat pressed herself against the cold glass of the cylinder, letting out a soft, mournful cry. A plea that transcended language.
{player_name}'s thoughts raced. Could he trust Eve's broken promise... or Lyrel's desperate hope?

options.text: Side with Eve. Help her keep her promise.
Side with Lyrel. Stop Eve at any cost.

steps.text: {player_name} drew his short sword. Not with conviction, but with a grim sense of finality. He moved to stand beside Eve.
I'm with you, Eve.
{player_name}... no. Not you, too.
You'd stand by and watch this happen? You'd help her?
It's the only way to be sure she's free.
Then I'll stop you both. Her soul deserves better than a pyre built on guilt.
The fight was brutal and short. A tragedy in three heartbeats.
Before Lyrel could even draw her bowstring, Eve was a blur of motion. There was a sharp clang, and Lyrel's bow flew from her hands.
Ligära!
{player_name} slammed his palm to the floor, and a binding rune flared to life, snaring Lyrel's ankles in cords of mana. She stumbled, falling to one knee.
This is a sin... Both of you... remember that.
Eve gave {player_name} a single, grim nod. There was no victory in it. Only a shared burden.
She turned back to the console, her path now clear.
{player_name} lunged forward, grabbing Eve's wrist just as her fingers made contact with the console.
Eve, no! I won't let you!
Let go of me, {player_name}.
This is not your promise to keep. Get out of my way.
Listen to him, Eve! Don't do this!
She tried to pull her arm free. When {player_name} held on, she moved.
Her other hand blurred, and the flat of her dagger slammed into {player_name}'s side. The blow sent him staggering back, gasping for air.
She was an S-rank assassin. He was nothing. A fly buzzing in the path of a storm.
Stay down. This is your only warning.
She turned back to the console, but {player_name} pushed himself up again, positioning his body between her and the controls.
You'll... have to go through me.
So be it.
She lunged, not with a dagger this time, but with a precise strike aimed at the nerve cluster in {player_name}'s neck. It was over.
Then, in that split-second before everything went dark, Anne the cat leapt from the floor onto {player_name}'s shoulder.
A blinding flash of cerulean light erupted from her, enveloping all of them. The sterile air of the lab was replaced by the smell of damp earth and pine.
They were outside, dozens of yards from the hidden entrance, thrown onto the forest floor. The world spun.
Behind them, the low hum of the Northern retrieval team's vehicles grew louder. They had the facility. And everything in it.
What... have you DONE?!
Her fury was a physical force, but they were beyond her reach now. The choice had been made for her.
{player_name} had saved her from committing a sin, but in doing so, had handed the North their miracle.
With Lyrel bound and the path clear, a chilling stillness fell over the chamber. Eve approached the console, her movements precise, devoid of hesitation.
This wasn't an act of passion. It was an execution.
Her fingers moved across the runic interface, inputting a sequence. The main screen flashed with crimson text: OVERLOAD PROTOCOL: FINAL CESSATION.
Fire can be survived. Ash can be gathered.
This time... I leave nothing behind.
Ah... there she is.
Not the hesitant wanderer. Not the jaded mercenary.
The Goddess of Death, returned to her throne! The one who makes the clean, hard choice that saves the rest of us from doubt!
His projection flickered, but his voice was ecstatic, like a zealot witnessing a miracle.
So beautiful... So perfect. You haven't lost your touch, Commander.
As Eve confirmed the command, a pained, high-pitched cry tore through the air.
Anne the cat suddenly arched her back, a faint blue light flickering around her. She shuddered violently, seizing on the cold stone floor.
Anne!
The cat collapsed, the knowing light in its eyes extinguished forever. A small, vital piece of the world had just vanished.
The stasis cylinder didn't explode. It filled with a silent, blinding white light. The hum intensified until it was the only thing in existence.
Through the glare, Anne Lysandria's form unraveled, dissolving into motes of pure energy until there was nothing left but light.
Critical failure alarms blared. The chamber groaned, and cracks spiderwebbed across the ceiling. The mana holding Lyrel's bonds flickered and died.
They're coming... let them find nothing but dust and echoes. A masterpiece of an ending! Until we meet again, my goddess.
Lyrel rose to her feet, staring at Eve with profound pity.
You did it. You killed hope itself. I hope the peace you've bought was worth the price.
Without another word, she turned and walked into the crumbling corridors, vanishing from their lives.
Eve! The whole place is coming down! We have to go!
Eve stood frozen, her mission complete. Her face a blank mask. {player_name} grabbed her arm, pulling her towards the exit as the world came crashing down around them.
They emerged into the cold light of dawn. The Northern soldiers were gone, having arrived to find only a collapsing ruin.
Eve sank to her knees amidst the rubble, her hands coated in dust.
It's over.
I saved her... didn't I?
{player_name} looked at the empty sky, at his mentor who had just erased a soul from the world. Roland's joyful praise echoed in his mind. He had no answer.
The rising sun felt cold.

Weeks passed. The Northern Kingdom, its secret weapon erased and its research buried, fell into political disarray. The threat of war subsided, replaced by a fragile peace born not of victory, but of exhaustion.
On a windswept cliff overlooking the sea near Porthumming, a new memorial stone had been placed.
Two simple, hand-carved wooden markers stood before it, placed in the soft earth.
One read: In Memory of Anne Lysandria. Beloved Hero. At Rest.
The other, smaller marker simply said: And for Anne. A Loyal Friend.
Gabe placed a small, wild sea-daisy at the base of the stone, his shoulders slumped with a grief that had finally found its place.
Funny, isn't it?
A few days after the North sent word... that she was gone... I found this tiny, half-starved kitten huddled by the docks.
I was so lost. I took her in. I... I named her Anne. It felt right. A way to keep her memory close.
He let out a long, weary sigh.
She lived with me for years. Never thought I'd lose them both on the same day.
But they're at peace now. Together, somewhere. You did right by them, Eve.
Eve said nothing. She just stared out at the endless grey ocean. She had kept her promise. She had saved her friend from a fate worse than death.
But in keeping that one, final promise, she had sacrificed every piece of herself she had started to reclaim.
The Eve who had begun to trust and feel was gone—buried alongside her friend. The person she was becoming had vanished, replaced by the familiar ghost of the soldier {player_name} first met.
The world was safer. Porthumming was safe. Gabe could finally move on.
But the vibrant colors of the world seemed muted now, as if a great light had been permanently extinguished. And somewhere, Roland was smiling.
The End The Mercy That Burned the World
The world snapped back into focus—the scent of pine, the chill of the night air. Behind them, the sounds of the Northern army mobilizing grew louder.
What... have you DONE?!
You took the choice from me! I had it handled! I was ending it!
You were ending *her*! There was another way!
Another way? To be captured? To let them turn her into their weapon? That was never an option! You've doomed her!
Lyrel stepped forward, her own anger tempered with a desperate plea.
She's right, {player_name}. We've handed her over. But Eve—killing her wasn't the answer either. There had to be something else.
There still is! Eve, look at me. Not the Commander. Eve.
The woman who taught me how to fight, who patched my wounds, who sits with a cat on her lap when she thinks no one is watching.
Is that person really willing to believe there's no hope left?
For a moment, the iron mask of the Revenant leader faltered. Doubt flickered in her eyes.
A crackle echoed from Eve's comm bead, which she hadn't deactivated. Roland's voice came through, no longer amused, but cold with disappointment.
I must admit, Commander... I am disappointed. You let sentiment cloud your judgment. You let a child and an idealist stay your hand.
You have failed the final test. You are not the goddess I thought you were.
Roland. It's over. Your plan failed.
No. The objective merely changes. My faith was in your ability to make the necessary choice. Since you cannot, I will prove my philosophy is correct.
I have accessed the facility's core systems. If a hero cannot be allowed to rest in peace... then she will be erased in the fires of necessity.
A deep, subterranean rumble shook the ground beneath their feet. A faint red glow began to pulse from the direction of the hidden entrance.
He's overloading the mana reactor... He's going to blow the entire facility!
That bastard... He'd rather destroy her than let her live.
Eve's fury was no longer directed at {player_name}. It had a new target. The choice was gone—now, it was a rescue mission.
He thinks it's over. He's wrong. There's a maintenance conduit about two hundred yards north of here. An old waterway. It'll lead to the lower levels.
He wants to show me the logic of destruction? Fine. I'll show him the stubbornness of hope.
We're with you.
Let's go. We're running out of time.
They found the core chamber just as the overload alarms reached a fever pitch. Runic conduits glowed cherry-red, straining to contain the building energy.
Roland's projection stood impassively near the main console.
So, you came back for one final, futile gesture. How sentimental.
This isn't sentiment, Roland. It's a choice. You taught me to end things. But you forgot the first rule of the Revenants: know your target.
That's not a 'vessel' in there. That's my friend. And I'm choosing to have faith in her.
This was her redemption. A full rejection of the cold calculus he worshiped.
You've grown soft. Weak. This world has no place for faith. Only for clean endings. In three minutes, you'll see I was right.
We can't stop it! The sequence is locked!
But... look! The energy regulators... they're shunting all the excess power towards the containment wing. It's designed to vent into the earth.
Vent... or be redirected?
An impossible, insane idea sparked between them.
Eve! If we can reroute the primary flow... we could channel the entire overload into the stasis pod!
It's a massive gamble! It could disintegrate her instantly, or...
...Or it could be the jolt needed to force a system restart. To wake her up. Do it.
Eve drew her daggers, placing herself between the console and the main entrance, ready to buy them the seconds they needed.
{player_name} and Lyrel worked in a frantic symphony of magic, their hands flying over the controls, weaving runes of redirection.
It's working, but the energy... it's too wild! It's pure destruction! Without a soul to anchor it, it'll tear her body apart!
Just as hope seemed lost, a small, furry shape darted past them.
Anne the cat sprang forward, landing gracefully atop the glass cylinder. A brilliant blue aura erupted from her small form, a beacon of pure spirit in the chaotic red glare of the chamber.
Anne...?
The raw, crimson torrent of energy from the reactor met the cat's serene blue light.
The blue aura enveloped the torrent, not stopping it, but calming it, guiding it—acting as a spiritual bridge between raw power and the sleeping soul within.
The light from the cat flickered and dimmed, its small body trembling under the immense strain. It was giving a piece of itself back, guiding the soul-fragment home.
The focused, now-stabilized energy surged into the pod. The alarms fell silent. For a beat, there was only a single, brilliant beam of white light.
The cylinder shattered. The facility began to tear itself apart. Through the chaos, a single, soft gasp.
They made it out just as the earth swallowed the last of the ruins, burying the North's secrets forever.
They found shelter in a hidden grove. Anne Lysandria was awake. She was frail, confused... but alive.
Eve...?
You look... so tired, my friend.
Tears welled in Eve's eyes, but for the first time, they weren't tears of grief. She reached out, taking Anne's hand.
Welcome back.
For a moment, Anne's kind eyes flickered, a flicker of something ancient and vast behind them. A soft, discordant whisper seemed to echo on the wind.
...so many... lost... where am I...
But the moment passed. Anne smiled weakly, and Eve smiled back—a genuine, heartfelt smile that reached her eyes. The soldier was gone, and the friend had returned.
A few weeks later...
They had found refuge in an old hunter's cabin deep in the unmarked territories. A fragile, quiet peace had settled over them.
Anne was growing stronger each day, and for the first time in a long time, the future felt less like a threat and more like a promise.
You know, Helmet Hair, we need to address something.
If it's about whose turn it is to fetch water, it's yours. Don't start, Tree-Hugger.
No, it's more serious. It's a branding issue. Your official title.
'The Goddess of Death'... it's officially retired. You hesitated. Goddesses of Death don't hesitate.
And what profound title have you come up with? 'Slightly-Less-Murderous Mercenary'?
I was thinking 'The Great Hesitator.' Has a nice ring to it. Or maybe 'Chief Cat-Herder,' in honor of our furry little deus ex machina.
{player_name} watched them, a genuine smile on his face. This was their new normal. Sharp-tongued, but without the venom. Anne watched from the doorway, a faint, amused smile on her own lips.
Keep talking and you'll be 'First-Rate Archery Target.'
Just call me Eve. It's enough.
It was the closest she'd ever come to admitting she was happy.
Lyrel watched Eve pour a cup of tea, a knowing, mischievous smile on her face.
You know, for someone who claims to need so much sleep, you and {player_name} have been keeping some very late watches these past few nights.
We're being thorough. This area isn't secure.
Oh, I'm sure you're being very... thorough.
It's just that the birds have been complaining. Apparently, all your late-night 'strategizing' is keeping them awake.
The birds told you that, did they?
They're terrible gossips. But they did mention that our resident 'Goddess of Death' looks significantly less murderous in the mornings now.
Eve didn't have a sharp comeback. She just hid a small smile behind her teacup, a faint blush on her cheeks. It was a new, lighter kind of normal.
And in that quiet moment of contentment, the knock came. Not a soldier's battering, but a polite, firm rap on the door.
Anne Lysandria. My name is General Kaelan of the Northern Command. I come in peace.
You have one minute to explain how you found us before I send you back in pieces.
There is a sub-dermal magical tracer placed in all high-value assets. We always knew where she was. We simply chose this moment to approach.
We are not here to take her. We are here to ask for her help.
He spoke of border skirmishes, of the Southern Alliance testing their defenses, of a nation losing hope without its symbol. It was a masterful, manipulative performance.
Why should I trust you? The North... it used me.
The old regime has been purged. Those responsible for 'Project Lazarus' have been held accountable. We are building a new North, one that needs its true hero to guide it.
...our duty... save them... it is not over...
I... I have to.
No. Anne, don't. It's a cage dressed as a throne. You don't owe them anything.
I owe it to them. The ones who died. The ones I hear every night.
This is my choice. Please... let me make it.
Slowly, painfully, Eve let go of Anne's arm.
This is a mistake.
I know. But it's mine to make.
Anne Lysandria, the Hero of the North, walked out of the cabin and stood beside the General, turning away from her friends.
They watched until she was gone.
Eve hadn't saved her from her fate. She had saved her for it.
Her redemption was real, but it had come at the cost of losing her friend all over again.
So what now?
She made her choice.
Now we get stronger. And we wait for the day she needs us to help her make a different one.
Later that night, long after Anne and Lyrel had fallen into an exhausted sleep, {player_name} found Eve by the embers of the fire.
She was keeping watch, as always, but her posture was different. The rigid tension of the soldier was gone. She looked... calm.
You should get some rest.
I don't think I could sleep if I tried. It's been a long time since a mission ended... like this.
She meant 'ended with hope'.
{player_name} sat down beside her, the warmth of the fire between them.
{player_name}.
Thank you.
We all did our part. Lyrel, the cat...
No. Not for that.
She turned to look at him, her eyes clear of the shadows he was so used to seeing.
Thank you... for stopping me. Back there in the lab.
I was ready to burn it all down again. To finish the job. To become that person again.
It was the most vulnerable he had ever seen her.
Your stupid, stubborn hope... you held onto it, even when I told you to let go. You pulled me back.
I never saw a monster, Eve. I just saw my friend, who was hurting.
A long silence stretched between them, filled only by the crackling fire. She looked down at her hands, then back up at him. Her gaze was soft, questioning.
Slowly, she began to lean in.

options.text: Meet her halfway.
Gently pull back. Keep it as friendship.

steps.text: It wasn't a passionate kiss, but one of profound relief and quiet acknowledgment. A promise.
She pulled back, a faint blush on her cheeks, looking more like the woman she might have been than the soldier she had become.
So... what now?
Now... we rest. And tomorrow, we figure it out.
Together.
Eve nodded, a real, true smile finally reaching her eyes. She leaned her head against his shoulder, closing her eyes, finally allowing herself a moment of peace.
In the heart of a broken world, they had found something whole.
He saw the question in her eyes. With a gentle smile, he placed a hand on her shoulder, stopping her advance. It wasn't a rejection, but a clarification.
You're my family, Eve. You, Lyrel, Anne... you're everything. Let's not make it complicated.
There was a flicker of something in her eyes—surprise, maybe a hint of disappointment—but it was replaced by a look of deep, profound gratitude and understanding.
She gave him a small, genuine nod.
Family... Yeah. I like the sound of that.
Thanks, {player_name}. For everything.
She didn't lean on his shoulder, but she did sit closer to the fire, the comfortable silence between them a testament to a different kind of unbreakable bond.
In the heart of a broken world, they had solidified their found family.
The air grew still the moment they passed the ancient stone markers. The vibrant greens of the outer woods gave way to a palette of ash, grey, and withered brown.
This was the Eldertide Forest, though Lyrel refused to call it that.
Welcome to the Heartwood Sanctuary.
Sanctuary for what? Ghosts?
For memory. And for what's still to come.
Lyrel moved with a light step that seemed to defy the oppressive silence. She ran her fingers along the trunk of a skeletal, leafless birch.
She's just sleeping. Her roots are still strong. Aren't they, old friend?
Cyan watched her, a mix of admiration and concern. Her optimism was a lone candle in a vast, dark room.

Eve, however, remained silent, her gaze sweeping over the dead landscape with the grim appraisal of a war veteran surveying a battlefield. She wasn't mocking Lyrel. She was mourning with her, in her own quiet way.
Look! Do you see? Right there.
She pointed to a patch of moss clinging to the base of a petrified oak. It was a sickly, pale green, but it was alive.
Life still lingers here. You just have to know how to listen for it.
She began to hum, a soft, melodic tune that felt ancient and sorrowful. The hollow wind seemed to whistle along, carrying the tune through the dead branches.
Her faith was absolute, but the silence of the forest was a heavy counter-argument.

options.text: You really believe it can be saved.
This place feels... hopeless.
Let's just focus on the mission.

steps.text: You see life everywhere, don't you?
Because it *is* everywhere. It's just quiet. Wounded. It needs someone to remind it how to sing again.
Her smile was genuine, a brief glimpse of the 'songbird' she used to be. She seemed grateful for the shared belief.
I don't know, Lyrel. This place... it feels like it's already gone.
Then we will have to be its hope. It is never too late, so long as the roots hold.
Her optimism returned, but it felt more like a shield she had just raised. A wall against his doubt.
We should keep moving. The light won't last forever in here.
Of course. You're right.
She nodded, her smile tightening slightly. She was here on a mission, but her heart was clearly on another.
They walked deeper, the silence broken only by the crunch of dead leaves under their boots and Lyrel's soft, persistent humming.
Let her have this.
What do you mean?
The hope. Let her have it for as long as she can. The fall is shorter that way.
Eve's words were a cold premonition. She knew what lay at the heart of a place like this.
Up ahead, Lyrel stopped. Her humming had ceased. The air had grown colder, and the scent of decay was stronger here.
We're here. The Worldroot.
Through the withered trees, Cyan could see a clearing, and in its center, the colossal, blackened form of a tree that looked like a giant's skeleton clawing at the sky.
The Worldroot was a monument to death. Taller than any spire in the capital, its branches were twisted, blackened claws. A great, gaping hollow in its trunk looked like a screaming mouth.
This was once the most sacred place in the Heartwood Sanctuary.
The heart of the forest. If I can heal the heart, the lifeblood will flow again.
That's not a wound, Lyrel. It's a corpse.
No. She's still breathing. I can feel it.
Lyrel stepped forward, her expression shifting from reverence to intense concentration. She placed both palms flat against the charred bark of the colossal tree.
She closed her eyes and began to chant in the ancient Elven tongue. The words were a soft, flowing melody, a stark contrast to the corrupted silence.
A gentle, golden-green light began to emanate from her hands, seeping into the dead wood. The air grew warm, and the scent of fresh spring leaves momentarily overpowered the smell of decay.
It's... it's working.
For a moment, it seemed like a miracle was unfolding. Faint veins of green light traced their way up the blackened trunk, like rivers of life returning to a barren land.
Lyrel's chant grew stronger, her brow furrowed with effort. Sweat beaded on her forehead.
Then, the forest pushed back.
A low, guttural groan echoed from deep within the hollow of the tree. The faint green veins of light flickered, then turned a sickly, violent purple.
The corruption wasn't just a passive decay. It was a hostile, living entity. And it was fighting her.
No... I can... I can push it back...
Lyrel, stop! Let go!
With a sound like splintering bone, a crack shot up the trunk of the Worldroot. From the new wound, a thick, blood-red sap began to ooze, steaming as it hit the ground.
The purple energy lashed out from the tree, snaking back along the stream of Lyrel's magic. It struck her arm with a sickening hiss.
Agh—!

She was thrown back, collapsing to the ground and clutching her arm. Where the energy had touched her, a pattern of blackened, spiderweb-thin veins now marred her skin—a miniature echo of the blighted tree.
Eve was at her side in an instant, grabbing her shoulders.
I told you to stop. Are you trying to get yourself killed?
Lyrel, your arm!
Lyrel stared at the new scar, then back at the weeping, bleeding tree. Her breath hitched. The crack in her hope was now as visible as the crack in the wood.
It... it fought back. I felt it... It's in so much pain...
But even now, faced with this violent rejection, her denial held.
It's just... more wounded than I thought. It can still heal. I just need to be stronger.
Cyan looked from the bleeding tree to the scar on Lyrel's arm. He knew, with a sinking certainty, that she was wrong.
The Worldroot couldn't be healed. It could only be mourned.
They made camp in a small, sheltered clearing. The fire pushed back the oppressive darkness, but not the silence.
Lyrel was tending to her bow, her movements a little too precise, her smile a little too bright. She refused to let anyone look at the blighted scar on her arm.
Eve watched her from across the fire, her face an unreadable mask of stone.
The wood here is too damp to burn well. It's lost its spirit. We'll need to gather more before—
Stop.
Stop what?
Stop pretending. Stop acting like a fresh bandage and a cheerful tune is going to fix that tree, or your arm, or any of this.
The air grew thick with tension. Cyan shifted, ready to intervene, but Eve's eyes were locked on Lyrel.
You think clinging to fairy tales is going to change what happened here?
Something in Lyrel finally snapped. The gentle, smiling mask didn't just crack; it shattered.
Fairy tales?
My belief that life is worth fighting for is a FAIRY TALE to you?
It is when the fight is already over. This forest is a graveyard, Lyrel. All you're doing is digging up the corpses and hurting yourself.
At least I'm TRYING! What are you doing, Eve? Besides walking through this sacred place with the same dead eyes you show everywhere else?
You've already given up! You look at this tragedy and all you see is an ending. I look at it and I see a reason to fight!
I have seen what 'fighting for a lost cause' does. It gets people killed. It turns heroes into martyrs and leaves nothing behind but stories that get children killed in the next war.
And what's the alternative?! To feel nothing? To burn everything you love so you don't have to watch it die?! That's not strength, Eve, that's cowardice!
The words hit Eve like a physical blow. Her face went pale. The campfire crackled, indifferent to the war of words.
That's enough! Both of you.
Cyan stood up, placing himself between them. The firelight cast long, dancing shadows, making them all look like ghosts.
This isn't helping. We're all tired. We're all on edge.
Lyrel stared at Eve, her chest heaving. The anger drained away, leaving only a raw, exposed grief. She turned away abruptly, wrapping her arms around herself.
I... I need some air.
She walked away from the firelight, disappearing into the shadows of the dead trees.
Eve didn't move. She just stared into the flames, her knuckles white where she gripped her knees.
The argument was over, but the wounds it had opened were still bleeding.
Dawn broke, but the light that filtered through the dead canopy was thin and grey. A fragile truce had settled over the camp, the kind born from exhaustion, not resolution.
The chasm from the night before remained. Eve was distant, Cyan was pensive, and Lyrel... Lyrel was smiling again.
It was a carefully constructed thing, that smile. A mask painted with the colors of hope, but it didn't quite reach her eyes.
Are you... ready to go?
Of course! The sooner we leave this sadness behind, the better.
The irony in her words hung heavy in the air. She was the one carrying the most sadness, a secret Cyan now shared.
Good. The air here is poison.
They packed in silence and began the final walk out of the Heartwood.
They reached the edge of the Blight, where the dead grey trunks gave way to the vibrant, living green of the outside world. It was like stepping from one world into another.
Lyrel stopped at the threshold, turning to look back one last time at the blighted sanctuary.
I'll be back for you. I promise.
As she spoke, a breeze, gentler than any they'd felt inside, rustled the high branches of a petrified oak.
A single, impossible leaf detached from a dead branch. It was a perfect emerald green, glowing with a soft, internal light.
It didn't fall. It drifted, spiraling down on the air currents as if guided, landing softly in Lyrel's outstretched palm.
The glow pulsed once, warm and alive against her skin, before fading, leaving just an ordinary, healthy leaf.
Tears welled in Lyrel's eyes, but this time, they weren't from grief.
You see?... It's not over.
The forest... it still breathes.
Eve watched the scene, her expression unreadable. She spoke quietly, her words meant only for Cyan.
It's not breathing. It's just taking a long time to die.
Two different worldviews, staring at the same miracle, seeing two different truths.
Lyrel clutched the leaf to her chest as if it were the most precious treasure in the world. She was smiling again, the songbird who refused to believe the song was over.
But Cyan, having seen her break, now knew the truth.
That smile was no longer just a beacon of hope. It was a shield.
And behind it, she was screaming along with the forest.
An hour passed. The unspoken argument hung in the air, heavy as a shroud. Eve hadn't moved, her silhouette a statue carved from stubborn silence.
But Lyrel hadn't returned. A cold knot of worry tightened in Cyan's gut.
I'm going to find her.
She doesn't want to be found.
Maybe. But she shouldn't be alone out here.
He left the relative safety of the firelight, pushing into the oppressive dark of the woods. The wind was picking up, and it seemed to carry faint sounds on its breath.
He followed the barely visible tracks, deeper into the forest's dead heart. It was then that he heard them, too.
Faint whispers, tangled in the rustle of dead leaves. Not words, but the echoes of feeling—pain, loss, confusion.
They grew stronger, drawing him toward a small, forgotten clearing. He stopped at the edge, hidden by a thicket of thorns, and saw her.

Lyrel stood before a colossal, ancient willow. Its branches drooped like a mourner's veil, and from dozens of them, a thick, opalescent sap leaked, glowing faintly in the moonlight. It looked, for all the world, like the tree was weeping.
She was transfixed, her head tilted as if listening to a conversation no one else could hear.
The whispers were clear here. Fragments of thought, the last vestiges of spirits fused to the wood.
...so cold... where is the sun... mother...
...the light... it tore us apart... help us...
Lyrel took a trembling step forward, her hand outstretched.
I hear you... I'm here...
And then, a single, clear voice, impossibly close, seemed to emanate from the bough directly in front of her. A voice that knew her.
Lyrel... why did you leave us?
That was the sound of her world breaking.
A choked sob tore from Lyrel's throat. Her knees gave way, and she slid down the trunk of the weeping willow, her hands flying to her mouth as if to hold back a scream.
The mask of serene hope didn't just crack; it shattered into a thousand pieces. This was not the gentle, optimistic elf from the party. This was a soul drowning in an ocean of grief.
I'm sorry... I'm so sorry...
I shouldn't have... I didn't know... Please, forgive me...
Her words were a desperate, fragmented prayer, a confession of guilt for a sin Cyan didn't understand.
Cyan stood frozen at the edge of the clearing, his heart aching. He finally understood.
Her hope wasn't denial. It was penance. Her smiles were an apology to the ghosts she heard every single day.
He started to step forward, to offer comfort, but stopped himself. This grief felt too sacred, too private. To intrude now would be a violation.
He took a slow, silent step back, leaving her to her sorrow.
As he retreated into the darkness, her broken sobs followed him, a secret he now carried, a burden he now shared.
They moved past the outer ruins into what felt like a different territory. The air grew heavy, watchful. The silence here wasn't empty; it was filled with presence.
Lyrel's steps, once light, were now hesitant. Her humming had long since stopped.
We're being watched. At least a dozen archers in the canopy.
Friends of yours, Lyrel?
They... were. A long time ago.
Before she could say more, the air hissed.
A volley of arrows rained down, embedding themselves in the ground around their feet. They weren't aimed to kill. They were a warning.
Leave this place, outsiders. The dead do not welcome visitors.
Eve's daggers were in her hands in a blur of motion, her body dropping into a low combat stance.
But before Eve could move, Lyrel stepped forward, her hand outstretched. A barrier of shimmering emerald light flared to life, shielding them.
Hold your arrows! I am Lyrel, daughter of the Heartwood! I have returned!

There was a moment of shocked silence from the trees. Then, figures began to drop to the ground, materializing from the shadows. Elves, clad in muted green and grey armor, their faces grim, their bows still half-drawn.
We know who you are.
The traitor speaks. After all these years, you dare to show your face here?
Captain Faelan... I am no traitor. I am here to heal the forest.
Heal it? The forest is dead! We performed the Rites of Severance. We cut ourselves off from its screams to survive! You dishonor our sacrifice by trying to wake the corpse!
His words dripped with a shared, painful history. Cyan began to understand. This wasn't anger; it was the lashing out of a deep, festering wound.
The Severance was a mistake! A choice born from fear! I stayed, I listened—
You stayed and wallowed in its agony! And now you bring *them*?
He gestured with his bow towards Cyan and Eve, his face contorting in disgust.
Humans. The very race whose arrogance and reckless magic murdered our home. You bring the arsonists to the gravesite and call it healing?
The accusation hung in the air, heavy and irrefutable. Lyrel's composure finally broke, tears welling in her eyes.
They are my friends. They are here to help. If you would only listen... the forest still lives! I can feel it!
All we feel is the scar where our heart used to be. A scar you keep trying to rip open.
Leave now, Lyrel. Take your pets and your misplaced hope, and never return. This is the only mercy our dead will grant you.
He gave a sharp signal, and without another word, the elven patrol melted back into the withered trees, leaving the party alone in the hostile silence.
The emerald barrier dissolved. Lyrel stood trembling, her head bowed. She was an exile in her own home.
They think I betrayed them.
Maybe... maybe they're right. I brought humans into Eldertide again.
You're trying to fix a mess they ran away from. If they're too blind to see that, it's their problem.
Easy for you to say. You weren't born with these roots... these memories. Every step here whispers what we lost because of...
She hesitated, her gaze falling on Cyan. She didn't say the words, but the meaning was clear: '...because of magic like yours.'

options.text: Let them whisper about me too.
It's not your fault.
Eve is right. Forget them.

steps.text: …Then let them whisper about me too.
What?
My Blink... it might look like the magic that scarred this forest. I know it does. And if they can’t see the difference, then let them blame me.
You’d carry that? For something you didn't do?
You're carrying this whole forest. For something you didn't do.
Silence descended, thick and heavy. The ancient trees seemed to lean in, listening. Lyrel studied Cyan's face, searching for a hint of mockery, but found only a maddening sincerity.
You are a very strange human, Cyan.
See? Told you he was weird.
The tension cracked. Lyrel's shoulders eased just a fraction. It wasn't a solution, but it was a shared burden. And for now, that was enough.
That's not fair, Lyrel. None of this is your fault.
Isn't it? I'm the one who keeps trying to open a wound they want to leave scarred over.
You're trying to heal it. There's a difference.
His words were meant to be comforting, but they felt like a dismissal of her pain. She gave him a tight, sad smile.
Thank you, Cyan. But it's not that simple.
She turned away, the distance between them feeling wider than before. The moment to connect had passed.
Eve has a point. If they're going to act like that, maybe they're not worth saving.
A flicker of hurt crossed Lyrel's face, so quick he almost missed it.
They are my people. And this is my home. They are always worth saving.
She spoke with a finality that shut down the conversation completely. Cyan realized he had just drawn a line between himself and her cause.
So this is the grand elven paradise you're always going on about? Looks a bit drafty.
It was a home, Eve. Not a fortress. Something I know you have trouble differentiating.
Fortresses have fewer holes in the roof. Just saying, Tree-Hugger.
And less soul. Come on, Helmet Hair. Even you must feel the memories here.
I feel a headache coming on, which is usually how your history lessons start.
Despite the sharp words, there was less heat in them than usual. It felt... practiced. Familiar.
Lyrel led them deeper into the heart of the old settlement.
They traveled deeper, the hostile tension of the guards giving way to a profound, echoing sadness. They had reached the heart of the old settlement.
White stone archways, elegant as swan necks, were cracked and stained. Silver birch trees stood like skeletal sentinels. This was not a ruin of war, but of heartbreak.
This was my home.
As she walked through the familiar paths, the very air seemed to sing to her, a faint, cracked melody from a forgotten time.
She approached a large, crescent-shaped wardstone, its surface covered in dormant, intricate runes. She hesitated, then gently placed her hand upon it.
Light. Laughter. A younger Lyrel, hair bright as spun moonlight, chasing other elven children through a vibrant, living sanctuary. The air hummed with joyous magic.
Then—a scream. A blinding, tearing light. The joyous hum twisted into a shriek of agony as the world turned white...
Lyrel snatched her hand back with a cry of pain. A wisp of black smoke rose from the stone, and her palm was red, as if burned. The wardstone now saw her as a foreign body.
You alright?
It doesn't remember me. I'm not who I used to be.
None of us are.
She is right, little songbird. The stone remembers who you were. It is you who has changed.

An old elf emerged from the shadow of a crumbling archway. He was ancient, his skin like bark, his eyes clouded with blindness. Black, corrupted veins, similar to the ones on the Worldroot, traced up his neck.
Elder Maerin.
So, the last believer returns. Chasing the song of a forest that no longer wishes to be sung.
He 'looked' towards Cyan and Eve, his blind eyes seeming to pierce right through them.
And you bring with you the echoes of the very storm that killed it.
We're here to help her.
Help? Child, this forest is not a wound to be mended. It is a ghost, and its pain is its final memory. To erase that pain would be to erase it completely. We chose to let it rest.
You chose to deny it! To give up! There is still time, Elder!
Time is all I have, little one. And I have watched this decay for decades. Your hope is a beautiful, cruel thing. Do not ask us to share in it.
He reached out a withered hand, placing it gently on her shoulder.

I will not stop you. Your heart is pure, and you have earned the right to find your own peace... or your own sorrow. But the other elves will not welcome you. Your presence reminds them of a choice they were forced to make.
His permission felt like a final farewell.
You still believe, don't you? Deep down?
Belief and denial wear the same mask when you're old enough, girl. Go now. Find your answer, and then leave us to our quiet end.
The elder turned and shuffled back into the shadows, leaving them alone in the heart of the ruins.
Lyrel stood silently for a long moment. She had been rejected by her past and dismissed by her future. All she had left was her own stubborn, breaking hope.
That night, as the others tried to rest, Lyrel stood looking up at the canopy, where the faint, sickly light of the corrupted magic pulsed.
The whispers returned, faint, pleading, calling her name.
From the shadows, Eve watched her. She saw the haunted, desperate look in Lyrel's eyes—the look of someone chasing ghosts.
It was a look she knew intimately. She had worn it herself for years.
When Lyrel finally turned, Eve closed her eyes, pretending to be asleep. She understood now. Lyrel wasn't a fool.
She was a survivor, just like her, walking the same path of grief—just starting from the opposite end.
The deeper they went, the stranger the forest became. The trees no longer grew—they *reached*, their branches leaning inward as if eavesdropping.
Massive, coiled roots breached the soil like the veins of a buried titan. The air itself buzzed faintly—wrong, alive, and filled with a terrible memory.
Anne the cat, perched on Cyan's shoulder, tried to blink forward. A faint spark of blue energy sputtered and died, absorbed by the heavy, unyielding air.
Anne? What's wrong?
Cyan raised his own hand, tracing a simple rune circle midair. The lines of mana fizzled into nothing before the shape could form.
My magic... it's being suppressed. Rejected.
It’s not you. The forest remembers what magic did here. It's defending itself.

Her voice trembled, not with fear, but with a strange reverence. Eve remained silent, her eyes constantly moving, her hand hovering near the hilt of her dagger—not from paranoia, but from the muscle memory of a place she never wanted to see again.

They arrived at a place where the corruption was thickest. The trees were unnaturally dense, their trunks twisted into shapes that resembled screaming faces. The ground pulsed with a faint, sickly warmth, like a feverish heartbeat.
It’s too quiet.
No birds... no insects. It's holding its breath.
Something's wrong. I'm going to try Rivirä. See what's under the surface.
Cyan focused, pushing past the oppressive aura. The world dissolved into the blue-grey ether of the life-seeing spell.
But what he saw was not the clean, distinct lights of living things. It was a chaotic, bleeding mess.
Thousands of fractured, tormented life signatures were smeared across the landscape, overlapping and tangled together. They were screaming in silence.
Gods... the life signals... they're everywhere. Fused together. Human, and... and something else. Plant? Earth?
Lyrel looked at Cyan, her expression one of profound sadness. This was not a story she had been told. It was a truth she had spent years piecing together.
It’s not an echo of the battle, Cyan. It’s the battle itself, still being fought.
What... what happened here? How do you know?
Lyrel took a deep breath, her voice taking on the hard-earned certainty of an investigator finally presenting her findings.
For years, I searched for answers. Why the Heartwood died so suddenly. The North's official story was a magical accident, a miscalculation. It was a lie.
I joined their guilds, climbed their ranks, all to get access to their archives. A redacted report here, a censored letter there... I found the truth.
As she spoke, Cyan watched Eve, who had turned away, her knuckles white where she gripped her dagger.
The Northern Kingdom wasn't losing the war, but they wanted a swift, decisive victory. They looked at a map and saw this forest not as a sacred sanctuary, but as a strategic asset.

Their plan was to teleport a thousand elite soldiers here, right behind the Southern Alliance's main front. They would establish a forward base, cut off supply lines, and perform a pincer attack. It would have ended the war in a month.
Eve flinched, a barely perceptible tremor. She knew the mission parameters.
But the forest's life magic was too strong, too wild. When the human mages forced the ritual, it shattered. The teleportation collapsed in on itself.

Of the thousand soldiers, seven hundred were fused instantly with the forest. Their bodies, their souls, their armor—all woven into the trees and soil. They became a part of the agony they had created.
The image from Rivirä slammed back into Cyan's mind—the screaming, tangled signals. That's what he had seen.

The survivors... the other three hundred... were warped. Twisted things, begging for death. The kingdom couldn't let the story of their strategic failure get out. It would have been a catastrophic blow to morale.
So they sent another unit. A covert team, their existence denied, tasked with 'sanitizing' the mission.
Cyan's eyes darted to Eve. Her shoulders were rigid, her face a mask of stone.

They were called the Revenant Division. Their orders were to contain the horror. They burned the screaming trees and killed anything that still moved. They buried the evidence under fire and steel, ensuring the official story remained 'a tragic accident'.
Lyrel fell silent. The truth was laid bare, a corpse in the center of the clearing.
They moved from the mass grave into a wide, unnatural clearing. This was not a natural feature of the forest. It was a scar.
The ground was bare in patches, oddly scorched and vitrified in others. The air was dead, and the silence was absolute—a pressurized void.
This is it. The place where the ritual was meant to happen. The epicenter.
They missed their mark by a few hundred meters. If they had landed here... perhaps it would have been a cleaner death.
Cyan felt a cold dread looking at the barren soil. But Eve... Eve was staring at a grotesquely warped oak tree at the edge of the clearing.
Half-swallowed by the gnarled, metallic-looking roots of the oak was the hilt of a blade. It was dull, weathered, but unmistakably military. Human-made. Northern steel.
A sword... one of the soldiers must have...
He trailed off. Eve had frozen, her face completely drained of color. Her eyes were locked on the hilt, a flicker of horrifying recognition in them.
Eve? You know that blade.
She didn't answer. She moved as if in a trance, stepping forward, her boots making no sound on the corrupted soil. She knelt, her hand reaching for the hilt.
Eve, don't! You don't know what touching it will—
But it was too late. Her fingers closed around the familiar grip of a standard-issue Revenant Division short sword.
The moment she pulled it free, the world broke.
A soundless, psychic scream ripped through the clearing. It wasn't a noise; it was a memory, a feeling—the collective agony of a thousand souls dying at once, forced into their minds.
Cyan's runes flared and died. Anne the cat collapsed. Lyrel dropped to her knees, gasping as waves of raw, undiluted anguish crashed through her.
Eve stood alone in the center of the psychic storm, the blade trembling in her hand. The forest was awake now. And it was screaming.
Ethereal lights flickered in the mist—the spectral forms of the elven dead. They did not speak. They only watched, their sorrow and anger a palpable force.
It's... it's remembering... The forest *knows* that blade... it knows *you*!
WHAT DID YOU DO?!
The large Elder spirit at the center of the phantoms did not open its mouth. Instead, it fixed its burning green eyes directly on Lyrel.
Lyrel gasped, her hands flying to her temples. Cyan could see no attack, but she flinched as if struck. It was a current of silent information, a memory being poured directly into her.
That blade... that insignia... We see the ghost of it on her armor...
She is one of the butchers. The commander of the Revenant Division.
She gave the order to burn the living and bury the dead. She is the one who silenced us.
Lyrel's eyes snapped open, wide with a horror that eclipsed everything else. The knowledge, branded onto her soul, was now hers to bear. She turned her gaze to Eve.
The blade... your armor... It was you.
They're saying... you were one of them. The... the Revenant Division.
The name, spoken by her, was a physical blow. The final, terrible piece of the puzzle slotted into place.
She took a stumbling step back, her face a canvas of disbelief and the deepest betrayal imaginable.
Eve... tell me it isn't true.
Eve finally looked at her, her face carved with a guilt so profound it was almost a physical presence. Her voice was flat, hollow—the sound of a confession she had made to herself a thousand times.
…It was war.
It was a MASSACRE! It was MURDER!
The wind howled, the spectral elves surged forward, and the ground itself seemed to tremble, responding to the verdict now delivered through their chosen proxy.
Cyan tried to intervene—'Lyrel, Eve, stop!'—but his voice was swallowed by the storm.
The hope of a healer and the guilt of a killer had finally collided. And the forest was ready to use its new weapon.
Eve... tell me it isn't true.

Eve finally looked at her, her face carved with a guilt so profound it was almost a physical presence. Her voice was flat, hollow—the sound of a confession she had made to herself a thousand times in the dead of night.
…It was war.
It was a MASSACRE! It was MURDER!
The wind howled, the spectral elves surged forward, and the ground itself seemed to tremble with the forest's rage.
Cyan tried to intervene—'Lyrel, Eve, stop!'—but his voice was swallowed by the storm.
The hope of a healer and the guilt of a killer had finally collided. And the forest was ready to be the executioner.
The forest was a living courtroom, and a verdict had been reached. The spectral elves flickered in the mist, their whispers a chorus of accusation.
You were there. All this time... the stories I told you... the pain... you knew. You knew and you said nothing.
What was there to say? That I'm sorry? Words don't unbury the dead.
You didn't bury them! You murdered them! You silenced them!
They were already screaming. Torn apart. My orders were to stop the contamination. To end the suffering.
Lyrel's breath hitched. The betrayal, the lies, the sheer scale of the horror—it was too much. The carefully built walls around her heart crumbled into dust.
And in that moment of absolute despair, the forest reached out.

A wave of emerald light pulsed from the ground, surging up into Lyrel. Her eyes began to glow with the same green fire as the Elder spirit's. The whispers of the forest coalesced, speaking through her.
LIAR.
You did not end suffering. You ended hope. You are the blight. The walking wound. And the forest demands a cleansing.
This was no longer just Lyrel. It was the collective rage of a thousand murdered souls, using her as their sword.
She raised her hands, and the ground itself erupted. Massive, thorned vines, thick as pythons, surged from the soil, surging directly towards Eve.
Eve! Move! Fight back!
But Eve didn't move. She didn't even raise the blade to defend herself. She stood her ground, watching the attack come, her face a mask of weary acceptance.
No.

The vines slammed into her, pinning her arms and legs, lifting her slightly off the ground. Thorns bit deep into her armor, and crimson blood began to seep through the cracks, dripping onto the forest floor.
Eve didn't scream. She just grunted in pain, her head slumping forward.
Then, with a metallic clang, she let the Revenant blade fall from her hand.
The forest, speaking through Lyrel, pulsed with triumph and rage.
Why do you not fight back, butcher? Where is the cold killer who silenced our children?
Eve lifted her head, her voice strained, but clear. Broken.
She died here. A long time ago.
If this is what I've earned... then let it be done. Let the forest take its price.
Her surrender was absolute. It was not a tactic. It was a confession.
The raw, honest guilt in her voice seemed to momentarily disrupt the forest's rage. The glowing in Lyrel's eyes flickered. A sliver of her own consciousness broke through the storm.
Why...? Why won't you fight me?
Because I already lost this war. You're just the one who's still bleeding from it.
The truth in those words, the shared pain, was more powerful than any attack. The fury in Lyrel's eyes wavered, replaced by a wave of confusion and her own overwhelming grief.
The vines holding Eve slackened slightly. The battle was no longer between a healer and a killer. It was between two survivors, drowning in the same sea of ghosts.
The forest held its breath. Eve hung limply in the grip of the thorned vines, her blood dripping onto the thirsty roots below. Her surrender had thrown the forest's rage into momentary confusion.
The burning green light in Lyrel's eyes flickered. For a heartbeat, Cyan saw the real Lyrel surface—a look of horrified confusion, her lips forming a silent 'No...'
But the forest's collective agony was too strong. It crushed her fleeting resistance, and the cold, vengeful light returned, brighter than before.
A confession is not an atonement. Guilt does not regrow what was burned.
Your debt must be paid. In blood. And in spirit.
The vines tightened their grip, and a sharp grunt of pain was forced from Eve's lips. This was not a quick death. It was a sentence.
The spectral elves surrounding them began to dissolve, their forms unraveling into streams of emerald and white light. They flowed from all directions towards Lyrel.

The light coalesced in her outstretched hands, weaving and hardening. Ancient wood, silver as moonlight and hard as stone, grew from the energy. A spectral bowstring, humming with contained power, strung itself taut.
The forest had forged its will into a weapon. An executioner's longbow.
Lyrel—or the entity wearing her face—raised the bow. Her movements were fluid, graceful, and utterly without emotion.
She drew the spectral string back. An arrow of pure, searing green energy materialized, its point aimed directly at Eve's heart. The air grew still. The howling wind died. The whispers ceased.
There was only the soft, terrible hum of the arrow, waiting to be loosed.
(I have to do something... NOW! But what? What can I possibly do?!)
Cyan stood frozen, caught between a friend ready to kill and a friend ready to die.
The forest had made its judgment. And its executioner was waiting.
The arrow of pure energy hummed, a note of finality in the raging silence. This was the last moment. The last chance.
Cyan's mind raced, his heart pounding a frantic rhythm against his ribs. He had to act. Now.

steps.text: Logic took over. The threat was the bow. The target was Lyrel. The answer was speed and precision.
His body moved before his heart could object.
Cyan Blinked—appearing in an instant behind Lyrel, hand already shaped into a knife-edge strike, aimed for the nerve cluster at the back of her neck.
Not to kill. Just to incapacitate. A clean, non-lethal solution.
But the forest doesn't read intent. It only feels the threat.
A violent burst of raw mana detonated from Lyrel's back, slamming into Cyan and throwing him against the writhing roots.
—CYAN!!
Eve's own guilt forgotten in a surge of protective instinct, she roared, tearing one arm free from the vines. She rushed forward—faster than her wounds should have allowed.
The forest, sensing Cyan was the immediate threat, changed its target. A dozen spear-tipped roots erupted from the ground, shooting directly towards him.
Eve shoved Cyan aside with her free hand—
—and the roots impaled her instead.
For a moment, everything stilled. The howling wind, the whispering spirits, the beating of Cyan's heart. All of it stopped.
Eve hung there, held aloft by the forest's thorns, her head bowed.
Lyrel...
The first time she ever said her name. It came out like a prayer.
Lyrel's glowing eyes widened. The green light faltered—human for a single, horrified heartbeat—as she saw what she had done.
This... isn't your fault. None of it is.
Heh... guess karma... never forgets, huh...
She coughed, blood trickling from her lips. Her eyes found Cyan's.
Cyan... I'm sorry.
Failed... to protect... my student...
Her hand, which had been reaching for him, fell limp. The light in her eyes went out.
Cyan stared, breath caught somewhere between his lungs and his throat. His mind refused to process what he was seeing.
Eve's blood soaked into the roots, and the forest drank it in. Veins of crimson spread through the green, spectral light of the spirits.
He didn't scream. He didn't move. His body refused to listen, as if the world itself had stopped turning.
The last flicker of the real Lyrel was gone. The eyes that looked at him now were ancient, cold, and utterly without mercy. The voice that spoke was a legion.
Humans. Destroy. All they touch.
Roots erupted around Cyan's feet. He didn't flinch. He didn't even notice.
Something warm slid down his cheek. He wasn't sure if it was his own blood, or just tears.
And then—
—the forest claimed him, too.
When dawn broke, there was no sound of birds. No wind in the leaves.
Only Eve's fallen dagger and Cyan's tracking pendant—tangled together in the unmoving roots, half-buried in the soil.
BAD END The Unforgiven Touch
Logic screamed 'attack.' Survival screamed 'run.' But his heart... his heart chose a different path.
He didn't draw his sword. He didn't raise a hand to cast a rune. He just looked at the friend trapped inside the storm.
He Blinked. Not behind her, not to the side, but directly in front of her—inside the lethal range of the bow, completely defenseless.
The forest, speaking through Lyrel, recoiled in confusion. This was not the response of a threat. It was the response of a sacrifice.
An aura of crushing force began to gather around him, but Cyan pushed through it, taking one slow, deliberate step forward. And then another.
It's okay. I'm not going to fight you.
I know you're in pain. All of you. Let me share the burden.
Before the forest's rage could form a coherent attack, he closed the final distance and wrapped his arms around her.
The world went silent. The howling wind, the spectral lights, the humming arrow—everything vanished.
There was only the feeling of his arms around her, a shield of pure, unconditional empathy against a storm of ancient pain.
This was a language the forest's rage did not understand. It was not violence. It was not fear. It was... connection.
The burning green light in her eyes flickered violently, then shattered like glass, revealing her own tear-filled, golden-green eyes beneath.

The spectral bow in her hands dissolved into motes of light. The vines holding Eve crumbled into dust. The spectral elves faded back into the mist, their whispers softening from a roar of rage to a sigh of release.
Lyrel's strength gave out, and she collapsed into his arms, sobbing. The possession was broken.
That... should not have worked.
I just... I trusted her.
Lyrel looked up from his shoulder, her face stained with tears, but her eyes were clear for the first time since they'd entered the forest's heart.
And I had it coming. We're even, Tree-Hugger.
The use of the old nickname was a peace offering. A return to a fragile, but now much deeper, normalcy.
The forest was no longer screaming. It was quiet, filled with a deep, echoing sorrow, but the rage was gone. It had found its release not in vengeance, but in an act of profound compassion.
You saved yourself. I just held the door.
She gave him a weak, watery, but completely genuine smile. The songbird, bruised and battered, was ready to sing again.
The group spends the night in silence — broken, guilty, and lost.
Eve and Lyrel reluctantly help, drawing runes and maintaining barriers.
The ritual succeeds — the forest stops screaming.
Eve finally apologizes — not for orders followed, but for not fighting them.
Lyrel forgives her, not because she must, but because she can’t heal the forest while hating someone still alive.
Cyan stands between them, both proud and exhausted.
Cyan & Anne the cat take point this time. The clearing hums like a broken circuit — faces and limbs still half-merged into wood. Eve and Lyrel just watch; both hollow from last night’s confrontation.
He kneels, tracing a rune under one of the warped “faces.” When he activates it, the bark ripples — the fused flesh separates slightly, and the surrounding wood begins to regrow, green and clean.
They start mapping out sigils across the clearing — Anne use teleportation skills to move the cancer out, Cyan stabilizing the mana, Eve and Lyrel lending raw power.
They form a massive array. Eve carves runes with her blades; Lyrel channels nature magic through the roots.
Cyan shouts instructions — crisp, methodical, the commander they didn’t know he could be.
As the light builds, distorted soldier-spirits begin to surface again, screaming.
Lyrel almost falters, but Eve catches her arm.
She doesn’t look away, and that’s all Lyrel needs to hear. They push through together.
The teleport completes. The fused remains vanish — ripped clean from the forest.
Roots collapse, then rise again, sprouting green.
The ground exhales. Silence.
Afterward, the four rest near the crater. The air smells of rain and new life.
Lyrel sits apart, still shaking. Eve approaches, slow, uncertain.
Eve gives the faintest nod — the first real one between them. No tears, no melodrama. Just quiet, mutual exhaustion and understanding.
The elders arrive, expecting disaster — instead they find the forest whole.
Eve stands back while Lyrel speaks for the group.
The elders bow — reluctant but sincere.
Morning light filters through healthy branches.
Anne sleeps against Cyan’s shoulder, drained but smiling.
Eve sharpens her blade — routine, grounding herself.
Lyrel watches the forest breathe again.
The party walks out together — Eve in front, Lyrel behind her, quiet but no longer broken.
The forest’s whispers fade, replaced by wind.
Cyan and Anne collapse in exhaustion, but smiling — they did it.
Eve stands quietly, her armor faintly reflecting the golden light.
Lyrel looks around, trembling, tears streaking her face… then suddenly bursts into laughter.
She starts running in circles, touching trees, hugging them, even kissing the bark.
Anne rolls her eyes.
Cyan can’t stop laughing.
Then Lyrel suddenly throws herself at Eve and hugs her tight — like a child clinging to her mother.
Eve freezes up, completely stiff.
Cyan walks up, smiling faintly.
Lyrel nods, still clinging to Eve’s arm.
Eve sighs — but doesn’t pull away.
The tension’s gone. What remains is the start of something new.

Not to kill, just to stop her.
